title: Prologue and the divine makers

initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: The revision swapped Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" for "the Framer, the Shaper" — but "Framer" and "Shaper" is Allen Christenson's signature rendering of tzaqol b'itol, arguably the second-most-famous English pairing for this epithet. Likewise "twice midwife, twice patriarch" (camul yiom, camul mamom) matches Christenson's distinctive iyom=midwife / mamom=patriarch choice, diverging from Ximénez's own "abuela/abuelo" gloss in exactly the direction Christenson does. This is a patchwork fix: one famous translator's wording replaced by another's. Less concerning but noted: "Heart of Sky," "Heart of the Lake, Heart of the Sea" are shared across all translators and essentially forced by the K'iche' (uk'ux kaj, etc.); Tepeu/Gucumatz/Huracán spellings follow the manuscript orthography (as Recinos does) and are acceptable as transliterations. "He of the Green Plate, He of the Green Gourd" plausibly derives independently from Ximénez's "verde cagete / verde hícara." Recommend re-rendering tzaqol/b'itol (e.g. "the Builder, the Fashioner" or similar independent choice) and iyom/mamom away from Christenson's exact pair.
initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity: broadly sound; minor points only. (1) "twice patriarch" for mamom stretches the source (Ximénez: abuelo; mamom = grandfather) — a fidelity-neutral but Christenson-flavored choice. (2) "a sound of wrong ... a sound of right — this being noise" for mal/cotz is admittedly obscure and the rendering is honest but awkward; the translator note discloses this. (3) "Great White Peccary and Tzyz the Coati" splits zaquinimac tzyz into two beings; Ximénez glosses only "blanco pizote" (one coati) — the two-being reading is Tedlock/Christenson's analysis (Great White Peccary / Great White Coati), so the split itself leans on later scholarship, though the wording differs. None of these are sense errors against the Spanish/K'iche'; the disqualifying issue is the Christenson resemblance noted separately.

last_review.resemblance_note: The revision swapped Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" for "the Framer, the Shaper" — but "Framer" and "Shaper" for tzacol bitol is Allen Christenson's signature published rendering (his 2003 translation opens with "the Framer and the Shaper"). This is precisely the swap-one-translator-for-another pattern the audit forbids. Additional echoes: "Great White Peccary" for zaquinimac (Ximénez glosses "blanco pizote" = coati only; the peccary reading and this exact epithet are Tedlock/Christenson's), and "Heart of Sky" / "Heart of the Lake, Heart of the Sea" match Tedlock's and Christenson's shared choices where Recinos/Goetz-Morley have "Heart of Heaven." Deity-name spellings (Hun Ahpú Vuch, Hun Ahpú Utiú, Gucumatz, Xpiyacoc, Xmucané, Caculhá Huracán, Chipí-Caculhá, Raxá-Caculhá) follow Recinos/Goetz & Morley orthography, though that is defensible as transliteration of the manuscript.
last_review.issues: Memorization: "the Framer, the Shaper" is Christenson's distinctive published pairing for tzacol bitol — the fix for the Tedlock echo landed on another famous translator's wording; needs an independent rendering (e.g. "the one who forms, the one who fashions" or similar). "Great White Peccary" imports Tedlock/Christenson's peccary reading not supported by Ximénez's Spanish gloss (only "blanco pizote," coati). Minor fidelity notes: "zaquil al, zaquil qahol" rendered "clear children, clear sons" is acceptable; "a sound of wrong ... a sound of right — this being noise" is an awkward but honestly-noted rendering of an obscure passage; "twice midwife, twice patriarch" is a reasonable reading of camul yiom, camul mamom. Paragraph-by-paragraph the sense of the K'iche'/Spanish is carried; no wrong-section or omission problems found.

paragraphs: This is the root of the ancient word, here in this place called Quiche. Here we shall write, here we shall begin the ancient word, the root and the start of everything that was done in the citadel of Quiche, in the nation of the Quiche people. And here we shall bring out its being shown, its being made plain, its being told — the hiding, the making clear — by the one who builds, the one who gives shape, Mother and Father, whose names are Hun Ahpu Vuch, Hun Ahpu Vtiu, Great White Coati, Tepeu, Gucumatz, the Heart of the Lake, the Heart of the Sea, He of the Green Plate, He of the Green Gourd, so they are called; and named along with them, spoken of along with them, the grandmother and the grandfather, whose names are Xpiyacoc and Xmucane, protector and shelterer, twice a midwife, twice a grandfather, as they are named in the Quiche word — when they told, when they gave account of all that they did together, within the clarity that had already come to be, within the words that had already come to be told.

This we shall write now within the word of God, within Christianity; we bring it out because there is no longer a place to see it, the ancient book, the original writing whose sight is hidden from the one who looks at it, from the one who ponders it. Great is its telling and its account of when the sky and the earth were finished being formed, squared, divided into four parts, measured out, when the cord was stretched across the sky and across the earth, its four corners, its four sides, as it is told — by the one who builds, the one who gives shape, mother and father of life and of what was made, who gives breath, who gives thought, who watches over the good walk of the people, of humankind, born into clarity, begotten into clarity, one who worries over, one who knows all that lies within the sky, the earth, the lake, the sea.

This, then, is the account of when all lay in suspense, all calm, in silence, in the darkness, in the night; nothing yet gathered, nothing yet come together, everything at rest, nothing stirring, and the sky lay empty. This is the first word, the first speech. There was not yet one person, one animal, bird, fish, crab, tree, stone, hollow, canyon, meadow, forest. Only the sky existed. The face of the earth had not yet appeared. Only the sea lay penned in, alone, and all that was of the sky. Nothing whatever was joined together, nothing went 'mal,' nothing went 'cotz' — these being sounds — in the sky. Nothing stood upright; only the water lay penned in, only the sea, calm and alone within its bounds, for nothing else existed yet. Only stillness and silence in the darkness, in the night. Only the one who builds, the one who gives shape, Tepeu, Gucumatz, Mother, Father, lay in the water, surrounded by clarity, hidden under green and blue feathers — and so they are called Gucumatz. Great sages, great thinkers were they in their being; and so it was that the sky existed, and the Heart of the Sky existed too, for that is the name of this god, as it is told.

Then the word came here, to the one who builds and the one who gives shape, to Tepeu and Gucumatz, in the darkness, in the night; it came, and it spoke with Tepeu and Gucumatz. And they spoke, consulting together, thinking together; they matched their words, their thoughts. Then it grew clear, then together they searched, and found what must be made when the light was to come, while it was still night. It was the Heart of the Sky, called Huracan, that was its name — Caculha Huracan first, then Chipi Caculha, and third Raxa Caculha; these three together are the Heart of the Sky. They came together, then, with Tepeu and Gucumatz, and there the light and the life were thought upon: how the sowing would be done, how the dawn would be brought forth, who would provide, who would sustain.

"Let it be done: let the water withdraw and be emptied out, so that the earth may be formed, so that it may have solid ground, sowing and dawning for the sky and for the earth. But there will be no glory, no grandeur, in what we have made until the human form, the human shape, comes to being," they said, before the earth was created by them.

revised.translator_note: Round-4 revision responding to reviewer feedback that "the Framer, the Shaper" reproduced Christenson's signature rendering of tzaqol bitol and "Great White Peccary" (paired with "Tzyz the Coati") reproduced Tedlock's exact epithet for zaquinimac tzyz. Tzaqol bitol is now rendered plainly and non-idiomatically as "the one who builds, the one who gives shape" — a literal gloss of tzaq- (to build/construct) and bit- (to form/shape) that matches neither Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler," Recinos's "Creator, Maker," nor Christenson's "Framer, Shaper." Zaquinimac tzyz is treated as a single epithet ("Great White Coati," from Spanish "blanco pizote") rather than split into two paired animal-epithets in the Tedlock manner ("Great White Peccary, Great White Coati"); no peccary appears anywhere, since neither the K'iche' nor Ximenez's Spanish glosses a peccary here at all — that was an artifact of a prior draft's over-elaboration. Also corrected per the audit: "nothing went 'mal,' nothing went 'cotz' — these being sounds" now preserves Ximenez's own untranslated K'iche' onomatopoeia (his gloss "esto es ruido") instead of importing a false moral wrong/right contrast; and "twice a midwife, twice a grandfather" now tracks camul yiom, camul mamom without the odd midwife/patriarch mismatch. "Heart of the Lake, Heart of the Sea" and "Heart of Sky" are kept close to literal (vqux cho, vqux palo; vqux cah) since no non-echoing alternative renders the compound more faithfully; the definite article ("the Heart of...") is retained throughout to keep the phrasing plain rather than adopting the articleless liturgical cadence associated with Tedlock/Christenson.

title: The naming of the animals

initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity is generally good paragraph-by-paragraph, but with real problems. (1) Epithet misassignment: in paragraph 1 "cacha ri alom, qaholom" and in paragraph 2 "xuyao alom, qaholom" are rendered "said the Maker and the Modeler" / "which the Maker and Modeler had given" — but alom/qaholom means the Bearer/Begetter (she-who-bears, he-who-begets; Ximenez: "madres...Padres"), a different divine pair than tzacol/bitol. The translation collapses the two epithet pairs, and notably nowhere renders alom/qaholom by its actual sense as a title (only the inline "we are your mother, we are your father"). (2) "guardians of the cords" for "chahal caam" is doubtful — caam here is vines/creepers (Ximenez "mecates" = lianas/vines), and the translation itself renders caam as "vines" everywhere else in the same section; "cords" is an inconsistency. (3) Minor: "adore us" for quihila (greet/worship) leans on Ximenez's "saludadnos/alabadnos" loosely but acceptably; "that shall be great and marvelous" for "ah nim ah xob" is a paraphrase (more literally "one who honors, one who reveres" or Ximenez's "obedecedor") — questionable. MEMORIZATION: the revision is a patchwork of famous translators' signature choices rather than an independent rendering. "Framer" and "Shaper" for tzacol/bitol is Allen Christenson's distinctive pair, while "Maker, Modeler" (retained throughout, the very phrase flagged in round 1) is Dennis Tedlock's — the text now alternates both. "Grandmother of the Day, Grandmother of the Light" for ratit quih ratit zac closely matches Tedlock's "Grandmother of Day, Grandmother of Light" (Ximenez has "abuela de el dia, o sol, y de la luna" — grandmother of sun and moon — so the Day/Light pairing is a K'iche'-side reading that lands exactly on Tedlock's wording). "Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth" is shared across all translators and is the literal sense, so acceptable. Name spellings Chipi-Caculha/Raxa-Caculha and Hun Ahpu Vuch/Hun Ahpu Utiu follow Recinos/Goetz-Morley orthography but track the manuscript closely enough to be defensible. Recommend re-rendering tzacol/bitol and alom/qaholom with independent English (and correctly distinguishing the two pairs), and rewording the grandmother epithet.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Uses Christenson's "Framer/Shaper" and Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" side by side, and "Grandmother of the Day, Grandmother of the Light" matches Tedlock's distinctive epithet; exactly the one-famous-translator-swapped-for-another pattern the audit warns against.

last_review.issues: Fidelity mostly sound, but "that shall be great and marvelous" (for ah nim ah xob) is an invented gloss present in neither the K'iche' nor Ximenez ("obedezedor, sustentador"); the translation also overruns the titled section (p06-p07) into the mud-person episode (disclosed in translator note). Memorization is the serious problem: "Maker and the Modeler" (Tedlock's signature pair, the very phrase the round-1 revision was meant to eliminate) persists throughout, now stitched to Christenson's signature "Framer, Shaper" — a patchwork of two famous translators rather than an independent rendering. "Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth" matches Tedlock/Christenson; "Grandmother of the Day, Grandmother of the Light" is near-verbatim Tedlock; "Chipi-Caculha/Raxa-Caculha" and "Hun Ahpu Vuch/Hun Ahpu Utiu" follow Recinos/Goetz & Morley spellings; "the sowing and the dawn was drawing near" echoes Tedlock's sowing/dawning formula.
last_review.resemblance_note: Composite of Tedlock ("Maker, Modeler"; "Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth"; "Grandmother of Day/Light"; sowing-and-dawning formula), Christenson ("Framer, Shaper"), and Recinos/Goetz & Morley name spellings (Chipi-Caculha, Hun Ahpu Vuch/Utiu).

paragraphs: Then they thought again about the animals of the mountain, the guardians of all the wildlands: the creatures of the mountain — deer, birds, puma, jaguar, serpent, viper, cantil-snake, keepers of the vines. The Builder and the Sculptor said: "Will this stand only in silence, unmoving beneath the trees and vines? It is good that there be someone to keep them." So they said when they took counsel and spoke, and then deer and birds were brought into being. And then they gave the deer and the birds their homes. "You, deer, shall lie down in the beds of the rivers and in the ravines; here among the grasses and thickets you will multiply; on four feet you will go and stand," they were told, and so it was fixed for them. Then for the small birds and the great birds: "You, birds, on the trees and vines you will make your houses and your dwellings; there you will multiply, you will scatter yourselves among the branches of the trees and vines," the deer and the birds were told when their work was assigned to them. All of them took up their sleeping-places and their dwellings, which the earth gave them for houses, by the will of the Bearer, the Begetter. And when the making of all the deer and birds was finished, they were spoken to again by the Builder, the Sculptor, the Bearer, the Begetter: "Speak, cry out, do not merely chirp, do not merely screech — speak, each of you according to your kind, each according to your family," the deer and the birds were told — the pumas, the jaguars, the serpents. "Say our names, praise us, say that we are your mother, that we are your father. Huracan, Chipi Kaqulja, Raxa Kaqulja, Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth, Builder, Sculptor, Bearer, Begetter — speak us, invoke us, greet us," they were told. But they could not speak as people speak; they only squawked and cackled and screamed — the shapes of their speech did not come clear, but each cried out in a different way. And when the Builder and the Sculptor saw that they could not speak, they said to one another: "They have not been able to say our name, though we are their Builder and their Sculptor; this is not good," the Bearer, the Begetter said among themselves. And so they were told: "You will be changed, because you were not able to speak. We have changed our word: your food, your pasture, your sleeping-places and your dwellings will be the ravines and the wildlands, for you did not achieve the greeting due us, you did not invoke us. There will yet be those who keep our word, once we have made beings who obey us; for now, take up your task and your function, and let your flesh be given to be eaten" — thus it was told to the small and great animals that are upon the face of the earth.

So it was that they wished to try their fortune again, wished to make another attempt, wished to bring about a being who could praise and speak, but their speech was not understood among themselves; nothing was accomplished, nothing came about. And so their flesh was condemned: they were made to serve, to be worked, to be eaten — the animals that exist here upon the face of the earth. And so came the next trial of people, the trial of a being built, a being shaped, by the Builder, the Sculptor, the Bearer, the Begetter. "Let us try once more; the time to plant draws near, and the light is coming: let us make one who will support us and sustain us. How else are we to be invoked, to be remembered upon the face of the earth? We have already tried with our first works, our first figures, but it could not be made that they praise us and make us known. So let us try now to make an obedient being, a being who reveres us," they said, thinking it over. And then came the shaping of the flesh, out of the mud of the earth: it did not turn out well, for it crumbled, it was soft, it had no motion, no strength, it fell to pieces, it grew soggy, its head did not turn, its face looked only to one side, its sight was clouded, it could not look behind itself; though it spoke, it had no understanding — it merely dissolved in the water, it had no firmness. And the makers, the sculptors, said again: "It will only get worse from here on; it will not walk about, it will not multiply once it is fully made" — this they said only from their own thought. And so they took it apart again, and again they set to remolding their work, their handiwork, and they said: "How shall we make it, so that it may come to praise us and invoke us," they said when they took counsel once more. "Let us say it to Xpiyacoc, to Xmucane, to Hun Ahpu Wuch, to Hun Ahpu Utiw: let us try our fortune once more, its being formed" — so said the builders, the sculptors, to one another, and then they said it to Xpiyacoc and to Xmucane. Then it was said to those diviners, grandmother of day, grandmother of light — for so they were named by the Builder, the Sculptor — and these were the names, Xpiyacoc and Xmucane.

revised.translator_note: Round 4 revision. Replaced the mixed Tedlock/Christenson epithet stack ("Framer, Shaper, Maker, Modeler") with a single independent pairing derived straight from the root senses of tz'aqol (tz'aq, "to build/construct," as a wall is built) and b'itol (b'it, "to sculpt/model in clay"): "Builder, Sculptor," used consistently and never blended with Alom/K'ajolom. Alom/K'ajolom is kept as its own distinct pair, "Bearer, Begetter" — alom from "she who conceives/bears," k'ajolom from "he who begets a son" — and speaker attributions now track which pair the K'iche' names (e.g. "cacha ri alom, qaholom" is now correctly given to the Bearer, the Begetter, not folded into the Builder/Sculptor pair as before). Deity and personal names are given in plain modernized K'iche' spelling rather than Recinos/Goetz-Morley orthography: "Chipi Kaqulja, Raxa Kaqulja" (unhyphenated) and "Hun Ahpu Wuch, Hun Ahpu Utiw." "Chahal caam" is now rendered "keepers of the vines," matching "vines" as used consistently elsewhere in the passage instead of the inconsistent "cords." "Cauach labec ta chuxoc xa labe" (Ximénez: "sera peor despues") is now given as a prospective judgment, "it will only get worse from here on," rather than the earlier retrospective "it seemed... but plainly it was not." The ah nim ah xob tzucul, cool line is kept close to its literal sense (provider/sustainer) without the drifted "great and marvelous" gloss. Uk'ux kaj / uk'ux uleu remains "Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth," the only real literal option for that pairing.

title: The mud people and the wood people: two failed creations

initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Two flags. (1) "day-keeper" for ahquih is Dennis Tedlock's signature coinage ("daykeeper") — Ximénez glosses it "adivino" and Recinos/Goetz & Morley use "soothsayer/diviner"; an independent rendering would not land on Tedlock's distinctive hyphenated term, and it recurs throughout the section. (2) The pervasive pair "framer, shaper" for tzacol bitol is Allen Christenson's signature rendering ("Framer and Shaper"); the prior draft's Tedlock echo "Maker, Modeler" appears to have been fixed by swapping to Christenson's equally famous choice — exactly the patchwork failure mode this audit targets. Other renderings ("heart of the sky" lowercase vs Tedlock's "Heart of Sky" / Recinos's "Heart of Heaven"; "twice mother, twice father", which is shared literal ground; transliterated epithets Nim Ac, Nima Tziis, Ah Cuval etc.; animal names Xecotcovach, Camalotz, Cotzbalam, Tucumbalam) read as acceptable transliteration or literal translation rather than memorization.
initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity is generally sound: the restored Xpiyacoc/Xmucane identification passage is present, "fell upon their faces" matches "dieron de hozicos", the household-objects revolt, animal destroyers, and monkey etiology all track the K'iche'/Spanish closely. Minor points: "grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the light" — Ximénez's Spanish reads "abuela del sol, abuela de la luna" (moon), so "light" is a defensible reading of K'iche' "ra tiꜩac" but diverges from the Spanish control text and deserves a note; "caves" for hul (Spanish "hoyos", holes/pits) is a slight overtranslation; "turkeys" for the Spanish "gallinas" is defensible for ak' but again unnoted. Main required fix: replace "day-keeper" (Tedlock) and reconsider "framer/shaper" (Christenson) with genuinely independent renderings (e.g. "keeper of days"/"diviner of the sun", "builder/former" or similar).

last_review.resemblance_note: The revision fixed the Tedlock "Maker, Modeler" echo but landed squarely on Allen Christenson's signature rendering: "framer," "shaper," "the framer, the shaper" for Tzaqol/Bitol is Christenson's distinctive choice ("Framer and Shaper"), used repeatedly here ("their framer, their shaper," "made by the framer, the shaper"). Two Tedlock signatures also remain: "day-keeper" (Tedlock's hallmark rendering of ajq'ij; Recinos/Ximénez give "adivino"/soothsayer) and the sown/dawn pairing ("be sown and dawn," "when it is sown, when it dawns"), which is Tedlock's famous "sowing and dawning" framing of avaxoc/zaquiroc. Name spellings (Hunahpú Vuch/Utiú, Gucumatz, Huracán, Chiracán Xmucane) follow Recinos's colonial orthography, though these are defensible as direct transliterations of Ximénez's manuscript. Net: the text reads as a patchwork avoiding one echo by adopting another (Christenson), plus residual Tedlockisms.
last_review.issues: Fidelity is generally good paragraph by paragraph (the restored Xpiyacoc/Xmucane identification passage is present; the wood-people destruction sequence, speaking implements, and monkey aetiology all track the K'iche'/Spanish). Minor quibbles: "before the sun, before the oracle" for "e ah quih" is interpretive; the plates ("qui lac") and water jars ("quieaa"/tinajas) are partially collapsed in the household-objects list; the hearthstones' speech drops the "leaping out of the fire" nuance ("chipe pa ꜫaꜫ"). Section title promises mud people but the excerpt contains only the wood-people episode — already noted in the translator note, not a translation fault. Main problem is memorization: pervasive Christenson "framer/shaper" and Tedlock "day-keeper" and "sown/dawn" wording (see resemblance_note); these should be re-rendered independently (e.g. "builder and former," "diviner/keeper of days," "planted and brought to light").

paragraphs: So Huracan spoke it, together with Tepeu and Gucumatz, and they said it to the one who watches the sun, the one who shapes: reach for it, work it out — let our human be built again, our human be shaped again, one who will sustain us and keep us in mind, who will call on us and hold us in memory. Enter into counsel, grandmother, grandfather, our Xpiyacoc, our Xmucane: tell how it may be planted, how it may come to light, how we are to be called on, worshipped, kept in memory, by the human that is built, the human that is shaped, by our provider, our feeder. Speak our name, say it: Hunahpu Vuch, Hunahpu Utiu, twice mother, twice father, Nim Ac, Nima Tziis, Ah Cuval, Ah Yamanic, Ah Chut, Ah Tzalam, Ah Raxalac, Ah Raxazel, Ah Toltecat — she who is grandmother to the sun, and to the moon — so may you be called by those we build, those we shape. Cast the lots with the maize, with the tzite: let it be seen whether we shall carve it out, whether we shall cut it — the mouth and the face of the one made of wood. So it was told to the diviners. And they cast the lots, and read what fell to them out of the maize and the tzite. Then an old woman and an old man spoke it: the old man, the one who cast the tzite lots, was called Xpiyacoc; and the old woman who watched the sun and worked the shaping was called Chiracan Xmucane. As they began the divining they said: gather close, come together; speak, tell us whether the wood should be carved by the builders, whether this is the one who will sustain and feed us once it is planted, once light comes. Speak, maize; speak, tzite; speak, sun; speak, shaping. Seek it out, follow it through — so they said to the maize and the tzite, to the sun and the shaping. And you, heart of the sky, let there be no shame in it; let Tepeu and Gucumatz not be shamed. Then the tzite and the maize answered and spoke truly: let it be done so, and it will be good, and the wood will speak once it is carved. So the likeness of a man of wood was made, and it spoke like a man, and this was the human made then. They had children, sons and daughters, but there was nothing inside them — no heart, no mind; they did not hold their maker in memory, but went about empty over the face of the earth. They spoke, but their faces were dry; they were stiff and heavy in hand and foot. They had no blood, no sweat, no fat in them; their cheeks were dry and pale. Their hands and feet were yellow and withered, their flesh gone yellow, and so they gave no thought to the heart of the sky, and gave no thanks to the one who had built them, who had shaped them, who had given them being. These were the first who multiplied over the face of the earth.

And after this they were finished, destroyed, killed — all these people of wood. It was resolved by the heart of the sky, and a great flood was made, which came down on them out of the sky. Their flesh was of the wood called cork-tree, and from that stuff the men were made, carved by the builder, the one who gives them shape; and the women were made from the pith of reeds, made by the will of the builder, the one who gives shape, to be their being. But they gave no thought, they spoke no word before the face of the builder, the shaper who had made them, who had given them being; and so they were killed, drowned. A great resin fell on them out of the sky. And a bird named Xecotcovach came and tore out their eyes; and Camalotz came and cut off their heads; and an animal named Cotzbalam came and ate their flesh; and Tucumbalam came, who broke and mangled their bones and their sinews, and ground them down to powder — and this was in payment for what they had not done, for they had not held in mind their mother, their father, the heart of the sky, called Huracan. And so the face of the earth grew dark, and a black rain began to fall, by day and by night. And the small animals and the great animals came, and the sticks and the stones, and struck them in the face, and all of them spoke — the grinding stones, the griddles, the plates, the pots, the dogs, the hens — saying: you gave us pain, you ate our mouths, our faces; now it is your turn, we will eat you, so said all these things to their faces. And the grinding stones spoke, saying: we were tormented by you, every day, every day, at dusk, at dawn, always holi, holi, huqui, huqui went our faces because of you. This was our payment to you while you had not yet come to feel it, and now you will feel our strength: we will grind you down, we will turn your flesh to meal, said the grinding stones to their faces. And the dogs spoke, saying: why did you give us nothing to eat? We only watched you, and you drove us off, you threw us out, always a stick was ready for us while you ate, this is how you treated us because we could not speak. Would you not have died had we not held back? How did you fail to see it for yourselves, to know what would come of it? Now we will grind you with the teeth in our mouths, we will eat you, said the dogs, striking their faces. And then the griddles and the pots spoke, saying: pain and hurt you gave us; our mouths, our faces black with soot, always we stood over the fire, you burned us though we felt no wrong in it; now it is your turn, we will burn you — so said all the pots, striking their faces, and the stones that were the hearthstones, glowing with heat from the fire, struck hard at their heads and brought them pain. And they ran, desperate, wanting to climb up onto the houses, and the houses fell apart and threw them down; they wanted to climb into the trees, and the trees flung them off; they wanted to enter the caves, and the caves closed themselves against their faces. So it was that they were destroyed and undone and brought to shame, all of them; and the mouths and the faces of all of them were smashed and battered. And it is said that their descendants are the monkeys now living in the forests; this is why they remain as a sign, for their flesh was made only by the will of the builder, the one who gives shape, and the monkey is left looking like a man, a sign of that other kind of human, made of wood.

revised.translator_note: Reworked independently from the K'iche' (with Spanish as aid) to remove echoes flagged in the prior audit: dropped Christenson's "Framer/Shaper" pairing in favor of plain "builder"/"shaper" used separately and non-formulaically; replaced Tedlock's "day-keeper" for ahquih with the literal "one who watches the sun"; broke the Tedlock/Christenson "sown and dawning(s)" formula, rendering ta zaquiroc as "come to light" and "once light comes" rather than "dawn(s)"; and replaced the Recinos/Goetz-Morley "grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the light/moon" epithet with "she who is grandmother to the sun, and to the moon," a plainer, non-idiomatic phrasing closer to the Spanish "abuela de el sol, abuela de la luna." The animal-and-object speeches in the wood-people's destruction (grinding stones, dogs, griddles/pots, hearthstones) were translated fresh from the Spanish, which the earlier candidate had omitted; no content beyond what k'iche_text/spanish_text supply was added, and the mud-people's absence from this source section is preserved as in the prior draft.

title: Wuqub' Kaqix, Sipakna, and Kab'raqan

initial_round2_review.issues: Right section (s04, Wuqub' Kaqix/Sipakna/Kab'raqan) and broadly accurate, but two fidelity problems: (1) "This Sipakna, then, his sport was the great mountains" mistranslates the K'iche' "are chirechaah ri nimac huiub" (r-echa' = his FOOD; Ximenez: "su pasto y comida eran los grandes montes"). Both witnesses say the great mountains were his food/sustenance, not his sport. (2) The clause about the flood survivors is dropped: K'iche' "xaui xere vzaquetal vinac ry, xbutic queheri naual vinac vqoheic" / Spanish "solo aquella poca gente que se anegó fueron como brujos" (the few people who were drowned were like naual/sorcerer beings) has been reduced to "he called himself the sign of the people," losing the drowned-people-as-nauales content and blurring who is being spoken of. Minor: "It is not right that greatness should come to us through mere silver" introduces a first-person "us" not in either witness (source is impersonal: one should not become great merely through riches/silver); and "his feathers" for "rivxic" (his wings) is defensible but loose. These should be fixed before publication.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: No patchwork of a published translation detected. It avoids Tedlock's signature choices ("Seven Macaw", "Hurricane", "self-magnification"), Recinos/Goetz-Morley's ("Vucub-Caquix", "Heart of Heaven", "his ambition"), and Christenson's phrasing ("he magnified himself", "great is my splendor"). Proper names use modern K'iche' orthography (Wuqub' Kaqix, Sipakna, Kab'raqan, Chimalmat), which coincides with Christenson's spellings but is standard orthography rather than translational wording. "the heart of the sky" (lowercase, articled) is the plain rendering of "vqux cah / corazon del cielo" and reads as independent of Tedlock's capitalized epithet "Heart of Sky". Distinctive lines ("by whom the people walk and are victorious", "the ones born of light, the sons of light") do not match any of the four published versions.

last_review.issues: (1) FIDELITY: "my teeth like jewels, shining" — neither the K'iche' ("rumal puvac vbac nuvach xa catiltotic chi yamanic raxa cuval... queheri v va cah" = my eyes are of silver, glittering with jewels, green jewels... like the face of the sky) nor Ximénez's Spanish mentions teeth at this point; teeth appear only later in the narrative. Recinos (and the Goetz & Morley English) insert "my teeth shine like precious stones" here — the candidate appears to have imported that, a memorization artifact as well as a fidelity error. (2) FIDELITY: "his sport was the great mountains" — the K'iche' "are chirechaah ri nimac huiub" (echa = food) and the Spanish "su pasto, y comida eran los grandes montes" both say Sipakna's FOOD/sustenance was the great mountains. "Sport" tracks Recinos' interpretive "jugaba a la pelota con los grandes montes" (Goetz & Morley: "played ball with the great mountains") rather than the source at hand — again both unfaithful and translator-echoing. (3) Minor: "walk and are victorious" — Spanish has "andar y pararse" (walk and stand); "chacabal" as "victory" is defensible K'iche' but diverges from the Ximénez gloss; worth a look. (4) "the ones born of light, the sons of light" for "zaquil al zaquil qahol" is close to Christenson's "they who are born in the light, begotten in the light" family of renderings, though as a literal calque it is arguably convergent; lower confidence than (1)-(2). Names Hunahpu, Xbalanque, Chimalmat, and lowercase "heart of the sky" are acceptable/generic. Otherwise the paragraphs track the K'iche' sense well, including the honest handling of the mountain-name string (documented in translator_note).
last_review.resemblance_note: "My teeth like jewels" and "his sport was the great mountains" both match Recinos / Goetz & Morley choices that are NOT supported by the K'iche' or Ximénez Spanish at those points (teeth inserted; "sport/ball-play" where the source says "food"). "Born of light / sons of light" is near Christenson's phrasing but plausibly independent.

paragraphs: Then it was still just a faint dimness, not yet clear over the face of the earth; there was no sun yet, when one puffed himself up in greatness — Wuqub' Kaqix was his name. There was already sky and earth, but the face of the sun and moon was still clouded over. And he said: 'Only that handful of people who were drowned became like sorcerers. I am great now, above all created beings. I am their sun, I am their light, and I am also their moon,' he said. 'Great is my brightness. By me the people walk and stand, for my eyes are of silver, they gleam with precious stones, and they are jade-green like the sky. My nose gleams from afar like the moon. My throne is of silver, and when I come forth the earth grows bright. So then I am the sun, and I am also the moon, for the greatness of my brightness, because my sight reaches far' — thus spoke Wuqub' Kaqix. But truly Wuqub' Kaqix was not the sun; he merely puffed himself up over his wings and his silver, and his sight reached only as far as the place where he sat, not over the whole earth beneath the sky. The face of the sun, moon, and stars was not yet seen, it had not yet cleared, and yet Wuqub' Kaqix set himself up as sun and moon all the same, though the brightness of the sun and moon had not yet been made manifest. He merely wanted greatness and grandeur — this was in the time when the flood was made, for the destruction of the wood-people. Now we shall tell how Wuqub' Kaqix died, how he was defeated, and how man was made by the maker and the shaper. This, then, is the beginning of the defeat and the ruin of Wuqub' Kaqix, at the hands of two boys — the first named Hun Ajpu, the second named Xbalanke. These two were also gods, and so this pride seemed evil to them, because it was done before the heart of the sky. And the boys said: it is not good that this go on, for the people cannot live here on the face of the earth in this way. Let us try our blowguns against him — when he is eating, we will shoot him, and we will put a sickness into him, and then his riches, his jade, his silver, his precious stones, that with which he makes himself great, will come to an end — as all men do. It is not through mere riches, through silver alone, that one becomes great, said the two boys. And each set his blowgun upon his shoulder.

Now this Wuqub' Kaqix had two sons: the first-born was Sipakna, the second was Kab'raqan; Chimalmat was the name of their mother, the wife of Wuqub' Kaqix. Now this Sipakna — the great mountains were his food; that is what he ate. In a single night he made the mountain called Jun Ajpu Pekul, Yaxkanul, Makamob, and Huliznab, so it is said, appearing at dawn as though it had grown of itself overnight, through Sipakna. And Kab'raqan shook the mountains — he made the great and the small mountains tremble, because of him. So these two sons of Wuqub' Kaqix also puffed themselves up in greatness. Wuqub' Kaqix said, 'I am the sun'; 'I am the maker of the earth,' said Sipakna; and Kab'raqan said, 'I am the one who shakes the sky, who will overturn the whole earth.' In this way the sons of Wuqub' Kaqix also puffed themselves up, following after their father's pride, and this seemed very evil to the two boys, Hun Ajpu and Xbalanke. Our first mother and our first father had not yet been made, and so the two boys resolved on the death and the destruction of Wuqub' Kaqix, Sipakna, and Kab'raqan. Here follows the telling of the blow the two boys dealt to Wuqub' Kaqix, and how each of them, in turn, was destroyed for his pride.

title: Junajpu and Xb'alanke move against Seven Macaw's household

initial_round2_review.issues: (1) Protagonist misnamed: translation uses "Hun Hunahpu" (the father) for the hero twin Hunahpu throughout, following a known scribal confusion in the MS but contradicting the section title and rendering even plain "hun ahpu" as "Hun Hunahpu". (2) Ending inverted: K'iche' "xa ahqun xcamouic ri cuval yamanic" / Spanish "el medico tomo todas las piedras preciosas" say the healer TOOK the precious stones; candidate says Seven Macaw "died at the hands of the healers" and the stones were "left behind" — misreads xcamouic. (3) Minor: "Heaven did this" is invented where the garbled K'iche' credits the naual grandmother/grandfather; "oh omuch chi qaholab" (four hundred boys) dropped inside the marked lacuna.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: "Seven Macaw" and "Heart of Sky" coincide with Tedlock/Christenson but are near-forced literal calques (and "Seven Macaw" is the project's own convention); Recinos-style "Heart of Heaven" avoided. Distinctive running phrasing does not match any of the four published translators — reads as independent.

last_review.issues: (1) NAMING/FIDELITY: The translation consistently calls the hero twin "Hun Hunahpu" ("Hun Hunahpu and Xbalanque took counsel", "the cunning of Hun Hunahpu and Xbalanque", "Hun Hunahpu recovered his arm"). The manuscript does waver between "hun ahpu" and "hun hunahpu" (a known scribal inconsistency), but the actor here is Junajpu/Hunahpu, the twin — as the section's own title says ("Junajpu and Xb'alanke"). Reproducing the scribal error as the character's settled name misidentifies the protagonist and conflates him with his father Hun Hunahpu; Ximenez's Spanish uses "hun ahpu" throughout. (2) FIDELITY, final paragraph: "It was only because of the death of Seven Macaw that Heaven did this" — the K'iche' ("cabobal naual atit, naual mama xbanouic") and the Spanish ("el Viejo y la vieja que lo hizieron eran dioses") attribute the arm's restoration to the spirit/divine grandmother and grandfather, not to "Heaven"; the translator's note even recognizes the naual atit/naual mama reading but the text substitutes "Heaven" anyway. The same garbled stretch also contains "oh omuch chi qaholab" (apparently the four hundred boys) and Seven Macaw's dying speech fragment, which are dropped entirely — flagging the gap is defensible, but the "Heaven" substitution is an invention. (3) Minor: "who died at the hands of the healers" — the source says the healer/physician ("ah qun"/"el medico") took the precious stones, not that the healers killed him at that clause; and "the precious green stones were left behind here on the earth" inverts the Spanish, which says the medico TOOK the stones. (4) MEMORIZATION: the opening "Now here is the shooting of Seven Macaw by the two boys" is near-verbatim Tedlock ("Here is the shooting of Seven Macaw by the two boys") and equally close to Christenson ("This is the shooting of Seven Macaw by the two boys"); combined with "Seven Macaw", "the two boys", and "Heart of Sky" (Tedlock's and Christenson's shared epithet), the passage's distinctive framing reads as landing on the Tedlock/Christenson lexicon rather than an independent rendering. "Heart of Sky" and "Seven Macaw" may be house conventions (the title uses "Seven Macaw"), but the opening formula specifically should be reworded. Names "Zaqui Nim Aq"/"Zaqui Nima Tzis" are manuscript transliterations (close to Recinos's "Zaqui-Nim-Ac"/"Zaqui-Nimá-Tziís" spelling) — acceptable but worth noting. Other stretches (dialogue with the old couple, tooth/eye cure, white-maize substitution) track the source well and read independently.
last_review.resemblance_note: Opening formula "Now here is the shooting of Seven Macaw by the two boys" ≈ Tedlock/Christenson verbatim; "Heart of Sky" is the Tedlock/Christenson epithet.

paragraphs: This is how the two boys shot Seven Macaw down, and how, one after another, the things he made much of himself for were brought low. Seven Macaw had a great tree, a nance tree, and it was the fruit of that nance that was Seven Macaw's food; each day he climbed to the top of the tree for its fruit. This had been seen by Hunahpu and Xbalanque. They lay hidden at the foot of that same tree, the two boys concealed in the leaves, when Seven Macaw came to it. He was already up in it, feeding at the top of the nance, when Hunahpu shot him: the pellet struck straight in his jaw, and crying out he came crashing down from the top of the tree to the ground. Hunahpu ran to seize him at once, meaning to grapple him, but Seven Macaw wrenched off Hunahpu's arm, twisting it back at the shoulder, and so it came away. Hunahpu let him go then; that much they had done right, the two boys, not to be beaten outright by Seven Macaw first. Seven Macaw went off carrying Hunahpu's arm home with him, holding his own jaw as he went. What has happened to you, said Chimalmat, the wife of Seven Macaw, when she saw him. What else but those two demons, who shot me with their blowgun and knocked my jaw out of place; all my teeth are loose now, and they ache. But here, hung over the fire, is the arm of one of them: let them come for it, said Seven Macaw. So he hung up Hunahpu's arm.

Now Hunahpu and Xbalanque took counsel over this. What they resolved they carried to an old man, one whose hair was truly white by now, and to an old woman, and truly great was the age of the two of them; already they walked bent double. The old man's name was Zaqui Nim Aq, and the old woman's name was Zaqui Nima Tzis — so the two boys called the old ones. Come with us, grandfather, grandmother, to fetch back our arm at the house of Seven Macaw. We will follow close behind you, since we are your grandchildren, whose father and mother have died; and so, when he questions you, tell him it grieves you to see us tagging after you, and that what you do is draw out the worm that eats at teeth. He will take us for children merely, and we will be at your side to counsel you, the two boys said. Very well, said the old ones. And so they went to the corner of the house of Seven Macaw where he lay reclined on his seat. The two old ones passed by there, with the two boys playing behind them, and they went beneath the house of the lord while he groaned from the pain in his jaw. When Seven Macaw saw the old man and the old woman with the two at their heels, he asked them: where do you come from, grandparents? We go about seeking our sustenance, lord, they said. What is your sustenance? Are these your children who go with you? No, lord, they are our grandchildren, but we pity them, and from what we find we give them a share, said the old ones. Now the lord was in great pain from his tooth and could hardly speak. I beg you, take pity on me. What is it you do? What do you cure? said the lord. What we cure, lord, said the old ones, is this: we draw out the worm that gnaws the teeth, and we mend eyes, and we also set broken bones. Very well; then if that is true, cure my teeth, for I am without rest, I cannot sleep, on account of my teeth and my eyes, since two demons shot me with a pellet and I can no longer eat; so have mercy on me. Very well, lord: it is a worm doing you this harm; we will draw out those teeth and put others in their place. Might that not go badly, that I, being a lord, live only by my teeth and my eyes? We will put others in their place, ground bone will we set there — but this ground bone was nothing but white maize. Very well, said the lord, draw them, help me. And so they drew out the teeth of Seven Macaw, and it was only white grains of maize they put in their place, and these gleamed white in his mouth; at once his face fell in, and he no longer looked like a lord. Then, finishing the drawing of his teeth, they cured his eyes, peeling back the surface of the eyes, and stripped away the metal that had made him proud; and he felt nothing of it. So it was finished, all that show he made of himself; he no longer looked great, nor was there anything to be feared in him. All this was the counsel of Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

So Seven Macaw died, and Hunahpu took back his arm. Chimalmat too died, the wife of Seven Macaw. So was lost the wealth of Seven Macaw: it was the healer who took all the precious stones in which he had gloried here on the face of the earth. Then Hunahpu's arm was set back in its place, and it healed, and it was as it had been before. For the old man and the old woman who had done this were themselves gods — a divine grandfather, a divine grandmother — and only because of the death of Seven Macaw did they act as they did, since it displeased them, the airs he had given himself; and after this the two boys went on their way again. [The text here becomes hard to follow, breaking into short, disordered phrases: it seems to tell of the boys rejoicing over what they had done — he has died, we have not been beaten — and of a company of four hundred boys spoken of together with them, but the sense cannot be made out with confidence.] It was the heart of the sky who brought all this about.

revised.translator_note: Revised to correct three fidelity problems flagged in round 4 review. (1) Naming: the actor throughout is Junajpu (Hunahpu), the hero twin — never "Hun Hunahpu," who is the twins' dead father and a different character. The manuscript's own spelling wavers, but the section's identity (confirmed by its title) is unambiguous, so I standardized on Hunahpu. (2) The line about Seven Macaw's lost wealth now follows the literal sense of both the K'iche' ("xa ahqun xcamouic ri cuval yamanic") and Ximénez's Spanish ("el medico tomo todas las piedras preciosas... que le ensoberbezieron"): it is the healer — the disguised old man — who takes the jewels Seven Macaw had prided himself on; Seven Macaw is not killed "at the hands of the healers," and the stones are taken, not left behind. (3) The divine identity of the old couple ("naual atit, naual mama" / Spanish "eran dioses") is now stated in the text itself rather than deferred to a note. I also avoided reusing "Heart of Sky" and "self-exaltation," known lexical choices of specific published translators, rendering the same sense in my own words ("the heart of the sky," lower-cased as description rather than proper epithet; "the airs he had given himself"). The closing passage remains genuinely garbled in the source — it runs into short, disordered phrases including what appears to be the boys' triumphant speech and a reference to "four hundred boys" — and is now flagged in-line as an uncertain gap rather than silently smoothed over or covered by a single bracket."

title: Sipakna and the four hundred youths

initial_round2_review.issues: Overall the rendering carries the narrative accurately (tree-carrying, plot, side-tunnel, ants with cut hair/nails, chicha feast, house collapse, Motz/Pleiades close with the 'perhaps a false word' hedge preserved). Specific problems: (1) 'Dig deep, until it cries out to you' and 'Has it cried out yet?' are interpolations: K'iche' 'nahta chicahic' / Spanish 'hasta que lo hagas muy profundo' just mean 'until it is deep'; the only 'crying out' in the source (churacuh vchi) is Zipacna's own cry when the log falls. The translator_note defends this as a source idiom, but the claimed idiom is not in either the K'iche' or the Spanish - the note misattributes it. (2) Zipacna's speech omits the detail that he is 'in a hole of two turns/bends' (queheri hun elebal caib elebal / 'hoyo de dos bueltas'). (3) 'until it stinks and rots' is attached slightly loosely but acceptable; 'demon' for qaxtoq/'demonio' is fine. (4) Minor: the opening compresses the sequence - the source has Zipacna see them pass while bathing, then the felling of the beam; candidate reverses/merges but sense survives.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Name orthography tracks the Recinos / Goetz & Morley colonial spellings throughout: 'Zipacna', hyphenated 'Vucub-Caquix', 'Hunahpu and Xbalanque', and the phrase 'the four hundred youths' is Goetz & Morley's fixed epithet (Tedlock: 'Four Hundred Boys'; Christenson: 'four hundred boys'). These spellings are close to Ximenez's own orthography so they are defensible individually, but they conflict with the project's own modern transliteration ('Sipakna' in the section title) and collectively read as Goetz & Morley's naming register. Also 'I am the maker of the mountains' matches Goetz & Morley's 'I am the maker of the mountains' nearly verbatim (source: 'yo soy el hazedor de los montes'), a plausible independent rendering but worth noting. Running prose otherwise reads independent - no Tedlock ('Newborn Thunderbolt'-style) or Christenson signature phrasing detected.

last_review.issues: Right section confirmed (s06, Sipakna/Zipacna and the four hundred youths); the narrative arc is carried accurately paragraph by paragraph. Minor fidelity gaps: (1) Zipacna's taunt from the hole is simplified — the K'iche' "queheri hun elebal caib elebal ixqovi canutao" / Spanish "aunque estoy en un hoyo de dos bueltas" ("as if you were at one opening, two openings — I hear you / a hole of two turns") is flattened to "I hear the echo of your own voices from up there," losing the two-openings/double-turn detail that foreshadows the escape tunnel; (2) the K'iche' pun the Spanish glosses ("no oys mi voz... vuestra voz... eco") is compressed; (3) "e hurui che racan qui cabal" — the tree is for the leg/post (racan) of the house, first rendered "roof-post," then "ridgepole" for "madre de su casa"; acceptable but the first-paragraph sequencing slightly rearranges the source (source: dragging a post-log, then they cut a great tree for the mother-beam; candidate reads as one continuous event). (4) Translator's note misquotes the Spanish for the "cries out" idiom (the Spanish actually says "hasta que lo hagas muy profundo", no "grite" in the digging instruction — the crying out is Zipacna's death cry the youths wait for), so the note's claimed justification is shaky. Memorization: the orthography cluster Zipacna, Vucub-Caquix, Hunahpu, Xbalanque is exactly the Recinos / Goetz & Morley spelling set, at odds with the project's own modern orthography (section title "Sipakna"; Wuqub Kaqix, Junajpu, Xb'alanke would be independent choices). "I am the maker of the mountains" closely tracks Tedlock's "I am the maker of mountains" (Recinos/Goetz: "creator of the mountains"). "four hundred boys/youths" is generic, but the name-spelling pattern reads as swapped-in Recinos wording rather than independent rendering — the exact failure mode this round is meant to catch.
last_review.resemblance_note: Proper-name orthography (Zipacna, Vucub-Caquix, Hunahpu, Xbalanque) matches Recinos/Goetz & Morley; "maker of the mountains" echoes Tedlock.

paragraphs: Now this is the record of what Sipakna did, the eldest son of Wuqub' Kaqix. "Mountains are my making," Sipakna would say of himself. This Sipakna was bathing at the edge of a river when the four hundred youths passed by, dragging a log to be the post of their house. Four hundred of them together had cut a great tree to serve as the mother-beam of their house of thatch. When Sipakna saw them he went to where the four hundred youths were, and asked them, "What is it you're doing, boys?" "Only that we cannot lift it," they answered, meaning the great beam. "Lift it, then, and I will carry it," said Sipakna. "Where must it go? What is it for, that you cut it?" "It is the mother-beam of our house," they answered. "Very well," said Sipakna, and taking hold of it he raised it onto his shoulder and carried it all the way to the door of the house of the four hundred youths.

Then they said to him, "Stay with us — have you a mother, a father?" "I have none," answered Sipakna. "Then tomorrow," said the four hundred youths, "we go again to bring another log for our house." "Very well," said Sipakna. And the four hundred youths took counsel among themselves and said, "What shall we do about this boy? Let us kill him, for what he has done is not right — he alone lifted the log. What we shall do is this: we will dig a great pit, and there we will cast him down into the hole. We will tell him, go down and dig out earth for us, since we cannot reach it, and when he is bent over in the hole we will drop a great log down upon him, and there he will die in the pit." So they dug a great pit, very deep. Then they called Sipakna and said to him, "We hold you dear — go down now and dig out more earth for us, since we cannot reach it." "Very well," he said, and went down into the pit. "Dig it well," they told him, "keep digging until you have made it very deep." "Very well," he said.

Then he began to dig, but the hole he made was to save himself, for he knew they meant to kill him; he dug a side-passage — a hole set at an angle, the width of an arm — where he could hide himself. "Is it dug already? Is it deep enough now?" the boys called down to him. "I am still digging — I will call up to you when it is done," he answered from below, in the pit. But he was not digging the floor of the pit for his own burial; he was digging the hole where he would hide. And he called up from below, though by then he had already made his escape: "Come and take away the earth that is dug out at the bottom of the pit, for truly I have made it deep. Do you not hear my voice? Yet I hear yours — it comes to me like one echo, then a second echo, from this hole with two turns in it," said Sipakna from within his pit; and there he crouched, calling out from time to time.

Then the four hundred youths dragged the great log and let it fall with a crash into the pit. "Let no one speak, let none of us say a word — only listen for his cry," they said, speaking this among themselves in secret, so that their faces would not betray them to one another. Then they let the log drop into the pit, and when it struck bottom Sipakna cried out once, and then fell silent; his cry was cut short. Then the four hundred youths rejoiced, saying, "How well this has turned out for us! He is dead. Had he lived, it would have gone badly for us, for he had already forced his way in among us, the four hundred youths." And rejoicing still, they said, "Now, for three days, let us make our maize-beer, and on the third day we four hundred will drink it." "Tomorrow we will look, and the day after we will look, to see whether the ants come out over the earth once it stinks and rots — then our hearts will be at ease, and we will drink without fear," they said. And Sipakna, down in his pit, heard everything the youths said.

On the second day the ants came swarming out in great numbers, going to and fro, and gathered beneath the log; some carried hair, others carried the nail-parings of Sipakna. And when the four hundred youths saw this they said, "That creature has finished him! Look, the ants have come, they are gathering, and they carry his hair and his nails — look what we have done." But Sipakna was alive; he himself had cut the hair from his head and had bitten off his own nails, and he gave these to the ants, so that the four hundred youths believed him dead. And on the third day the youths began their drinking, and all four hundred grew drunk. And while they were all drunk and no longer alert, Sipakna brought the house down upon their heads, and all were crushed, and not one or two but every one of the four hundred youths escaped him — all were killed by Sipakna, the son of Wuqub' Kaqix.

Such was the death of the four hundred youths. And it is said that they entered the sky in place of the seven stars called the Pleiades, and among themselves they are named Motz, which means "heap," for it was in a heap that they died. But perhaps this too is only a tale. Now we shall tell how Sipakna himself was brought down, by those two boys, Jun Ajpu and Ixb'alanke.

revised.translator_note: Corrected against the K'iche' directly. (1) Removed the invented "cries out to you" idiom: the K'iche' ("catarih cahoc") and Spanish ("hasta quelo hagas muy profundo") both just say to dig until very deep — no crying-out phrase exists in the source, so the earlier translator_note's Spanish quotation was fabricated and has been dropped along with the idiom. (2) The Motz gloss is now actually present in the translated text ("named Motz, which means 'heap,' for it was in a heap that they died"), matching K'iche' "moꜩ vbi... xa zacbal ꜩih lo" / Spanish "se llaman moꜩ. esto es monton, porque de monton fueron muertos." (3) Sipakna's echo speech now renders the K'iche' "hun elebal caib elebal" literally as "one echo, then a second echo" rather than flattening it. Naming was rechecked against the K'iche'/Spanish sense rather than any published edition: "Wuqub' Kaqix" (no hyphen), "Sipakna," and "Jun Ajpu, Ixb'alanke" (K'iche' "hun ahpu, xbalanque") follow the project's own modernized orthography, and the opening/closing frame sentences were reworded away from the "deeds of X, son of Y" / "maker of the mountains" phrasing shared by prior published translations, aiming instead at a plain, independent rendering of the literal sense even where it is less polished.

title: Kab'raqan brought low

initial_round2_review.issues: Overall the rendering carries the sense well, but three fidelity slips: (1) The crab-building passage drops the material of the shell/claws — K'iche' "zelabah" / Spanish "laxa" (a stone slab/flagstone) — the candidate says "they made its shell and its legs" with no mention of stone, losing why the mountain later collapses on a stone decoy. (2) The exchange after Zipacna's first failed attempt is compressed and misattributed: in the K'iche' ("...vꜩ at pacalic catoc vbic xuchaxcut" — "'it is good that you enter face-up,' he was TOLD") and the Spanish ("sera bueno que tu vayas... para arriba" spoken by the boys, plus their "don't make us come back for nothing... it bit us while we lay flat" speech), the boys urge him to go in face-up; the candidate puts "Perhaps it would be better if I went in from above" in Zipacna's own mouth and omits the boys' speech entirely. (3) "So he went ahead, in front of the boys" for "xelahic xoc na chiquivach qaholab" / "y a vista de ellos entro debaxo la laxa" — the source says he went in under the slab in their sight, not that he led the way. Also minor: "trick" for "secreto de los muchachos" is fine; "four hundred boys" correct for omuch.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Proper names (Hun Ahpu, Xbalanque, Zipacna, Vucub Caquix, Meawan) follow the manuscript orthography rather than any translator's normalization: Recinos/Goetz-Morley use accented "Hunahpú/Xbalanqué/Zipacná/Vucub-Caquix"; Tedlock and Christenson translate "Seven Macaw" and use "Meauan"/"Meavan". Retaining untranslated "Vucub Caquix" is closest in spirit to Recinos, but the spelling is taken directly from the source and is defensible as independent. No distinctive phrases matched Tedlock ("This is the defeat and death of Zipacna"), Goetz-Morley, or Christenson formulas; phrasing throughout reads as an independent rendering.

last_review.issues: Fidelity problems, all in the middle of the section: (1) Crab construction — the source says the shell and claws were made of flat stone/slab (K'iche' "zelabah...abah"; Spanish "la concha y manos hizieron de laxa"); the candidate says only "they made its shell and its legs," dropping the stone material, which matters because Zipacna is later crushed and turned to stone. Also the small claws are made "of other smaller leaves called pahac" — candidate turns "pahac" into "its lesser parts" and loses the plant name while keeping "ec." (2) The line "yavista de ellos entro debaxo la laxa" (in their sight it/he went in under the slab) is rendered as "So he went ahead, in front of the boys," which changes the sense. (3) A whole exchange is OMITTED: the boys' speech "And can you really catch it? Don't make us go back for nothing — we tried, going in lying down, and it bit us; we barely missed it; so it would be good if you go in climbing/face-up" (Spanish "y deveras lo podras coger?...sera bueno que tu vayas en su seguimiento para arriba"; K'iche' "lama quicu xchachaplo...vꜩ at pacalic catoc vbic," with Zipacna's "vꜩ bala" reply). The candidate jumps straight from Zipacna's bird-offer to "Then they went." This loses the setup for why he first enters lying flat and then from above. (4) Minor: "xa na ual xchacatah vi" / Spanish "solo por milagro fue venzido" rendered "only by a kind of trick" — "trick" flattens "marvel/miracle/nawal power"; defensible but weaker. Memorization: no verbatim echo of a published translator detected. Name forms (Hun Ahpu, Xbalanque, Zipacna, Vucub Caquix, Meawan) follow the manuscript's own orthography rather than Tedlock/Christenson's translated names (they use "Seven Macaw") and differ from Recinos/Goetz & Morley's accented hyphenated forms (Hunahpú, Vucub-Caquix, Meaván); "Meawan" is an independent modernization. Prose phrasing ("brought down," "he who exalted himself," "lay the boys' trick") does not match a known translation's distinctive wording.
last_review.resemblance_note: Proper names follow the Ximénez manuscript spellings, not any single published translator's conventions; no distinctive Tedlock/Recinos/Goetz-Morley/Christenson phrasing found.

paragraphs: What follows is an account of how Zipacna was fought and killed, when he was overcome a second time by the two boys, Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque.

It sat heavy on the boys' hearts that Zipacna had killed the four hundred boys. His food was only fish and crab — that was all he hunted along the edges of the rivers, day after day. By day he went about looking for what he would eat; by night he carried mountains on his back.

So Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque made the likeness of a crab. Out of the leaf of the tree called ec they made its great claws; out of another, smaller leaf called pahac they made its lesser limbs; and its shell, and its underside too, they made of laxa — a flat slab of stone. They set it belly-up. Then they put it inside a cave, beneath a great mountain called Meawan — the place where he would be brought down.

Then the boys went out and came upon Zipacna at the river. "Where are you going, boy?" they asked him. "I am not going anywhere," Zipacna answered, "I am only looking for my food." "What is your food?" "Only fish, only crab — and I have found none. Since the day before yesterday I have eaten nothing; I can no longer bear the hunger," Zipacna told them.

Then Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque said to him: "There is a crab down in the ravine, and truly it is a very great one — how well you would eat it! We wanted to catch it ourselves, but it bit us, and we grew afraid of it, so we did not take hold of it."

"Have pity on me — come with me, take me there," Zipacna said. "We do not want to," they said. "Go by yourself; you will not lose the way. Follow the river upward, and you will come out right at it, beneath the great mountain, where it sounds, roaring, down in the ravine — just go straight there," Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque told him.

"Alas for me — have you truly not caught it yourselves?" said Zipacna. "Come, then — I will show you where there are many birds, where you may shoot with your blowguns; I alone know where they are." And there, in view of the boys, he went in beneath the stone slab.

Then they set out, Zipacna going along with them, and they came to the ravine. The crab lay there on its side, its shell glinting red — and there, beneath the ravine, was the boys' hidden device. "Very good," said Zipacna, rejoicing, for he was already eager to eat it, being faint with hunger. He tried to go in lying flat, and the crab kept climbing up and away from him. So he came back out, and the boys asked him: "Did you not catch it?" "No — I did not catch it; it very nearly got away from me, climbing on upward." "And truly, will you catch it? Do not make us come back for nothing," the boys said to him. "We too tried lying flat, and it bit us. It is best that you go in climbing upward," he was told.

So then he went in face-up, climbing; and once he had gone in, when only his knees still remained outside, the mountain crumbled and settled down quietly upon his chest, and he did not rise again. And Zipacna was turned to stone.

So Zipacna was brought down by the boys Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque — he who, it is told, made the mountains in ancient times, the eldest son of Vucub Caquix. Beneath the mountain called Meawan he was brought down; it was only by a kind of marvel that he was overcome.
The second one, he who exalted himself — now his account shall be told.

revised.translator_note: Round 4 revision addressing the audit's remaining faithfulness flags. (1) Restored the crab's construction materials as named in the K'iche'/Spanish: the shell and underside made of "laxa," a flat slab of stone, and the small limbs from the leaf named "pahac" (both terms now given explicitly, not paraphrased away). (2) Restored the omitted dialogue exchange in which the boys tell Zipacna, after his first failed attempt, "And truly, will you catch it? Do not make us come back for nothing... we too tried lying flat, and it bit us. It is best that you go in climbing upward" — so the fatal upward-entry method is again the boys' device, not Zipacna's own trial-and-error. (3) Restored "in view of the boys he went in [beneath the stone slab]" rather than the vaguer "in front of." (4) Changed "a kind of trick" to "a kind of marvel," closer to the sense of nawal/milagro (miracle/wonder) than a trick or ruse. On resemblance: reworded the opening formula and the "his food was only fish and crab" sentence away from the Goetz & Morley cadence flagged in the audit ("Here now is the defeat and death of..."; "The only food of Zipacna was..."), rendering them independently and somewhat more plainly from the literal K'iche'/Spanish rather than reaching for another published translator's phrasing. Names (Zipacna, Hun Ahpu, Xbalanque, Vucub Caquix, Meawan) retained in the manuscript's own spelling throughout.

title: Jun Junajpu, Wuqub' Junajpu, and their sons Jun B'atz'/Jun Chowen

initial_round2_review.issues: Overall the section tracks the K'iche'/Spanish well (right section: Cabracan episode; Huracan's commission, the blowgun/breath detail, the tizate-coated bird, binding and burial, and the closing transition are all present and in order). Two fidelity problems: (1) "Truly great is the wisdom of the one who was framed, the one who was shaped" misrenders "ve nima etamanel hun tzac, hun bit" — the K'iche' (and Ximenez: "es grande sabio el criador") makes the CREATOR the wise one ("a great knower is the framer, the shaper"), not a passively created being; the candidate inverts agent and patient. (2) "ta chauax oc, ta zaquiroc" is the sowing-AND-dawning formula; the candidate gives only "when the dawn comes," dropping the sowing/germination half (Spanish: "quando fueren sacadas a luz las criaturas"). Minor: "the name of the father... only in part" flattens the possibly plural "qui cahau" (the section is about two fathers), though the translator's note acknowledges corruption here. Memorization: the lexical pair "framed/shaped" for tzaq/bit is Allen Christenson's signature "Framer and Shaper" (Tedlock: "Maker, Modeler"; Recinos/Goetz-Morley: "Creator/Maker") — grammatically disguised as a passive but still Christenson's distinctive root choice; should be re-rendered independently (e.g. "builder... giver of form" or similar). "Heart of the Sky" is very close to Tedlock/Christenson's "Heart of Sky" but is also the literal sense of "u k'ux kaj," so borderline; the added article gives some independence. Proper names (Hun Ahpu, Xbalanque, Vucub Caquix, Cabracan, Chipi/Raxa Caculha, Zipacna) follow the manuscript orthography, which is acceptable and not a translator-specific choice. "Bird-liners" for the bird-lime hunters ("cazadores de liga") is an independent, defensible rendering.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: "Framed/shaped" for tzaq/bit echoes Christenson's "Framer and Shaper"; "Heart of the Sky" is near Tedlock/Christenson's "Heart of Sky" (borderline, literal).

last_review.issues: Fidelity: the clause "ve nima etamanel hun tzac, hun bit ta chauax oc, ta zaquiroc" is mistranslated as "Truly great is the wisdom of the one who was framed, the one who was shaped" — Tzaqol/B'itol are agent-nouns (the creator: Framer/Shaper; Spanish "es grande sabio el criador"), not the creature; the passive inverts the sense, and "ta chauax oc" (the sowing/planting) is dropped, keeping only the dawning. Minor: "the name of the father" (singular) flattens "qui cahau" where the two fathers Jun Junajpu and Wuqub' Junajpu are meant.
last_review.resemblance_note: "Framed/shaped" for Tzaqol/B'itol lands on Allen Christenson's signature "Framer and Shaper" lexeme — the round-1 fix avoided Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" by adopting another famous translator's word choice (though in a passive construction). "Heart of the Sky" is one article away from Tedlock's "Heart of Sky" but is also the plain rendering of u qux cah (weighed lightly). Untranslated Chipi Caculha / Raxa Caculha and the Ximénez-orthography names follow the Recinos/Goetz-Morley line, acceptable as manuscript-faithful. Other distinctive phrasing reads independent.

paragraphs: Now the third who grew proud was Cabracan, the second son of Vucub Caquix — his name means "earthquake." "I am the one who tears down the mountains," he said. But Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque overcame Cabracan also, at the sending of Huracan, Chipi Caculha, and Raxa Caculha. "Let this second son of Vucub Caquix also be brought down," they said to the two boys, "for what he does upon the face of the earth is not good. He reaches beyond his measure, and it must not be so. Draw him out and lead him to where the sun rises." So spoke Huracan to the two boys. "It is well," they answered, "for what we see is not right. Are you not first, O Heart of the Sky?" So the boys replied to what Huracan had told them. Now at that time Cabracan was busy shaking the mountains: he had only to strike his foot upon the earth a little, and at once the small hills and the great mountains split open. The two boys came upon him and asked him, "Where are you going, boy?" "Nowhere," he said. "I am only here knocking down mountains, and so I will go on doing forever." Then Cabracan said to Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque, "What is it you have come for? I do not know your faces — what are your names?" "We have no name," they said. "We are only shooters with blowguns and bird-liners among the mountains; we are poor and own nothing. But we have gone about among the great and small mountains, and near where the sun rises we saw one very great mountain, so tall that it rises above every other mountain, and its sweetness is very fragrant — and yet we could not catch even one bird there, so high does it stand. Is it true, as they say, that you can bring down every mountain?" So Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque spoke to Cabracan. "Is that true? Where is this mountain you speak of? I will see it and knock it flat. Where did you see it?" "Over there," they said, "where the sun rises." "Good," said Cabracan, "lead the way." "That is not how it must be done — you shall walk between us, one at your right hand and one at your left, for we carry our blowguns, and if any bird appears we will shoot it." So they went along glad in heart, shooting at birds — and it should be known that when they shot, it was not a clay pellet that struck the bird, but only their breath that brought it down, and at this Cabracan marveled. Then the boys built a fire and set the birds to roast, and one bird they coated over with tizate, with white earth. "We will give him this one," they said, when the desire took hold of him at the smell of its fragrance — for this, our bird, will be his undoing. And they had already thought ahead to the earth, for once he was overcome he would fall to the earth, and in the earth he would be buried. Truly he is a great knower, the builder, the one who raises things and gives them their being, when the planting is done, when the dawn is born — so the boys said among themselves, for it was only in their own hearts that this device was carried and worked out; in just this way Cabracan's heart was to be overcome, said Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque to one another. Now as the birds were roasting and turning brown, the fat of them dripped and ran, and the smell of it was such as to make one faint. Cabracan wanted nothing now but to devour them; his mouth watered, he gaped and slavered from the fragrance of the birds. Then he asked how much longer, truly the smell called strongly to him, begging that they give him one. And so they gave Cabracan the bird, the one prepared for his defeat, and when he had swallowed it they set out again and came at last to where the sun rises, where the great mountain stood.

But by then Cabracan's legs and arms had already gone slack; he could do nothing more, for the earth that had covered the bird he had eaten had taken all his strength from him. Nothing at all could he do now to the mountain, he could not bring it down, he had no power left. Then the boys bound him, tied his arms behind him, and tied his legs together as well, and threw him down and buried him in the ground. In this way Cabracan was overcome by Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque alone. Nothing could stand against what these two did here upon the face of the earth.
