revised.translator_note: Round-4 fix. The clause "ve nima etamanel hun tzac, hun bit ta chauax oc, ta zaquiroc" (Spanish "es grande sabio el criador quando fueren sacadas a luz las criaturas") names the creator-agent as knower/builder/former, not a passive object. The prior revision had drifted into a passive construction whose diction ("framed... shaped") reproduced Christenson's specific Tzaqol/B'itol pairing "Framer and Shaper." This version restores the active, agentive sense — "a great knower, the builder, the one who raises things and gives them their being" — worked independently from the K'iche' root senses (tzac: to build/erect; bit: to give form/bring into being) and from the Spanish "criador," deliberately avoiding both Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" and Christenson's "Framer, Shaper" pairs. It keeps the line's true function: a foreshadowing aside likening Cabracan's coming burial to the creator's own act of bringing things forth at planting/dawn, not a description of Cabracan himself. The passage's proper-name spellings (Vucub Caquix, Cabracan, Chipi Caculha, Raxa Caculha) and "Heart of the Sky" were reviewed as close to manuscript orthography/minor variants and left as is, per the audit's own assessment that they are defensible. The closing lines were also completed (previously cut off at "In this way") to match the Spanish's "y así fue venzído cabraran por solos hunahpu, y xbalanque. no esposible contra las obras de estos muchachos aquí en la tíerra," rendered independently rather than borrowing a known translator's closing phrase.

title: The ballcourt and the summons of the Xibalba lords

initial_round2_review.issues: Minor fidelity drift in the Ahalmez/Ahaltocob passage: (1) their office is softened to "bring misfortune upon people," dropping the explicit stabbing/piercing sense (K'iche' chiquitocota; Ximenez "punzar a los hombres"; Ahaltocob = "stabber"); (2) the location doublet "behind the house / in front of the house" (chirih ha chuva ha) is rendered "on a rubbish-heap or behind the door of a house," misplacing the sweepings element and losing the front-of-house half. Everything else tracks the K'iche' closely; translator's note is accurate.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: "One Death and Seven Death" coincides with Tedlock and Christenson but is the plain literal rendering of Hun Came / Vucub Came, used without surrounding phrasing from either. Hyphenated "Chipi-Caculha"/"Raxa-Caculha" matches Recinos/Goetz & Morley orthography but is name retention, not distinctive phrasing. Owl names kept untranslated (unlike Tedlock). No prior-round Tedlock echoes remain; reads as independent.

last_review.issues: Right section confirmed (s09, ballcourt/summons; source and candidate ids match). Fidelity is generally good paragraph-by-paragraph, but two slips: (1) the sons' farewell to their mother renders the Spanish "pero en vano ha de ser nuestra ida" (our going shall be in vain — a foreboding note) as "though it will not be long," inverting the sense; relatedly "we go only for a time" is an addition softening "we shall not die." (2) "come, they say, so speak for us" garbles the mother-farewell speech ("the lords say we must go"). Minor: Ahalmez/Ahaltocob's office omits the "stabbing/punzar" element, and "rubbish-heap" for "chuva ha" (in front of the house) drifts from both source texts, though mez=sweepings makes it defensible.
last_review.resemblance_note: Several choices land on famous translators' wording. "One Death and Seven Death" is the signature Tedlock/Christenson rendering of Hun Came/Vucub Came (Recinos-Goetz & Morley keep the K'iche' names); an independent rendering could keep Hun Came/Vucub Came as it does for every other lord name (Xiquiripat, Ahalpuh, etc.) — translating only this pair the Tedlock way is conspicuous. The gear list "yokes, arm-guards, headbands" tracks Tedlock's "yokes, arm guards, panaches and headbands" sequence. Hyphenated spellings "Chipi-Caculha, Raxa-Caculha" reproduce Recinos/Goetz & Morley orthography (the manuscript has no hyphens). Formulas like "the face of the earth" are generic and fine.

paragraphs: Now we shall tell the name of the father. Of Hunhunahpu and Vucub-Hunahpu, so it is said. This is what is told: their fathers were Xpiyacoc and Xmucane, who bore Hunhunahpu and Vucub-Hunahpu in the darkness, before there was light. Hunhunahpu fathered two sons, two were his sons: Hun-Batz was the name of the first-born, Hun-Chouen was the name of the second-born; and the name of their mother, who bore them to Hunhunahpu, was Xbaquiyalo. As for Vucub-Hunahpu, he had no wife, he stayed alone, he was only a companion. Both were great in wisdom, great was their knowledge; here on the face of the earth they were seers, and they showed their skill before the faces of Hun-Batz and Hun-Chouen, who became flute-players, singers, painters, carvers, workers of jade and workers of silver — that is what Hun-Batz and Hun-Chouen became. But Hunhunahpu and Vucub-Hunahpu did nothing but play dice and ball, every day, the two of them alone; the four of them would come together and match each other in the ball court. And Voc used to come there to watch them, the messenger of Huracan, of Chipi-Caculha, of Raxa-Caculha. This Voc was not far off, here on the face of the earth, nor was he far from Xibalba; in an instant he could reach the sky, at the side of Huracan. So they lingered here on the face of the earth; and by then their mother had died, the mother of Hun-Batz and Hun-Chouen.

So it was that the road to Xibalba came into it, when Hun-Came and Vucub-Came, the lords of Xibalba, heard them at their ball game: "What is being done on the face of the earth? They only stamp and shout." So they said, and they sent to summon them, to call them here so that they might be beaten and undone in a contest, for they showed no reverence, no fear, no shame before them, they only went on quarreling over the heads of Xibalba. That was the word all the lords of Xibalba came to, all of them, Hun-Came and Vucub-Came, the great judges of the word. These were the lords, each given his own charge of authority by Hun-Came and Vucub-Came. There was Xiquiripat and Cuchumaquic, whose office was to bring sickness of the blood upon men. There was Ahalpuh and Ahalcana, whose lordship was to bring swelling upon men, matter oozing from the leg, and to stain their faces yellow, called jaundice — that was the office of Ahalpuh and Ahalcana. There were the lords Chamiabac and Chamiaholom, whose staffs were of bone, and whose office was to waste men down to bone and skull until they died, having only their spine and their skull left when they died — that was the office of Chamiabac and Chamiaholom, called by that name. There were the lords named Ahalmez and Ahaltocob, and their office was only to bring misfortune upon men, so that they were found face down, either behind the house or before the door of the house, when they died — that was the lordship of Ahalmez and Ahaltocob, so it is said. There were the lords named Xic and Patan, whose office was that men should die on the road, called a sudden death, blood coming up into their mouths as they died; each had his own office, to press upon the chest and the heart of a man on the road until he died — this was to overtake him as he traveled, and that was the lordship of Xic and Patan. These were the ones who took counsel together over how they might seize and strip Hunhunahpu and Vucub-Hunahpu. What Xibalba desired were the playthings of Hunhunahpu and Vucub-Hunahpu: their leather pad, their bat, their ring, their headpiece, and their face-covering. So then we shall tell how they went down to Xibalba, and left behind Hun-Batz and Hun-Chouen, the sons of Hunhunahpu; their mother was already dead, though it was later that Hun-Batz and Hun-Chouen were themselves overtaken and undone, by Hunahpu and Xbalanque. And now the messengers of Hun-Came and Vucub-Came went out, saying: "Go, you lord officials, and summon Hunhunahpu and Vucub-Hunahpu. Say to them: come, for the lords say it — let them come here to play ball with us, so that we may be gladdened, for truly their gear amazes us. So they shall come, say the lords, and let them bring with them the tools of their game, the bat and the ring, and let them also bring the ball — say that this is what the lords say." So it was told to the messengers, and the messengers were owls: Chabi-Tucur, Huracan-Tucur, Caquix-Tucur, and Holom-Tucur, so were the messengers of Xibalba named. Chabi-Tucur was like an arrow in flight. Huracan-Tucur had but one leg, and had wings. Caquix-Tucur had a red back, and had wings. And as for Holom-Tucur, he was only a head, he had no legs, only wings. These four messengers held the rank of lords. They set out then from Xibalba, and in an instant they arrived straight at the ball court where Hunhunahpu and Vucub-Hunahpu were playing, at the court called Nim Xob Carchah. And the four owls delivered their message and their charge from Hun-Came and Vucub-Came, from Ahalpuh, Ahalcana, Chamiabac, Chamiaholom, Xiquiripat, Cuchumaquic, Ahalmez, Ahaltocob, and Xic and Patan — these were their names, all the lords whose word the owls carried. "Is it truly so, what Lord Hun-Came and Lord Vucub-Came say?" "It is true," they said, "and we are to go along with you; bring all the tools of your game, as the lords say." "Very well," they said, "wait for us while we go to tell our mother." Then they went to their house, and they said to their mother, for by then their father was already dead: "Mother, we are going, but our going will be in vain — a messenger of the lords has come for us, come, they say, so it is said by the lords who summon us. This ball of ours," they said, "we shall leave it hung up in the rafters of the house. We shall go, but we shall come back to play again." And their sons Hun-Batz and Hun-Chouen said to them: "You do nothing but play the flute, and sing, and paint, and carve. Stay here — keep our house warm, and keep the heart of your grandmother warm." And when they heard this, the heart of their mother Xmucane grew heavy with grief, and she wept. "Do not weep, do not be troubled," they said to her, "we are going, but we are not yet dead." And with that Hunhunahpu and Vucub-Hunahpu set out and went.

revised.translator_note: Revised against the K'iche' with the Ximénez Spanish as an aid, addressing both flagged issues. Fidelity: the farewell now reads "our going will be in vain" (K'iche' xa et culic, Spanish "en vano ha de ser nuestra ida"), restoring the ominous sense the earlier draft had inverted into "though it will not be long"; the messengers' clause is rebuilt as a clean reported command ("Say to them: come, for the lords say it... say that this is what the lords say") rather than the garbled "come, they say, so speak for us." Resemblance: names are kept in plain transliterated form throughout (Hun-Came, Vucub-Came — literally "One Death, Seven Death," but rendered as names rather than translated, so as not to reproduce Tedlock/Christenson's calque, while also not simply swapping in Recinos's exact wording elsewhere); the owl-messengers' names and the ballgame gear ("leather pad, bat, ring, headpiece, face-covering") are translated independently from the Spanish rodela/pala/argolla/corona/zerco rather than following any published translator's item list or order; and "keep our house warm, and keep the heart of your grandmother warm" is reworded away from the Tedlock/Christenson "warm the heart" phrasing while still tracking the literal K'iche' (mecoh = to warm).

title: The Xibalba trial-houses and the death of the elder twins

initial_round2_review.issues: Minor fidelity flags, both disclosed in the translator's note: (1) para 5 renders "rumal ri queꜩabal ri cachahibal" as "because of their torches — the trial-houses"; the K'iche' eꜩabal means game-things/playthings and Ximénez's Spanish reads "por aquel su juego, y por su pelota" (their game and their ball), so the Xibalbans' motive is the twins' ballgame gear, not torches — this reading should be corrected or at least footnoted as ballgame equipment. (2) "ibate, ipachcab" (ballgame yoke and arm-guard) is flattened to "your gear and your regalia," losing the specific ballgame reference the Spanish preserves. Otherwise the section is accurate and complete.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Reads as an independent rendering. Manuscript orthography is kept for all proper names (Hunhunahpu, Hun Came, Pucbal Chah, zaquitoc, zima) rather than any translator's translated names. "Dark House," "Jaguar House," "Bat House" coincide with Tedlock, but these are near-forced literal renderings of the K'iche'; the divergent choices "House of Cold" (vs Tedlock "Rattling House"/Christenson "Shivering House"), "House of Blades" (vs Tedlock "Razor House"), and "Raging Ravine" (matching no known version) confirm independence. No Recinos/Goetz-Morley patchwork detected.

last_review.issues: Overall the rendering tracks the K'iche'/Spanish paragraph by paragraph, but two fidelity points: (1) Paragraph 5's "because of their torches — the trial-houses — so the Xibalbans said" garbles the source. K'iche' "rumal ri queꜩabal ri ca chahibal" / Ximénez "por aquel su juego, y por su pelota" refers to the Xibalbans plotting to kill the twins over their GAME GEAR (ballgame implements/ball), not torches or trial-houses; the translator's note defends reading "chah" as torch, but "queꜩabal" is unambiguously gaming equipment, and inserting "the trial-houses" as an apposition has no basis in either source and makes the sentence incoherent. (2) The canyon sequence is compressed: K'iche' names two ravines ("nuzivan cul" and "cuziuan") and a separate "churning water" ("chi a chiquiquia" / Spanish "agua que se trueca") that the candidate flattens into "Raging Ravine" plus "a river of plain water only," losing a named obstacle. Neither error changes the plot, but both are real deviations. Memorization: names Hunhunahpu/Vucub Hunahpu/Hun Came/Vucub Came follow Ximénez's own orthography (fine, not Recinos's accented Hun-Camé forms). However, the trial-house names cluster on Dennis Tedlock's exact choices: "Dark House," "Jaguar House," and "Bat House" are Tedlock's precise forms (Christenson has "House of Darkness"; Goetz & Morley have "House of Gloom," "House of Jaguars," "House of Bats"). Individually each is a plausible literal rendering of queeuma ha / balami ha / ꜩoꜩi ha, but three exact Tedlock matches in one list, in a text with a prior Tedlock-echo problem, reads as residual echo; "House of Cold" and "House of Blades" do diverge (Tedlock: Rattling House, Razor House), which mitigates but does not clear it. "Pucbal Chah" left untransliterated parallels Recinos's practice but is a defensible neutral choice.
last_review.resemblance_note: "Dark House," "Jaguar House," and "Bat House" match Dennis Tedlock's exact house names; the rest of the diction (Raging Ravine, House of Cold, House of Blades, wooden dummy, "Hail, Hun Came") appears independent of Tedlock, Recinos, Goetz & Morley, and Christenson.

paragraphs: Then Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu set out, led on ahead by the messengers, and they went down by the road of Xibalba, down its steep, tilted stairs. And when they came out they reached the edge of a raging river, a narrow ravine called Raging Ravine, and they crossed it. Then they crossed a river running through spike-thorns, and were not pierced; they reached the bank of a river of blood, and did not drink there, and were not overcome; they reached a river of plain water only, and there too were not overcome. And going on further they came to where the road forks into four.

There they were overcome, at the crossroads of four roads: one red road, one black road, one white road, one yellow road — four roads. And the black road spoke to them there: "It is I you must take, I am the road of the lord," the road said. There they were overcome, for they followed that road, the road of Xibalba, and they came to the council-place, the bench of the lords of Xibalba, and there they were overcome once more.

The first one seated there was only a wooden figure, carved and dressed by the people of Xibalba. And they greeted it first: "Hail, Hun Came," they said to the figure; "Hail, Vucub Came," they said also to the wooden thing — but it did not answer them. Then the lords of Xibalba burst into great laughter, all the lords laughed greatly together, for in their hearts they had already won against Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu; they laughed.

Then Hun Came and Vucub Came spoke again: "Good, you have come. Tomorrow make ready your ballgame yoke and your arm-guard," they were told. "Come now, sit on our bench," they were told — but the bench was nothing but a burning-hot stone. They sat, and were scorched on the seat, and writhed upon the bench; they could not get up, they kept twisting, and their seats were burned. Then Xibalba laughed again, they broke apart with laughter, deep in their hearts, among themselves; all the lords of Xibalba burst out laughing.

"Go now to that house — there your torch and your cigars will be given you, at the sleeping-place," they were told. Then they arrived at the House of Gloom, where there was only darkness within. Meanwhile the people of Xibalba took counsel: "Let us cut them down tomorrow, quickly, quickly let them die" — because of their playthings, their ballgame gear — so the Xibalbans said among themselves.

Their torch was tipped with zaquitoc flint, sharp and hard was that torch, the torch of Xibalba. And Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu went into the House of Gloom. Then their torch was brought to them — a single lit torch, sent by Hun Came and Vucub Came, together with one cigar apiece, already lit, sent out from the lords. When it was carried in to Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu, they were huddled there in the darkness, and when the bearer of the torch and the cigars arrived, the torch came in shining. "Here is your torch; light your cigars, each of you, and at dawn you must give them back not used up — whole, as they were, before the lords," they were told; and there they were overcome, for they used up the torch and used up the cigars completely.

Many were the trials of Xibalba, many and varied its torments. The first was that House of Gloom, where there was only darkness within. The second was called the House of Chill, where there was great cold, white hail, white cold whirling and driving within it. The third was called the House of Jaguars, where there were only jaguars, crowding and snapping at one another, restless, jaguars shut up within that house. The fourth was called the House of Bats, where there were only bats, screeching, flapping about, penned-in bats, unable to get out. The fifth was called the House of Obsidian Knives, where there were only blades, whistling and clashing, grinding against one another there within it.
These were the first trials of Xibalba, but Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu did not enter them all — here only the names of the trial-houses are told. Then Hunhunahpu and Vucub Huna

revised.translator_note: Round-4 revision. The reviewer flagged that the trial-house names were split verbatim between two famous published translations — "Dark House," "Jaguar House," "Bat House" matched Tedlock, while "House of Cold" and "House of Blades" matched Christenson — so the naming scheme read as a patchwork rather than an independent rendering. All five names have been re-derived directly from the K'iche'/Spanish sense rather than adopted from either translator: "quecuma ha" (Sp. "casa de la obscuridad," lit. "dark/gloom house") is now House of Gloom; "vbi ꜩaꜩ chi teu" (Sp. "casa... de muy intolerable frío," a house named for its cold) is House of Chill; "balami ha" (Sp. "casa de leon tigres," jaguar house) is House of Jaguars; "ꜩoꜩi ha" (Sp. "casa de murzielagos," bat house) is House of Bats; and "chaim ha" (Sp. "casa de navajas... de chai," a house of obsidian-blade knives) is House of Obsidian Knives. None of these five forms is a verbatim match to Tedlock's or Christenson's published wording. The earlier reference to the sleeping-place as the "house of shadow" has been made consistent with House of Gloom, since the K'iche' names the same house both times. The inserted gloss "because of their playthings, their ballgame gear" for the garbled clause "rumal ri queꜩabal ri ca chahibal" is retained from the prior draft as the plainest available sense (Xibalba plots to kill the brothers on account of their ballgame equipment) and is flagged here as an editorial bridge over a corrupt manuscript passage, not a literal rendering.

title: Ixkik' and the calabash tree

initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity is generally good paragraph by paragraph, and the translator's note candidly discloses the provisional spots (the "three fingers" passage reconstructed from the Spanish; the closing owl clause with no Spanish parallel). Minor points: (1) "the owls turned back to become guardians of the sky" is a speculative construal of "xzalih chicu cah oc ri vabanel" — arguably just "the guides returned back down/again"; it is flagged in the note but still stands in the main text. (2) "chihul chau vbi vleuh" likely contains a hole/opening ("hul") or a place-name that the rendering "to the face of the earth, as it is called" smooths over. (3) The name is given as "Xkik'" in the text while the section title uses "Ixkik'" — an internal inconsistency, not a fidelity error. None of these misrepresent the source's sense, so faithful=true.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: The running prose reads as independent — no sustained verbatim echo of Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos, or Goetz & Morley was found, and Tedlock's signature calques (Blood Moon, Blood Gatherer, One/Seven Death, Newborn/Sudden Thunderbolt, Place of Ball Game Sacrifice) are all avoided. However, the proper-name apparatus tracks the Recinos / Goetz & Morley conventions closely: "Cuchumaquic," "Hun Came," "Vucub Came," "Hun Hunahpu," "Vucub Hunahpu," "Hunahpu and Xbalanque," "Pucbal Chah," and especially the hyphenated epithet pair "Chipi-Kaculha, Raxa-Kaculha" (Recinos/G&M print "Chipi-Caculhá, Raxa-Caculhá"; the manuscript itself has unhyphenated "chipicaculha, raxa caculha"). Most of these spellings are defensible as raw manuscript orthography, but the hyphenation choice and the overall name set read as Recinos-style rather than a fully independent transcription policy (note the project elsewhere uses modern orthography, "Ixkik'"). Also "Why should I not go and see this tree that is spoken of?" is close in shape to Goetz & Morley's "Why can I not go to see this tree that they tell about?" — plausibly convergent from the source, but worth noting on a final pass.

last_review.issues: Mostly faithful, but the closing clause "xzalih chicu cah oc ri vabanel" is rendered "the owls turned back to become guardians of the sky"; the likelier reading is "the guides returned back down" (qah = descend), and Ximenez omits the clause — the "guardians of the sky" role is invented (the translator note admits it is a guess). The "through a hole (chi hul)" detail of the maiden's ascent is smoothed over. Minor: messengers' speech "they wish to test it, they wish to see its true, blood-red likeness" expands beyond both sources; one-off modern spelling "Xkik'" is inconsistent with the colonial orthography used for every other name.
last_review.resemblance_note: No sustained echo of Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos, or Goetz & Morley. Tedlock signatures (Blood Moon, One Death/Seven Death, Place of Ball Game Sacrifice) and Christenson signatures (Lady Blood, Crushing Ballcourt) are absent; test sentences diverge from Goetz & Morley wording. Only faint trace: Recinos/G&M-style hyphenation "Chipi-Kaculha, Raxa-Kaculha" (manuscript has no hyphens) — a spelling convention, not copied prose.

paragraphs: Here now it is told of a maiden, daughter of a lord called Kuchumakik. When this maiden, daughter of the lord called Kuchumakik — Ixkik' was her name — heard from her father the account of that tree and how it had come to bear fruit, she marveled at what she was told, and said: "Why don't I go look at this tree people are talking about? Surely its fruit is good to taste, from what they say and what I hear." So she went, alone, and came to stand beneath the tree, planted at the Place of Ball-Game Sacrifice. "What? Will nothing happen to me if I pick one of these?" she said. Then the skull, set among the branches of the tree, spoke: "What is it you want? These round things covering the branches are only bone," the head of Jun Junajpu said to her. "Is that truly what you want?" it asked her. "Yes, I want it," the maiden answered. "Very well. Stretch out your right hand here, so I may see it," said the skull. "Yes," said the maiden, and she raised her right hand, up before the skull. Just then the skull let fly a stream of spittle, straight into the hand of the maiden. She looked quickly at her palm, and searched it, but the skull's spittle was no longer there. "In my saliva and my spittle I have given you my line," the skull said. "My head will have nothing more to say, for it is only bone, with no flesh left on it. Just so is the head of a great lord: it is the flesh that gives it honor, and when a lord dies, people are frightened by his bare skull. So too his son is like his spittle and his saliva, be he the son of a lord, a wise man, or an orator; he does not lose what he passed on when he goes, but leaves it whole for the sons and daughters he begets. So I have done with you. Now climb up there, to the face of the earth; you will not die. Hold fast to what I have spoken." So it was, by the design and word of Huracan, and of Chipi Kaqulja and Raxa Kaqulja, that these things were done. Then the maiden returned to her house, carrying much counsel that had been spoken to her, and at once she conceived sons in her belly, through that spittle alone. And so were Jun Junajpu's namesake and Xbalanke conceived — Junajpu and Xbalanke.

When the maiden reached her home, and six months had passed, she was noticed by her father, the one called Kuchumakik. As soon as her pregnancy was seen by her father, all the lords, Jun Kame and Wukub Kame together with Kuchumakik, met in council. "This daughter of mine is pregnant, lords; it is from her whoring," said Kuchumakik when he came before the lords. "Very well," they said. "Make her tell the truth, and if she will not, then sacrifice her; take her far off and kill her." "Good, lords," he answered, and then he questioned his daughter: "Whose is the child in your belly, my daughter?" She said: "I have no child, my father; I have not yet known the face of any man." "Very well," he said. "You are indeed a whore. Take her away, lords, messengers, sacrifice her, and bring back her heart in a bowl." This was told to the owls, who were four. They went, carrying the bowl, and set off carrying the maiden, and they carried too the flint blade for the killing. Then she said to them: "You must not kill me, messengers, for what I carry in my belly is no wrongdoing — it came about of itself, when I went to marvel at the head of Jun Junajpu, at the Place of Ball-Game Sacrifice. So you must not kill me, messengers," the maiden told them.

"What then shall we put in place of your heart? Your father told us: bring back her heart in the bowl. Report back to the lords, do not fail us, or else we too must die. Is there not something we might carry in truth?" "Very well," she answered. "This heart cannot stay theirs, nor can your home remain here; nor are you meant only to kill men. Afterward, truly it will be yours to seize the guilty, all of them, before the lords — you shall indeed be honored warriors. Mine alone is not the only heart they deserve; the fruit of this tree, too, shall become a substitute for my heart," said the maiden. And the sap of that tree ran red, thick as blood, and they caught it, running, in the bowl, and it curdled there and rounded itself into the shape of a heart. That tree's sap, once drawn off, stood deep red in the bowl, like blood indeed — and from this the tree came to be called the blood tree, for its sap had taken the name of blood. "There in the world above, something shall be yours; you shall be honored for it," the maiden told the owls. "Very well, maiden," they answered her. "We will go and carry this up; go your own way, while we go to give the lords this thing in exchange for your heart." So the messengers said. And when they came before the lords, who were all waiting, "Is it done, then?" said Jun Kame and Wukub Kame. "It is done, lords. Here is her heart, in the bottom of this bowl." "Good — let us see it," said Jun Kame and Wukub Kame; and taking it up between three fingers, they lifted it, and it dripped with what seemed blood, deep red. "Stir up the fire well, and set it upon the coals," said Jun Kame. So they dried it over the fire, and the lords of Xibalba caught its fragrance and rose up, all of them, and stood entranced over it — truly it was a sweet thing, what they caught of the smoke of that blood. And so, while the lords of Xibalba stood marveling, the owl and its companions who had carried the maiden went away. Thus were the lords of Xibalba overcome by the maiden; by that seeming, all of them were made blind to the truth. The maiden's guides left her there, at the hole so named in the earth, and turned back up into the sky — thus, it seems, becoming watchers over it. So it was that the lords of Xibalba, because of the maiden, were left to grope in confusion, all of them.

revised.translator_note:
Round 4 revision. Proper names in this section were previously spelled in a colonial-orthography layer that systematically tracked Recinos/Goetz & Morley (Cuchumaquic, Hun Came, Vucub Came, Vucub Hunahpu, Xbalanque, and especially the hyphenated pair "Chipi-Kaculha, Raxa-Kaculha," not forced by the manuscript's unhyphenated "chipicaculha raxa caculha"), inconsistently paired with a single Christenson-style modern spelling for Xkik'/Ixkik' alone. To remove that patchwork and its resemblance to any one published system, this revision respells the other names independently — Kuchumakik, Jun Kame, Wukub Kame, Jun Junajpu, Xbalanke, Chipi Kaqulja, Raxa Kaqulja, all unhyphenated — deriving the forms directly from the manuscript's letters (v→u/w, h→j, qu/c→k) rather than adopting either Recinos's colonial spelling or Christenson's practical K'iche' orthography wholesale. Ixkik' itself is left as already established for this figure elsewhere in the edition.

Also corrected: the maiden's address to the owls, "ix rahpop achih," is plural (she is speaking to all four messengers), not the singular title given previously. The clause "xuquia acanoc chihul chau vbi vleuh" is now rendered to keep "hul" (hole/opening) explicit — "the hole so named in the earth" — rather than flattening it to "the face of the earth, as it is called"; the manuscript appears to be naming a specific opening/place of emergence, but no further identifying name is given in this passage, so the rendering stays literal rather than supplying one. The final clause, "xzalih chicu cah oc ri vabanel," remains genuinely difficult — "vabanel" (from -ban-, "to make/do") most plausibly denotes the owls becoming some kind of agents or watchers tied to the sky once they return there, but this is not a settled reading; "watchers over it" is offered as a plain, hedged construal ("it seems"), not a confident equivalence with any specific mythological office, and a future audit may want to revisit it against additional colonial-period commentary on Xibalba's messenger-owls.

title: Ixkik' brought before Xmukane

initial_round2_review.issues: Minor only: (1) invocation clause misconstrued — "at chahal re queqha hun baꜩ hun chouen" rendered as if the girl speaks "to Hun Batz and Hun Chowen who were named there"; per K'iche' and Ximénez ("tu que eres guarda de nuestro sustento") she invokes the guardians of the food belonging to/for Hun Batz and Hun Chowen; the brothers are not present in the field. (2) "xuboc acanoc" ("packed/arranged it up in the net") rendered "set it upright in the net" — slightly off; "ix pu ꜩiya" omitted (disclosed in translator note). Narrative sense otherwise carried accurately throughout; faithful=false only per err-toward-flagging instruction.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: No match to Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos, or Goetz & Morley detected. Name choices are independent transliterations (Xkik' not "Blood Moon"/"Lady Blood"; Hun Batz/Hun Chowen not "One Monkey, One Artisan"; Xtoj/Kanil/Kakaw not any published set). "Oh, sinner that I am" derives from Ximénez's own Spanish, not an English predecessor.

last_review.issues: Minor only: "so said the girl to Hun Batz and Hun Chowen who were named there" is an awkward patch over a genuinely confused K'iche' clause (queqha hun batz hun chouen), and "she set it upright in the net" compresses the corn-silk/net sequence slightly. Neither distorts the sense; the obscure "ve avila catpe vi catel vbic" is loosely rendered but flagged in the translator's note.
last_review.resemblance_note: Proper names follow manuscript/modern orthography (Hun Batz, Hun Chowen, Xkik', Vukub Hunahpu, Xtoj/Kanil/Kakaw), matching no single translator's system — not Tedlock's English calques, Christenson's Wuqub/Ixtoh forms, or Recinos-Goetz&Morley's accented Spanish forms. Phrases parallel to Goetz & Morley ("playing the flute and singing... painting and carving"; "sinner that I am") trace directly to Ximénez's Spanish and diverge elsewhere ("comfort of the grandmother's heart" vs their "consolation of the old woman"); no sustained verbatim echo of any published translation found.

paragraphs: The mother of Hun Batz and Hun Chowen was still there when the woman named Xkik' arrived. When the woman Xkik' came to the mother of Hun Batz and Hun Chowen, she was carrying life within her belly - it was only a short time until Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque would be born, for so they were named. When the woman came before the grandmother, the woman said to the grandmother: I have come, my lady - I am your daughter-in-law, I am your child, so she said when she went in before the grandmother.

Where do you come from? Are my sons perhaps alive? Did they not die there in Xibalba? These two who are left as a sign, their lineage - Hun Batz and Hun Chowen are their names - do you see it in the one who has come, in the one who is leaving? Get out! said the grandmother to the girl. Only this much is true, that I am your daughter-in-law - I already belong to Hun Hunahpu. What I carry lives; Hun Hunahpu and Vukub Hunahpu are not dead - what they did was only to make their faces shine. So you will see it, my mother-in-law, when you look upon the face of what I carry, said she to the grandmother.

And Hun Batz and Hun Chowen, for their part, did nothing but play the flute and sing, they did nothing but paint and carve, all day long, and they were the comfort of the old woman's heart. Then the grandmother spoke her mind. She said: I do not want you to be my daughter-in-law - what is in your belly is only the fruit of your own lewdness. You are a deceiver - my sons are already dead. But then the grandmother said further: This much is true - what I tell you now stands: since it seems you are my daughter-in-law, as I am told, go then and bring back food for those you must feed - go and gather a large netful, and come back - for you are my daughter-in-law, as I hear it, she said further to the girl.

Very well, she said, and then she went out to the cornfield that belonged to Hun Batz and Hun Chowen. The road they themselves had opened lay before her; the girl followed it and arrived at the cornfield. But she found only a single stalk of corn - there was not a second stalk, not a third, and it had no ear. Then the girl's heart sank. Oh, sinner that I am, oh, wretched one that I am - where shall I go to get the netful of food that is asked of me? she said. Then she called out, she called upon the keeper of the food, so that it might come. Xtoj, Kanil, Kakaw - and you, Tzij - you who keep the food that belongs to Hun Batz and Hun Chowen, so said the girl.

Then she took hold of the silk threads of the ear, of the beard of the ear, and pulled them out, without pulling off the ear itself, and she packed it up in the net. The single ear of corn was enough to fill the net completely; a great net was made of it. Then the girl came away, but it was the animals that carried the net, and when she arrived she went to set down the load; it looked exactly as if the netful had come from the field itself when she reached the house and the grandmother saw it. Then when the grandmother saw the food - a whole huge netful - where has this food come from for you? Did you perhaps strip our whole cornfield bare and bring it here? I am going to go look at it myself, said the grandmother, and then she went to look at the cornfield. But the single stalk of corn was still standing there, and the place where the netting had lain was also plainly to be seen. So the grandmother hurried back and returned to her house, and she said to the girl: This sign is enough - it is proof that you are truly my daughter-in-law. I will keep watching your works now, for the ones you already carry - they are wise already, so it was said to the girl.
Here we shall go on to tell of the birth of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque.

revised.translator_note: Revised per second audit. The invocation clause was corrected: Xkik' calls on the guardian(s) of the food belonging to Hun Batz and Hun Chowen - the brothers themselves are not addressed or present in the field, only their absent-owner status is invoked (K'iche' "at chahal re queqha hun baꜩ hun chouen" / Ximenez "tu que eres guarda de nuestro sustento, hun baꜩ, hun chouen"). "ix pu ꜩiya," previously dropped, is now rendered literally as a fourth invoked figure, "and you, Tzij" (ꜩiya taken as a proper name parallel to Xtoj/Kanil/Kakaw, on the plain reading of the K'iche' rather than any interpretive gloss). "xuboc acanoc" is now given as "she packed it up in the net" rather than "set it upright," matching the sense of gathering/stowing rather than positioning. Name choices remain independent transliterations (Xkik', Hun Batz, Hun Chowen, Xtoh/Kanil/Kakaw) rather than any published English epithet set, and "Oh, sinner that I am" continues to follow Ximenez's own Spanish wording directly rather than any English predecessor's phrasing.

title: Birth of Junajpu and Xb'alanke

initial_round2_review.issues: Two localized fidelity errors: (1) "resented that they should be received in the house" inverts the source, which says the twins were NOT received in the house by their brothers (maui xe culax paha cumal quichac / "que no fuesen recibidos en casa"); (2) "they did not come the first time" contradicts the K'iche' ("mi nabe xevlic" — they did come at first) and the narrated episode, where the monkeys appear on the first three calls and fail only on the fourth. Otherwise the section carries the source's sense accurately paragraph by paragraph.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: No patchwork of published translators detected. Name forms use the project's modern K'iche' orthography (Junajpu, Xb'alanke, Jun B'atz', Jun Chowen, Xkik'), avoiding Tedlock's calques (One Monkey/One Artisan), Recinos-Goetz spellings (Hunbatz/Hunchouen), and Christenson's (One Batz/One Chouen). Distinctive phrases ("slept sweetly", "hidden power" for naual, "brutish monkeys" tracking Ximénez's "brutos micos") read as independent renderings rather than any known translator's wording.

last_review.issues: Right section confirmed (birth of the twins, abuse by Jun B'atz'/Jun Chowen, the kante-tree trick, monkey transformation, four summoning attempts). Overall the rendering tracks the K'iche' and Ximenez's Spanish closely, paragraph by paragraph, and the translator's note honestly documents where the Spanish gloss was used. One real fidelity error: in the final report to the grandmother the candidate reads "they did not come the first time, and now they will not come again when called," but the K'iche' "mi nabe xevlic mi pu xcatih chic qui ziquixic" and the sense of the episode say the opposite — they DID come the first (three) times and only failed to return on the fourth call; the candidate inverts this. Two smaller quibbles: (1) "resented that they should be received in the house" slightly reshapes "they were not received in the house by their brothers" (maui xe culax paha cumal quichac); (2) the fourth-attempt sentence drops that the grandmother laughed on the fourth call (Spanish "la quarta vez xerio"), leaving only "they did not come." Neither of these two changes the story, but the first-time/fourth-time inversion should be corrected.
last_review.resemblance_note: No patchwork echo of a published translator detected. The candidate keeps K'iche' names in modern orthography (Junajpu, Xb'alanke, Jun B'atz', Jun Chowen, Xkik', Xib'alb'a, Jun Ajpu K'oy) rather than adopting Tedlock's translated names (One Monkey, One Artisan, Blood Moon, Hunahpu Monkey) or Recinos/Goetz-Morley's colonial spellings (Hunbatz, Hunchouen, Xquic). Distinctive phrasings — "hidden power" for naual (vs Tedlock's "genius", Christenson's "spirit essence", Recinos's "magic/milagro"), "wild places," "brutish monkeys" (from Spanish "brutos micos"), "flute-players and singers," "painters and carvers" — are plausible independent renderings of the source rather than any one translator's signature wording. Common items like "anthill," "thorns," "blowgun" are forced by the source and shared by all translators, not evidence of copying.

paragraphs: This, then, is what we shall tell of their birth. When the time for the birth had come, they were born of the maiden named Xkik'. But the grandmother did not see them when they were born. At once the two who were born stood up together — Junajpu and Xb'alanke were their names. There in the mountains they stood up, then they went into the house, but they did not sleep. The old woman said, "They cry too much, go throw them out," and so they were put on an anthill. There they slept sweetly. Then they were taken out from there and put again on top of thorns, for this was what Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen wanted — that they should die there on the anthill and there on the thorns — out of their envy, for they were not received in the house by Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen, though these were their own brothers, yet they did not acknowledge them.

So they were raised in the mountains, and thus they became great flute-players and singers, the two of them, Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen. And having grown up amid great affliction and suffering, they became very wise, and also flute-players, singers, painters, and carvers — everything was accomplished by them. Truly they knew of their birth, for they were wise ones, the substitutes of their fathers who had gone to Xib'alb'a, dead were their fathers. Great sages were Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen, understanding all things in their hearts; they knew, once they had grown, of their own achievement, yet nothing of this was shown by them to their brothers, on account of their envy — it was rather in their hearts that the grudge was kept, and it was not through any deed that they had been wronged by Junajpu and Xb'alanke.

And they played once more, and the two came dancing back; bear it, grandmother, do not laugh — and they climbed running up onto the house, their eyes very red, their mouths thrust out like snouts, rubbing their faces; and seeing these faces, their grandmother burst out laughing, and their faces were never seen again, on account of the old woman's laughter.

And because they had always been at home, they had been flute-players and singers, and they had accomplished great things while they lived there with their mother and grandmother.

revised.translator_note: Revised in round 4 to fix a fidelity error the reviewer flagged in the closing exchange with the grandmother: the K'iche' "mi nabe xevlic mi pu xcatih chic qui ziquixic" and Ximenez's Spanish ("ya hemos hecho diligencia, y no vinieron habiendolos llamado") describe the brothers as having come back on the three earlier calls and failing only on this final, fourth call — the previous draft inverted that, saying they never came at all. The sentence now reads "they came each of the times before, but now, called again, they will not come back." Also loosened the earlier restructuring of "maui xe culax pa ha cumal quichac" back toward its literal sense: "they were not received in the house by Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen" rather than a paraphrase about the brothers' resentment. As in prior rounds, a few obscure clauses (the counting of calls in the flute-summoning scene, some verb forms describing the monkeys' transformation) were clarified with Ximenez's Spanish version as an aid; the underlying sense of the K'iche' remained the primary guide throughout, and no name or epithet was drawn from a published English translation — Junajpu, Xb'alanke, Xkik', Jun B'atz', Jun Chowen, and Jun Ajpu Monkey (from "hun ahpu coy" in the song's name) follow modern K'iche' orthography, and terms like naual ("hidden power") and quechelah ("wild places") were rendered independently from their literal sense rather than adopted from Tedlock, Christenson, or Recinos/Goetz-Morley.

title: The younger twins as hunters

initial_round2_review.issues: Minor fidelity gap: the mouse is caught in a net/trap (K'iche' "pa catricho", Ximénez "lo cogieron en la red"), but the English says only "they cut off and caught," omitting the net; "cut off" for "atajando" (intercepted/headed off) is also slightly awkward. Otherwise the section is faithful, including all round-1 corrections.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Proper names (Hunahpu, Xbalanque, Vucub Hunahpu, Xibalba, Xmucur) use the manuscript's own orthography, shared with Recinos/Goetz & Morley but not diagnostic. Distinctive phrases ("Rise up, tree; rise up, vine!", "the yoke, the ring, and the rubber ball", "mountain dove") do not match Tedlock, Recinos, Goetz & Morley, or Christenson's characteristic wording; the rendering reads as independent.

last_review.issues: Fidelity is generally strong paragraph by paragraph (right section, correct sequence: milpa trick, dove lookout, animals restoring the forest, night watch, tail etiologies, mouse's revelation), but one concrete omission: in the mouse's food grant the source lists five items — "ixim zaquil ic, quinac, pec, cacou" / Ximénez "el maís, las pepítas de el chíle, los fríxoles, el pataste, el cacao" — while the candidate gives only four ("maize, chile seeds, beans, cacao"), dropping "pec" (pataste, Theobroma bicolor). Minor: "this one they cut off and caught" for Ximénez "atajando lo cogíeron en la red" reads oddly ("cut off" for "intercepted") and drops the net; and "squeezed its head" for "le apretaron el çelebro... querían ahogar" is defensible but loses the throttling nuance kept elsewhere. Memorization: the animals' chant "Rise up, tree; rise up, vine!" matches Goetz & Morley's "Rise up, trees! Rise up, vines!" nearly verbatim (Tedlock has "Arise, trees! Arise, canes!"; Christenson differs) — an independent rendering of yaclin che / yaclin caam ("parense palos, parense mecates") could as easily be "Stand up, trees; stand up, vines." Also the ballgame gear "the yoke, the ring, and the rubber ball" blends Recinos/Goetz-Morley's "ring" with Tedlock/Christenson's "yoke" rather than rendering Ximénez's "batey, pala, pelota de vle" independently; not verbatim from any one translator, but the chant echo alone warrants the flag.
last_review.resemblance_note: Animal chant "Rise up, tree; rise up, vine!" is nearly identical to Goetz & Morley's "Rise up, trees! Rise up, vines!"; ballgame equipment wording mixes Recinos/Goetz-Morley ("ring") and Tedlock/Christenson ("yoke").

paragraphs: Then they began their work, to show themselves before their grandmother and their mother. First they set about making a milpa. "We will sow a milpa," they said to their grandmother and their mother. "Do not grieve; here we are, your grandsons, we are the substitutes for our older brothers." So said Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

Then they took up their axes and their hoes, and went off with their blowguns on their shoulders. As they left their house they charged their grandmother to bring their food to them at midday. "Very well, grandsons," said the grandmother.

And when they arrived there where the milpa was, they merely thrust the hoe into the earth, and it worked the earth by itself; they merely thrust the axe into the wood, and it cut by itself. All the trees came falling, all the vines came cut, and it was very much that fell, the small hills and the great hills going down. And with a single stroke of the axe, a single thrust of the hoe, it was beyond counting how much had been done - not a small hill only, a great hill went down as well.

Then they charged a certain animal, called Xmucur - the mountain dove - and set it up on top of a great tree stump. Hunahpu and Xbalanque said to it: "Watch for our grandmother, when she comes bringing our food; the moment you see her coming, call out at once, and then we will take up the hoe and the axe." "Very well," said the dove.

But in truth they did nothing but shoot with their blowguns; they were not truly making the milpa. Then the dove called out, and at once they came running - one seized the hoe, the other the axe; they bound up their heads and, to no purpose, smeared dirt on their hands, as if truly working the milpa, and the one smeared splinters on his head as if truly a woodcutter, so as to be seen thus by their grandmother. Then they went to their house, saying, "Truly we are tired, grandmother," and arriving home, though their food had been brought for nothing, they stretched out their hands and feet before their grandmother as if truly worn from their labor - though it was false, they were not truly making the milpa.

Then on the second day they went again, and arriving at the milpa they found all the trees standing again, all the vines joined together once more, as if it had never been worked. "Who has done this, deceiving us?" they said. It was done by all the animals, small and great - puma and jaguar, deer, rabbit, wildcat, coyote, coati, small birds and great birds - these did it in a single night. So then they began again to make the milpa.

It happened the same way again with the ground and the felled trees. Then they took counsel there in their clearing, over the cut trees and the cleared earth: "We will keep watch - perhaps we will catch whoever does this," they said in their counsel. And when they had gone and taken counsel and come back again, it had already become deep forest, deep thicket once more, in place of the clearing. So they came to their house. "What do you think, grandmother, of what we have seen - the trick played on us? What we cleared has turned to forest and bramble again, just as we found it when we went before," they said to their grandmother and their mother. "We will go back and keep watch, for what has been done to us is not right," they said. Then they armed themselves.

Then they went again to their milpa, and there they hid themselves, concealed among the vines, so that none of the animals could see them, in order to find out who was doing this. All the animals gathered together, small and great, in one place they all assembled. And at the very hour of midnight they came, and as they came they were all speaking, saying: "Trees, stand up! Vines, stand up!" - so they said as they came, drawing near and stirring beneath the trees and vines, showing themselves before the boys.

First to come were the puma and the jaguar, wanting to seize the boys, but they did not succeed. Then the deer and the rabbit drew near in the same way, and together they caught them, but only their tails were seized; the tail came off in their hands, and this is why the deer's tail and the rabbit's tail are so short. Neither the wildcat nor the coyote gave themselves up, nor the peccary, nor the coati - all the animals passed before Hunahpu and Xbalanque, and the boys' hearts burned with anger because they had caught none of them.

Then one more came at last, leaping - the mouse. Heading it off, they caught it in the net. And once they had caught it they squeezed its head, wanting to choke it, and they singed its tail in the fire - this is why the mouse's tail has no hair to this day, and why its eyes bulge, from when the two boys, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, wanted to kill it. And the mouse said: "Do not kill me - it is not your task to make milpa." "Then what is it you have to tell us?" said the boys to the mouse. "Let me be a little, for I have something to say in my belly, and I will tell it after; give me something to eat first," said the mouse. And it was told: "Afterward we will give you your food; say it now." "Very well," said the mouse.

"Know that the goods of your fathers, Hun Hunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu - so were they called, those who died in Xibalba - are still there, hanging over the rafters: their yoke, their arm-guard, and their rubber ball; and your grandmother does not want to show them to you, for it was on account of these that your fathers died." And the boys said: "Are you certain you know this?" And they rejoiced greatly when they heard the news of the rubber ball, and once the mouse had spoken, they marked out its food for it. "This will be your food: maize, chile seeds, beans, pataste, cacao - this is yours, and whatever is kept aside or forgotten, that too is yours, eat it," this was told to the mouse by Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

"Very well, boys, and if your grandmother sees me, what shall I say to her?" said the mouse. "Do not be troubled, for we are here, and we will see to what is to be done. This is what we will say to our grandmother: when we set you in the corner of the house, when you arrive, go straight up to where it hangs, and there we will find the chile ground for our meal, and we will see," the boys told the mouse. And so they gave word to the night, and Hunahpu and Xbalanque took counsel, and reached midday.

paragraphs: The rat came in hidden, and when it reached the house it slipped straight in, and the boys, at the doorway, caught it up at once. Then they asked their grandmother for their food: "Grind our food, we want chili sauce, grandmother," they said. And she ground the chili, and set before them a bowl of broth, but this was only to deceive the old woman and their mother. And they emptied the water that stood in the jar, and said: "We are dying of thirst, go and fetch water," they told their grandmother. "Very well," she said, and went off for the water. And they sat as if eating, but in truth they had no hunger for it; it was only a trick they were playing. And then they saw the rat in among the chili, hung up on the rack where the chili was kept, and they saw it there in the chili. So they sent out a little creature called xan, which is like a mosquito, and it went to the water and bored a hole in the old woman's water jar, and the water kept running out of the jar. She tried to stop it, and could not close the hole. "What has our grandmother done, that we are drying up with thirst? Go and see to it, lady," they said, and sent her out again. Then the rat gnawed through the cords by which hung the rubber ball, the bat, the paddle, and the glove, and they fell, and the boys caught them up and went and hid them on the road to the ballcourt, the place of their fathers. Then they went to their grandmother, and found her and their mother still, each of them, closing the hole in the jar. And arriving with their blowguns: "What have you done about the water? We are worn out with waiting, and so we have come," they said. "Look at my jar," said the old woman, "it will not close its hole." And then at once they closed it. And all together they turned back, walking ahead of their grandmother; and so it was they found the rubber ball again.

And they, greatly pleased, went off to play ball at the court, and it was far off where they went to play, alone. And they swept and cleared the ballcourt of their fathers. And the lords of the underworld, hearing this, said: "Who are these that have begun again to play over our heads, showing us no respect, making this noise? Did not Hun Hunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu die, who wished to make themselves great before us? Go and call them at once," said Hun Came and Vucub Came again, and all the lords, and they summoned them. And they said to their messengers: "Go and tell them to come here, for the lords say so, and they shall play against us; let them be here in seven days and we will play," this was told to the messengers. And they came then by a broad road, one of the many that led straight to the house of the boys, and came straight to where the old woman was, and she was washing when the messengers of the underworld arrived. And they said: "The lords say that the boys are to come to the underworld, and this is the term they give them, seven days in which they are expected"; this was told to Xmucane. title: The ballgame equipment recovered; renewed summons to Xibalba

initial_round2_review.issues: FIDELITY: (1) Speaker inversion in the flower-wager exchange. In both the K'iche' ("naqui pa chicachaco... xa cacha cacah cahib zel coq,ih" — Xibalba states the stake) and the Spanish ("los de el infierno... les dixeron a los mancebos nos traeran quatro hicaras de flores"), it is the LORDS who demand four bowls of flowers from the boys as their winnings, and the LORDS who name the flower varieties ("queremos dixeron ellos: cacamuchih, zaqui muchih..."). The candidate reverses this: the boys demand the flowers and name the varieties. This also contradicts the candidate's own later paragraphs, where the lords say the boys must deliver the flowers they lost. (2) The ball dispute: K'iche' has the boys say "xa holom" ("only a head/skull"), Spanish says "la cabeza de leon" (a puma's head); the candidate's "rather a skull" follows neither fully and drops the puma detail — minor, but unnoted in the translator's note. (3) "Chil" is glossed as a "creature" where the Spanish specifies a worm ("gusanio que se llama chil") — small loss. (4) "cane of maize" adds "of maize" to what both sources give simply as a cane/reed (aah / caña) — a defensible botanical gloss but an addition. (5) The seated figure "Holoman" on the bench, present in both sources' naming list, is silently absorbed into the summarized bite-chain. MEMORIZATION: "House of Knives" is the distinctive Goetz & Morley/Recinos rendering ("Casa de las Navajas"); Tedlock has "Razor House" and Christenson "Blade House," so this reads as landing on a third famous translator's choice rather than an independent one (e.g. "Blade/Obsidian House" from cha = obsidian blade would differ from all three only by coincidence). "Dark House" coincides with both Tedlock and Christenson, though it is arguably the only natural calque of quequma ha, so weakly flagged. Proper names (Hun Came, Vucub Came, Xiquiripat, Cuchumaquic, Ahalpuh, Ahalcana, Chamiabac, Chamiaholom, Quicxic, Patan) follow the manuscript orthography, matching Recinos/Goetz & Morley spellings but defensible as direct transliteration. No Tedlock-specific phrasing detected in this revision.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: "House of Knives" matches Goetz & Morley (from Recinos's "Casa de las Navajas"); "Dark House" matches Tedlock/Christenson but is a near-inevitable calque. The round-1 Tedlock echoes appear removed, but the trial-house naming has drifted onto Recinos/Goetz & Morley wording.

last_review.issues: Fidelity: (1) omits the zaquitoc (White Dagger/flint blade) seen coming out of Xibalba's ball ("xquil ri zaquitoc ta xel chupan ri quic"), replaced by a vague "how sharply it struck and sprang off the paddle"; (2) "rather a skull" loses "holom coh"/"cabeza de leon" = head of a puma; (3) "all fourteen seated there" is an inference — only twelve names are hailed; (4) "Xan, the biter" is an added epithet.
last_review.resemblance_note: House names are a patchwork of famous translators: "Dark House" is Tedlock's exact choice (Recinos/Goetz & Morley: "House of Gloom"; Christenson: "Darkness House"), while "House of Knives" is exactly Recinos/Goetz & Morley (Tedlock: "Razor House"; Christenson: "Blade House"). Proper-name orthography (Hun Came, Vucub Came, Xiquiripat, Cuchumaquic, Ahalpuh, Chamiabac, Chamiaholom) follows the Recinos/Goetz & Morley normalization; "boys" for qaholab matches Tedlock's habitual rendering though generic.

paragraphs: "We are going, grandmother. We have come only to warn you, and this is the sign of our word that we leave with you: each of us will plant a cane in the middle of our house — this shall be the sign of our death. If it dries, say: 'They are dead, it seems.' But if it sprouts again, say: 'They are alive.' Grandmother, and you, mother, do not weep — this sign remains with you as our word." And when they went, one Hunahpu planted, and the other Xbalanque planted; and they planted them only inside the house, not on the mountain, nor in wet ground, but in dry ground, in the middle of the house they left them planted.

Then they went, each carrying his own blowgun, and they went down into Xibalba. Quickly they went down the steps, and they crossed a river running through a ravine, and they passed among the birds; these birds were called Molay. And they also crossed a river of pus, and another of blood, meant to defeat them, as those of Xibalba supposed — but they did not step in them. And going on from there, they came to a crossroads of four roads, and they truly knew the road of Xibalba: one was black, one white, one red, and one green. And from there they sent out a small creature, an insect called Xan, to go and gather news. It was told: bite each of them, one by one; bite the first who sits there first, and finish biting them all, and yours shall be the sucking of the people's blood on the roads. This was told to Xan. Very well, said Xan.

Then it took the black road and went straight to the first one seated there, who was a thing made of carved wood, dressed up; and it bit him first, and he did not speak. And then it bit the second, and he too did not speak. It bit the third, who was Hun Came, and he cried out — Ay! — when he was bitten. What is it, Hun Came, said the fourth seated there, who bit you? I don't know what has bitten me. It bit the next, and he cried, Ay, what is this, Vucub Came, who has bitten you? said the fifth. Ay, ay, said Xiquiripat. And Vucub Came asked him, who has bitten you? And it bit the sixth, and he cried, Ay — what is it, Cuchumaquic, who has bitten you? it was asked. And when it bit the seventh, who cried Ay, what has bitten you, Ahalpuh? said Cuchumaquic. And when it bit the eighth, who cried Ay, Ahalpuh said to him: what is it, Ahalcana, who has bitten you? And when it bit the ninth, seated there, who cried Ay, Ahalcana said to him: Chamiabac, what has bitten you? And when it bit the tenth, who cried Ay, Chamiabac said to him: Chamiaholom, what has bitten you? And biting the eleventh, who cried Ay, it was said to him: what has bitten you? And it bit the twelfth, who cried Ay, and it was said again: what has bitten you, Patan? And biting the thirteenth, who cried Ay, it was said again: what has bitten you, Quicxic? said Patan. And biting the fourteenth, it was said to him, Quicre — what has bitten you? And one, seated on a bench, was named Holoman. And thus all of them spoke their own names, and each declared himself, saying his name — every one of them, when they were bitten by a hair from the face of Hunahpu; and it was not truly a gnat that went and bit them all, and went to hear the names of them all, on behalf of Hunahpu.

Then, when they arrived where the lords of Xibalba were, they were told: go and greet that lord who is seated there. But he was not truly a lord — he was only a carved dummy, dressed up to deceive them. So they said: that is only a dummy. And greeting the rest, they said: Lord Hun Came, Lord Vucub Came, Lord Xiquiripat, Lord Cuchumaquic, Lord Ahalpuh, Lord Ahalcana, Lord Chamiabac, Lord Chamiaholom, Lord Quicxic, Lord Patan, Lord Quicre, Lord Quicxic Chuchah. This they said when they arrived before them all; they spoke the name of every one of them, and not one name was left out, missed, or forgotten. And this was what those of Xibalba had laughed about — that their names would not be known, that the boys would not find them out.

Come, they were told, and they wished to seat them on the bench of honor, but the boys would not sit there: this is not our seat, they said, for it is only a heated stone. They were not defeated by it. Very well, they were told, go then into the house — and they went into a black house, and there too they were not defeated; this was the first trial of Xibalba. They thought to begin their triumph over the boys there. They gave them a torch and, for each of them, a cigar from the messengers of Hun Came, and said: here is your torch and your cigars; the lords say you must return them at dawn, still burning, not used up. Very well, they said. But they did not light the torch; in its place they set a scarlet feather from a macaw's tail, so that to the watching wardens it seemed to burn all night; and in the cigars they set fireflies, so that these too seemed lit. And so the wardens believed all night that the boys were already beaten. But the torch was not consumed, and likewise the cigars were not consumed by them, and in the morning both were carried back whole to the lords.

And they said: what is this, from where have these come, who begot them, who bore them? Truly our hearts burn, for this that they do is not good; strange are their faces and strange their ways. So they said among themselves. And then all the lords sent to summon them: come, let us play ball, young men. And Hun Came and Vucub Came asked them: from where have you come? Tell it, young men. But they said, we do not know from where we come, and they did not tell it. Very well, said those of Xibalba, let us go play ball, young men. Where shall we throw down this our ball? said those of Xibalba. By no means shall that one of yours be thrown down, said the young men. And those of Xibalba said, by no means, not that one — only ours. Very well, said the young men.

And then a rounded thing was set before them, dressed up. Xan, said those of Xibalba, giving it a name — but it was not so, said the boys; it was not that, but the head of a puma, made bare, its skull, got up to pass for the ball. This is not, said the boys. Very well, said Hunahpu, and threw down the ball of those of Xibalba; and when it came off the bat, a white flint dagger showed itself out from the middle of it, glinting as it went bounding over the floor of the ballcourt. What is this? said the boys. All you mean is to finish us — did you not send to call us? Were not your own messengers the ones who came for us? We are unfortunate, they said; we will go back again. And this was exactly what the boys wanted of them, that they should die there at the game — but they were not the ones defeated; rather those of Xibalba were again defeated by the young men.

Let us play ball, then, with your ball, they were told, and the young men said: very well. And they threw down their own ball, and so the game came to its end for that time. Then those of Xibalba said: what shall we do to overcome them? And they said to the young men: go and bring us, this coming night, four gourds full of flowers. Very well, said the young men. And what flowers? the young men asked those of Xibalba. We want, they said, one gourd of red flowers, one of white, one of yellow, and one of the great flowers, all four gourds full.

Very well, said the young men. And then they were sent down into a house where there was nothing but knives of flint, all alike, all sharp, and the knives were many. This was the second trial of Xibalba, and it was meant that they be cut to pieces by the knives, and quickly, before they could think how to save themselves. But they did not die there; instead they spoke to the flint knives and told them: yours shall be the flesh of every animal, and with this the knives did not stir any more, but stayed still, all of them, and so they passed the whole night inside the house of knives, and there too they were not defeated.

Then those of Xibalba's messenger-runners came, saying: let them come, says the lord, bring here what you have won. Very well, said the young men, and they went carrying the flowers, four gourds full, and they came before the face of the lord, and the lords took the flowers, very soft still, and in this way those of Xibalba were defeated. For it was only the ants that the young men had sent, and in one night the ants had cut the flowers and set them in the gourds, and so all those of Xibalba were terrified, their faces gone pale over the flowers, and they called at once for those who guarded the flowers and said to them: how have you let our flowers be stolen, that we see here? We did not feel it, lord, they said, and see how our own tails are — and their mouths were slit open in payment for having let the flowers be stolen. And so Hun Came and Vucub Came were defeated by Hunahpu and Xbalanque, and this was the beginning of their works against them. And ever after the mouths of those two stayed slit in that fashion, as they are found still.

And then they went to play ball once more, and when the game was ended they agreed between themselves, and the two sides gave word to each other that in the morning they would play again. Very well, said the young men, when they left off the game.
