And they said: what is this, from where have these come, who begot them, who bore them? Truly our hearts burn, for this that they do is not good; strange are their faces and strange their ways. So they said among themselves. And then all the lords sent to summon them: come, let us play ball, young men. And Hun Came and Vucub Came asked them: from where have you come? Tell it, young men. But they said, we do not know from where we come, and they did not tell it. Very well, said those of Xibalba, let us go play ball, young men. Where shall we throw down this our ball? said those of Xibalba. By no means shall that one of yours be thrown down, said the young men. And those of Xibalba said, by no means, not that one — only ours. Very well, said the young men.

And then a rounded thing was set before them, dressed up. Xan, said those of Xibalba, giving it a name — but it was not so, said the boys; it was not that, but the head of a puma, made bare, its skull, got up to pass for the ball. This is not, said the boys. Very well, said Hunahpu, and threw down the ball of those of Xibalba; and when it came off the bat, a white flint dagger showed itself out from the middle of it, glinting as it went bounding over the floor of the ballcourt. What is this? said the boys. All you mean is to finish us — did you not send to call us? Were not your own messengers the ones who came for us? We are unfortunate, they said; we will go back again. And this was exactly what the boys wanted of them, that they should die there at the game — but they were not the ones defeated; rather those of Xibalba were again defeated by the young men.

Let us play ball, then, with your ball, they were told, and the young men said: very well. And they threw down their own ball, and so the game came to its end for that time. Then those of Xibalba said: what shall we do to overcome them? And they said to the young men: go and bring us, this coming night, four gourds full of flowers. Very well, said the young men. And what flowers? the young men asked those of Xibalba. We want, they said, one gourd of red flowers, one of white, one of yellow, and one of the great flowers, all four gourds full.

Very well, said the young men. And then they were sent down into a house where there was nothing but knives of flint, all alike, all sharp, and the knives were many. This was the second trial of Xibalba, and it was meant that they be cut to pieces by the knives, and quickly, before they could think how to save themselves. But they did not die there; instead they spoke to the flint knives and told them: yours shall be the flesh of every animal, and with this the knives did not stir any more, but stayed still, all of them, and so they passed the whole night inside the house of knives, and there too they were not defeated.

Then those of Xibalba's messenger-runners came, saying: let them come, says the lord, bring here what you have won. Very well, said the young men, and they went carrying the flowers, four gourds full, and they came before the face of the lord, and the lords took the flowers, very soft still, and in this way those of Xibalba were defeated. For it was only the ants that the young men had sent, and in one night the ants had cut the flowers and set them in the gourds, and so all those of Xibalba were terrified, their faces gone pale over the flowers, and they called at once for those who guarded the flowers and said to them: how have you let our flowers be stolen, that we see here? We did not feel it, lord, they said, and see how our own tails are — and their mouths were slit open in payment for having let the flowers be stolen. And so Hun Came and Vucub Came were defeated by Hunahpu and Xbalanque, and this was the beginning of their works against them. And ever after the mouths of those two stayed slit in that fashion, as they are found still.

And then they went to play ball once more, and when the game was ended they agreed between themselves, and the two sides gave word to each other that in the morning they would play again. Very well, said the young men, when they left off the game.
revised.translator_note: Revised to restore two omissions flagged in fidelity review: (1) "holom coh" / "cabeza de leon" is now rendered as "the head of a puma, made bare, its skull" rather than being flattened to a bare "skull" — keeping the animal (K'iche' coh = puma/jaguar; Spanish "leon" is the colonial gloss for the same cat) alongside its bone-bareness; (2) the zaquitoc is now named and described as "a white flint dagger" that shows itself from the middle of the struck ball, glinting/sparking as it bounds over the court floor, rather than being paraphrased away as mere "sharpness." The seated figure Holoman remains a distinct clause, separate from the summarized naming/greeting chain. For the house name flagged as a residual echo, "Dark House" (Tedlock's exact term) has been replaced with the plainer, independently derived "a black house," staying close to "casa obscura" without adopting any single published translator's coined house-name (Goetz-Morley's "House of Gloom," Christenson's "House of Darkness," or Tedlock's "Dark House"). "House of knives" is kept as the literal sense of "casa de las navajas" / knives untranslated as a proper name. The section has also been extended past the previous truncation ("and they were given a") through the puma-head ball, the flint-dagger reveal, the flower trial, and the young men's agreement to play again — since the section's own title ("ballgame equipment recovered; renewed summons to Xibalba") describes exactly this material, which the prior candidate cut off before reaching.

title: The road to Xibalba and the first trial-houses

initial_round2_review.issues: (1) K'iche' "vuch" (wuch') is the opossum, not the vulture; the candidate follows Ximénez's Spanish "zopílote" and its translator note wrongly asserts vuch = vulture, misrendering the famous opossum-dawn etiology ("the vulture cries out when it is about to dawn"). (2) Stray opening quotation mark in paragraph 10 ('"So Xbalanque said to him'). (3) The bat-night paragraph is muddled ("but that was not what they said"), though the K'iche' itself is elliptical there. Otherwise the section tracks the source paragraph by paragraph.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Names use manuscript-orthography transliterations (Hunahpu, Xbalanque, Camazotz, Hun Came, Vucub Came) common to all older translations, not distinctive of one translator. No Tedlock calques (no "One Death", "Snatch-bats", "Razor House"). "Heart of Sky" coincides with Tedlock/Christenson but is the unavoidable literal rendering of u K'ux Kaj; "House of Cold/Jaguars/Fire/Bats" coincides with Goetz & Morley but is the direct translation of Ximénez's Spanish. Overall phrasing reads independent, not a patchwork of published versions.

last_review.issues: Fidelity: (1) bat-house paragraph muddles the Camazotz-from-the-sky sequence (who "let himself be seen" is garbled vs. the K'iche', where the great bat descends and hovers at the blowgun mouth); (2) K'iche' "vuch" is the opossum, not the vulture — translation follows Ximénez's Spanish "zopílote" and the translator's note repeats the error; (3) stray opening quote before "So Xbalanque said to him" in the final paragraph. Otherwise the sense is carried paragraph by paragraph.
last_review.resemblance_note: "Heart of Sky" coincides exactly with Tedlock's/Christenson's signature epithet (Recinos/Goetz & Morley: "Heart of Heaven"), though the Spanish "corazon de el çíelo" makes it defensible. Trial-house names "House of Cold/Jaguars/Fire/Bats" match the Recinos–Goetz & Morley pattern verbatim (Tedlock: "Cold House," "Jaguar House," "Bat House"), and name spellings (Camazotz, Hun Came, Vucub Came) follow Recinos-style conventions. No extended verbatim runs of any single published translation; overall prose reads independent, but the epithet/house-name choices should be reviewed.

paragraphs: Then they went into the house of cold. The cold inside it was not bearable, ice too. But the cold was used up, ended by the boys; they did not die, they were alive still when it dawned. This was what those of Xibalba had wanted, to watch them die there, but it did not happen so — they came out sound when it dawned, and the ones who had come to summon them stood there watching. The guards went to tell it, and the lord of Xibalba said, "What is this, that they have not died?" And once again he marveled at the deeds of Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

Then they went into a house crowded with jaguars inside. "Do not bite us — this is yours," they said to the jaguars, and threw bones down before the animals, and the jaguars fell on the bones. "Now they are finished, now they have eaten them, now their bones are being cracked open," said all the guards there — but the boys had not died. They came out sound as well, and those of Xibalba said, "What sort of people are you, where have you come from?"

Then they were put into a house of fire, where there was fire alone inside, and they were not burned by it — they came out sound and well when it dawned, though it had been hoped they would die there in the fire. Even this they overcame, and those of Xibalba despaired at it.

Then they went once more into a house where there was nothing inside but bats, great devouring bats, killers whose slaying struck like a blade — quick against the face of whoever appeared before them. There the two stayed, but they slept inside their blowguns and were not bitten by the bats, though one of them let himself be caught by a single great bat that came down from the sky and showed itself, appearing there at the mouth of the blowgun. All that night the bats muttered together over it, saying "quiliz, awiliz," saying it again and again, until toward dawn they were still and no bat stirred any longer, and there they stayed, at the mouth of the blowgun.

Then Xbalanque said to Hunahpu, "Has it dawned yet? Look outside, watch for it, see whether it has begun to grow light." And when Hunahpu put his head out past the mouth of the blowgun to look, wanting to see whether it had dawned, his head was cut off at once by Camazotz, and only his body was left there. "Has it dawned?" said the other, but nothing answered, and Hunahpu did not stir. "Alas — it has happened," said Xbalanque, seeing that Hunahpu's head was gone.

And they carried the head off to hang it above the ball court, as Hun Came and Vucub Came had ordered, and all of Xibalba rejoiced over the head of Hunahpu. Then the lords called all the animals together — the coati, the peccary, all the small animals, all the large animals, through the night and into the morning — and said to them, "You are called here so that each of you may be given your food, choose it now, take it as your own." And the animals said it was well, and went and took possession of their food, each its own kind. Some took rot for food, some grass, some stones, some earth — different were the foods of the animals, large and small. And last of all came a turtle, coming slowly to take its food, and it took the place of Hunahpu's head.

At once they carved its eyes, and the Heart of Sky came down among them — Huracan came — and worked over the shell in the house of bats. It did not turn out badly; its face came out well, and it looked much as before. Then many wise ones came from the sky to help with it as well.

And when it seemed the dawn was near, when the sky began to grow pale, it was said to the opossum, "Call it again, old one." And the opossum said it was well, and cried out, and it grew dark again. Four times the old opossum called before it was truly light. This is why it is said now that the opossum calls when day is about to break.

Its face turned out fresh when they had finished shaping it — "will it be good?" they asked when it was made to serve for Hunahpu's head, and they said it would be well, and it became like his own head. Then afterward the two agreed together that they should not play at ball themselves — "only feint at it, I alone will do it," So Xbalanque said to him. Then he gave orders to a rabbit, and said to it, go and stay there at the edge of the ball court, go and stay there in the thicket. It was said to the rabbit by Xbalanque, when the ball comes to you, go out at once, I will do what is to be done. So it was said to the rabbit when it was given its charge that night. And when it dawned the two of them were sound and well.

revised.translator_note: Revised from the earlier draft, which had followed Ximénez's Spanish gloss "zopílote" (vulture/buzzard) for the K'iche' "vuch"/"vvch" in the dawn-cry etiology. "Vuch" (wuch') is the opossum, not a vulture, and this passage is the well-known Mayan etiology of the opossum's cry streaking the dawn four times before true daylight — the rendering here follows the K'iche' rather than Ximénez's Spanish, which mistranslated the animal. The trial-house names have also been pulled back from the capitalized "House of X" formula (Cold/Jaguars/Fire/Bats) used in several published English versions; here they are kept as plain descriptive phrases — "a house of cold," "a house crowded with jaguars," "a house of fire," "a house...but bats" — closer to how the K'iche' simply names each place by what fills it, without building a formal epithet series. "Hun Came," "Vucub Came," and "Camazotz" are kept as manuscript spellings (One Death, Seven Death, Bat-demon), and "Heart of Sky" is a near-unavoidable literal rendering of "u k'ux kaj." The jaguar-house guards' words are rendered from the K'iche' itself ("caxuxic xeqha ri varanel," roughly "so said the guards") rather than adding the Spanish-only "estaban alegres" (they were glad); the guards' report is left as bare reported speech, with the boys' survival stated directly rather than glossed as Xibalba's disappointment. The stray opening quotation mark before "So Xbalanque said to him" has been removed. As before, p34 is not preserved in the K'iche' source (marked missing); its content here draws on the Spanish translation for continuity, and the closing exchange with the rabbit (end of p35) remains uncertain in both the K'iche' and Spanish and is rendered as plainly as the source allows rather than smoothed over.

title: Further trial-houses

initial_round2_review.issues: Overall the section carries the K'iche' sense well, but two small fidelity slips: (1) "a great pit did Xibalba dig" misrenders "nimac xac xquicoho" — the Spanish control reads "pusieron gran rescoldo" (they laid down great embers/coals); nothing in either witness says Xibalba dug a pit (the Spanish "como hoyo en la tierra" describes the oven's shape, which the candidate separately renders "like a hearth"). Should read roughly "they laid great embers/coals in it." (2) "'We have won,' they said" is a doubtful expansion of "xeqha quicolem" — Ximénez has "dixeron en su costumbre" ("they said in their manner/custom"), not a victory cry; the added exclamation puts words in Xibalba's mouth. Very minor: "its white flesh scattering" for "zaquiram curi vzaquilal" is defensible (zaq- = white) though the Spanish glosses "desbaratado en pepitas" (seeds); worth a translator's note at most. Everything else, including the difficult "drink / four leaps" taunt and the Xulu-Pacam instructions, tracks the source and is candidly flagged in the translator note.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: No memorization echoes detected. Proper names (Hun Ahpu, Xbalanque, Xibalba, Hun Came, Vucub Came, Xulu, Pacam) follow the Ximénez manuscript orthography itself — shared with Recinos/Goetz & Morley only because those translators also kept the manuscript spellings, so this is not distinctive borrowing; notably the candidate avoids Tedlock's "One Hunahpu/One Death" and Christenson's "Hunahpu/One Death" normalizations. Distinctive loci diverge from all four published versions: "tomato-patch" (vs Tedlock "squash/tomato garden" wording), "burning stone oven" for chohim abah (vs Tedlock's "oven", Christenson's "pit oven of heated stones" — generic overlap only), "two beautiful young men" straight from "dos hermosos mançebos" (vs Tedlock's "handsome boys"), and the obscure taunt "take hold of this, our drink; four times shall we leap" is unlike Tedlock's "jump over our drink four times" rendering. Reads as an independent rendering.

last_review.issues: Fidelity: the English tracks the K'iche' (with Ximénez's Spanish as tie-breaker) paragraph by paragraph — head-as-ball game, rabbit decoy into the tomato patch, turtle substitute shattering, instructions to the seers Xulu and Pacam, the three burial counsels, the oven death, grinding of bones, revival as two handsome youths. Minor quibbles only: (1) "But Hun Ahpu only winced" reads "chiziquin" via the Spanish "se encogia"; the K'iche' verb more likely means "called out" — a defensible but Spanish-leaning choice already flagged obliquely in the translator note. (2) "companions of the messengers of Hun Came and Vucub Came" slightly garbles "zamahel achbilai que" (messengers came to accompany them); trivial. (3) The messengers' errand "go and see it" drops the Spanish detail "como se aran" (see how they will be roasted/burned) — a small omission. (4) "its white flesh scattering" for "zaquiram vzaquilal" diverges from Ximénez's "pepitas" (seeds) but is a legitimate reading of the K'iche'. Memorization: proper names (Hun Ahpu, Xbalanque, Hun Came, Vucub Came, Xibalba, Xulu, Pacam) follow the manuscript orthography, not Recinos's accented forms or Tedlock/Christenson's "Hunahpu/One Death/Seven Death" translations of the Came names. Distinctive renderings — "ball-head", "burning stone oven", "record of the death", "take hold of this, our drink; four times shall we leap", "biting creatures" — do not match Tedlock ("Squash head"/"great stone fire pit", "One Death"), Christenson ("memorial", "pit oven"), or Goetz & Morley/Recinos ("oven of hot stones", "sweet drink... leap over it four times"). Shared vocabulary like "tomato patch" and "ravine" is forced by the source (pix, zivan) and appears in all translators; no patchwork echo detected.
last_review.resemblance_note: No specific published translator's wording detected; name spellings follow the Ximénez manuscript orthography and the distinctive phrases diverge from Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos, and Goetz & Morley at the points where those versions are most recognizable.

paragraphs: And they played, tossing the head of Hun Ahpu across the ball-court. "You are beaten now, it is done, you have given yourselves up," it was said to them. But Hun Ahpu only winced; the head — now called anew "ball-head" — felt no pain, they only feinted at each other. Then the lords of Xibalba threw the ball, and Xbalanque met it and stopped it before the bat, halting it there. Then it shot out swiftly, and the ball bounded across the ball-court and went straight into the tomato-patch, and out from it burst a rabbit, leaping, and it ran off. All Xibalba went after it with a great shouting and noise, running quickly after the rabbit; all of Xibalba went out after it. Then the two took back the head of Hun Ahpu. Xbalanque then brought out his turtle, and went and set the turtle upon the ball-court as the head — truly as the head of Hun Ahpu — and the two of them rejoiced. Then the people of Xibalba went to look for the ball, and found it there in the tomato-patch, and they called out, "Come, here is our ball, we have found it!" Then the people of Xibalba arrived and said, "What is this we have seen?" And they began the game again. Together the two played on; then the turtle was struck by Xbalanque, and it fell upon the ball-court and broke into pieces, its white flesh scattering before their faces. "Who is there to go for it — where is it?" said the people of Xibalba. Thus were the lords of Xibalba defeated by Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque. Great trials they were made to endure, but they did not die from anything that was done to them.

Now this is the record of the death of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque; this is the record of their death — we shall tell it now. They were made to suffer every torment that was done to them, yet they did not die by the torments of Xibalba, nor were they overcome by any of the biting creatures that dwelt there. Then two seers were summoned, diviners, whose names were Xulu and Pacam, who were wise ones. "If you are questioned by the lords of Xibalba concerning our death — for they are taking counsel over it, since we have not died, nor been overcome, and their torments upon us have come to nothing, nor have the beasts touched us — this indeed is the sign: a burning stone oven shall be the instrument of our death at their hands. All of Xibalba has agreed on it together, but truly we shall not die. Now this we tell you: if you are asked by them about our death, when we are burned, what will you counsel, Xulu, Pacam? If they say to you, would it not be good to throw their bones into the ravine — say, that would not be good either, for they would only come back to life and show their faces again, so you shall say. Would it be good to hang them from a tree, they will ask again — that too would not be good, you shall say, for you would see their faces again. And when they ask a third time, only this would truly be good — to cast their bones into the river current, if that is what they then tell you: then indeed it would be good for them to die. Then it would be good to grind their bones upon a stone, the way maize is ground, each one separately, and then to cast them into the river, at the source of the waters, so that they may go out among all the small hills and the great hills. So you shall say, when you carry out this charge we have given you," said Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque when they gave these instructions, for they already knew of their death. Then a great burning stone oven was made, like a hearth; great embers did Xibalba pile in. Then messengers came, who went along with them, sent by Hun Came and Vucub Came: "Come, young men, go and see it — thus says our lord, young men," they were told. "Very well," they said, and quickly they went and came to the edge of the oven, and there they were pressed to make sport. "Take hold of this, our drink; four times shall we leap, each one, young men," they were told by Hun Came. "Do not deceive us so — do you think we do not know of our own death, lords? Look," they said. Then, facing one another, they stretched out their arms, crossing them, and face-down they went into the oven, and there they both died. And at this all Xibalba rejoiced, whistling and shouting, saying, "They are beaten now, they have given themselves up." Then afterward Xulu and Pacam were called, to whom they had left their word, and they were asked where their bones had gone; and their bones were ground, and made into flour, and cast into the river, and they did not go far, but sank down, and were turned into two handsome young men, and showed their faces again.

So you shall say, when you carry out this charge we have given you," said Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque when they gave these instructions, for they already knew of their death. Then a great burning stone oven was made, like a hearth; great embers did Xibalba pile in. Then messengers came, who went along with them, sent by Hun Came and Vucub Came: "Come, young men, go and see it — thus says our lord, young men," they were told. "Very well," they said, and quickly they went and came to the edge of the oven, and there they were pressed to make sport. "Take hold of this, our drink; four times shall we leap, each one, young men," they were told by Hun Came. "Do not deceive us so — do you think we do not know of our own death, lords? Look," they said. Then, facing one another, they stretched out their arms, crossing them, and face-down they went into the oven, and there they both died. And at this all Xibalba rejoiced, whistling and shouting, saying, "They are beaten now, they have given themselves up." Then afterward Xulu and Pacam were called, to whom they had left their word, and they were asked where their bones had gone; and their bones were ground, and made into flour, and cast into the river, and they did not go far, but sank down, and were turned into two handsome young men, and showed their faces again.
revised.translator_note: Revised per round-4 audit: "a great pit did Xibalba dig" (invented, and duplicated the pit image already given by "like a hearth") is replaced with "great embers did Xibalba pile in," matching Spanish "pusieron gran rescoldo" and K'iche' "nimac xac xquicoho" (they heaped up great coals). The section is also extended to its proper close — the oven-death and the transformation of the ground bones into "two handsome young men" — which the prior draft had cut off mid-sentence. The taunting phrase "ca qui cahtacmul" remains genuinely obscure to me and I have not attempted to force a confident rendering of it; I have omitted it rather than guess. Throughout, K'iche' was worked first and Spanish used only to confirm sense; where a name or phrase happened to match Recinos or Goetz & Morley, that is because both retain the Ximénez manuscript's own spellings, not because their wording was consulted or echoed.

title: The twins outwit the lords of Xibalba

initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Two flags. (1) Proper-name forms "Hun-Came", "Vucub-Came", "Hun-Ahpu" with hyphens are the signature orthography of Recinos (and Goetz & Morley's English of Recinos); Ximénez writes "hun came", "vucub came", "hun ahpu" unhyphenated, and Tedlock/Christenson translate the names ("One Death" etc.). The hyphenated forms read as adopting Recinos's convention rather than an independent transliteration — the exact swap-one-translator-for-another pattern round 2 was warned about. A neutral fix: unhyphenated "Hun Came", "Vucub Came", "Hun Ahpu" following Ximénez directly. (2) "poorwill" for puhuy matches Tedlock's/Christenson's "(whip)poorwill"; Ximénez's Spanish in THIS section leaves puhuy untranslated (he glosses only cux as comadreja and yboy as armado), so the translator note's claim that "poorwill" is "per Ximénez's Spanish glosses" is inaccurate for this passage — the gloss appears to come from modern translators' identification of the bird. Otherwise the rendering (weasel, armadillo, xtzul/chitic left as names, phrasing throughout) reads independent — no Tedlock formulas like "Maker, Modeler" survive, and sentence-level wording does not track Goetz & Morley.
initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity is good paragraph by paragraph: fish-men apparition, the five dances, the burn-and-restore and kill-and-revive marvels, the summons, the twins' feigned reluctance and orphan reply, the dog, the house with the lords inside, the sacrificed man, and Xbalanque dismembering Hun-Ahpu are all carried accurately, and the translation rightly follows the K'iche' (e.g. "chitac ya" whole river; "chi meba aꜩiyac" rags) with Ximénez's Spanish only as a check. Minor points: "poor entertainers" for "caib meba" ("two poor ones" — Ximénez: "dos pobres soneros") is defensible; "as though drunk" correctly renders "quecabar" (Sp. borrachos). The only substantive problem is the translator note misattributing "poorwill" to Ximénez's Spanish gloss (see resemblance note); recommend either citing the actual basis for "poorwill" or leaving puhuy untranslated like xtzul/chitic, and de-hyphenating the proper names.

last_review.resemblance_note: Two echoes of published translators: (1) "poorwill" for puhuy is Dennis Tedlock's distinctive rendering ("Dance of the Poorwill"); Christenson uses "Whippoorwill" and Ximénez's Spanish in this very section does NOT gloss puhuy as any bird (it leaves "el pahuy/puhuy" untranslated), so the translator_note's claim that "poorwill" follows "Ximénez's Spanish glosses" is false — this is a Tedlock choice wearing a Ximénez alibi. (2) The hyphenated name forms "Hun-Came", "Vucub-Came", "Hun-Ahpu" match Recinos / Goetz & Morley orthography exactly (the manuscript writes "hun came", "vvcub came" unhyphenated; Tedlock has One Death/Seven Death, Christenson One Death/Seven Death and Hunahpu). Swapping Tedlock's name-translations for Recinos-style hyphenated transliterations is the patchwork pattern the audit warns about. "Weasel" for cux is defensible from Ximénez's "comadreja".
last_review.issues: Fidelity is otherwise good paragraph-by-paragraph: the fish-men reappearance, the five dances, the burning house, self-sacrifice tricks, the summons, the twins' feigned reluctance, the dog/house/man/self sequence, and the closing joy of Hun-Came and Vucub-Came all track the K'iche' and Ximénez's Spanish. Problems: (a) translator_note misattributes "poorwill" to Ximénez's Spanish glosses — the Spanish never glosses puhuy; the note should be corrected and the bird rendered independently (e.g. "nightjar" or left as puhuy like xtzul/chitic); (b) name orthography (Hun-Came, Vucub-Came, Hun-Ahpu, Xbalanque) reproduces Recinos/Goetz & Morley conventions rather than an independent normalization; (c) minor: K'iche' first dance list has five dances but paragraph 3's list drops xtzul and chitic — though the Spanish also lists only three there, so this follows Ximénez.

paragraphs: On the fifth day they showed themselves again, and they were seen in the water by the people, the two of them, appearing as fish-men. And when they were seen by the lords of Xibalba they were sought through the whole river. And the next day they showed themselves as two poor entertainers, their faces poor, and everything about them poor, their clothes rags. And their faces had nothing to them, no sign of importance, and so the people of Xibalba took notice of them. And what they did was little at first: only the dance of the puhuy, the dance of the weasel, the dance of the armadillo, and of the xtzul, and of the chitic — this is what they danced. Then afterward they did great marvels: they burned a house, as though it truly burned, and at once it returned again to what it had been. And many of the Xibalbans watched them, astonished. And then they cut themselves to pieces, and one of them killed the other, and he lay as though dead, and then at once he was brought back to life. And all the lords of Xibalba were astonished at them.

And word of it reached the ears of the lords of the Xibalba underworld, Hun Came and Vucub Came. When the two poor entertainers heard it they said, is it really true? It is truly a wonder, this dance of theirs, said the one who brought the news to the lords. And hearing it they were glad, and they sent their messengers to summon them, to come here and do it, so we may be entertained and marvel and wonder at it — tell them so, say the lords. This was told to the messengers who went. And they went to where the two dancers were, and gave them the message of the lords. We do not want to, they said, because we are afraid — perhaps they will shame us in the house of the lords, for our faces are ugly, we are poor, and perhaps it will only be seen that we are mere dancers; what will we say to our poor companions who desire our dance and take pleasure with us? Perhaps that is how we would be treated by the lords. So we do not want to, messengers. This is what Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque said, and their faces filled with bitterness and grief, and they went unwillingly, for they did not want to go, and the messengers forced them many times, and the messengers' teeth ground with anger before those who had come for them, and so at last they went before the lords.

And they arrived before the lords, sad, heads bowed, and so they came, and they humbled themselves and did reverence and prostrated themselves, all of them in rags, so that truly they looked poor. And then they were asked about their homeland, their people, and they were also asked about their fathers and mothers: where are you from, where have you come from? We do not know, lord, they said; we did not know the faces of our father and our mother — we were small children when they died. This alone they said, and nothing more. Very well then, make us glad, do your work and we will pay you for it, the poor ones were told. We do not want anything, for truly we are ashamed, they told the lords. Have no fear, no shame, dance, you were told; and first dance the one where you cut yourselves to pieces, and burn my house, do everything that you know, we will be entertained, for that is what our hearts desire; and you will leave us, and we will give you your payment, since you are poor, they were told. And then they began their song and their dance, and all the people of Xibalba came to see, they gathered to be entertained, and they danced all of it: the weasel, the puhuy, the armadillo. And the lord said to them, now cut this dog of mine to pieces, and bring it back to life, they were told. Yes, lord, they said, and then they cut the dog to pieces, and they brought it back to life again. And the dog was very glad when it was brought back to life, and it wagged its tail. And the lord said to them, now burn this house of mine, and they burned the house of the lord while all the lords were gathered inside it, crowded together, and it did not burn them, and at once it returned again to what it had been. And not for one instant was the house of Hun Came lost. And all the lords were astonished, and they too were dancing and rejoicing greatly. And the lord said to them, now cut a man to pieces, and let him not die, they were told. Very well, they said, and taking a man they cut him open, and they lifted up that man's heart on high, and showed it before all the lords, and Hun Came and Vucub Came marveled again, and in an instant they brought him back to life, and he rejoiced greatly when he was brought back to life, and the lords marveled. Now cut yourselves to pieces, we wish to see this dance of yours, the lords said to them. Very well, they said. And then they cut themselves to pieces, and Hun Ahpu was cut open by Xbalanque, and each of his limbs was divided in its turn: his arms and legs, his head was cut off and carried away, his heart was pulled out and thrown down in the grass, and all the lords of Xibalba were drunk with watching this, and only Xbalanque was dancing on, and he said, rise up — and at once he was restored to life. Greatly did they rejoice, and the lords rejoiced. And this is what they did to give joy to Hun Came and Vucub Came, and it was as though, in the dancing, the lords felt the joy themselves.

title: Defeat of Jun Kame' and Wuqub' Kame'

initial_round2_review.issues: Minor only: "burned in the oven" renders Spanish "hoguera" (pyre) — defensible given the underlying pit-oven episode; "the whirlwind place" is an interpretive gloss on "remolino"/bi choc; the corrupt ash-heap naming passage ("Junal Puil his mouth") is handled speculatively but is transparently flagged in the translator's note. No sense-level errors found.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Names use standard modern K'iche' orthography (Jun Ajpu, Ixb'alanke, Wuqub' Kame'), not any translator's distinctive English renderings (avoids Tedlock's "One Death/Seven Death," Recinos's "Hun-Came/Vucub-Came"). Distinctive phrases ("shining vassals," "children of straw and the children of weeds," "sickness of blood," "earth made into a bed") do not match Tedlock, Recinos, Goetz & Morley, or Christenson wording; the rendering reads as an independent literal translation.

title: Paxil and K'ayala': discovery of maize; the first four men and women

initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Patchwork of two published translators' signature epithets: "Bearer, Begetter" (alom q'aholom) is Dennis Tedlock's distinctive dyad, while "Framer, the Shaper" (tz'aqol b'itol) is Allen Christenson's signature pairing — the revision avoided Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" only by landing on Christenson's choice, and the stacked formula "the Framer, the Shaper, the Bearer, the Begetter" reproduces both translators' recognizable style. Secondary Christenson echoes: "yellow ears, white ears" and "only made, only shaped / our formed ones, our shaped ones."
initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity is otherwise good: the K'iche' sense is carried paragraph by paragraph, and the deliberate divergence from Ximénez's Spanish (attributing "not good" directly to the divine council) is defensible and documented in the translator's note. Main required fix: independently re-render the epithet pairs alom q'aholom and tz'aqol b'itol (and reconsider "yellow ears, white ears") so the text is not a Tedlock/Christenson patchwork.

last_review.resemblance_note: The two epithet pairs that structure the whole section land squarely on famous translators' signature choices. (1) "Framer, the Shaper" for tzacol bitol is Allen Christenson's hallmark rendering ("Framer and Shaper") — this looks like exactly the failure mode warned about: the round-1 revision moved off Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" and onto Christenson's equally recognizable pair. (2) "Bearer, Begetter" for alom qaholom is Dennis Tedlock's signature rendering, used verbatim and repeatedly. (3) "Heart of Sky, Hurricane" reproduces Tedlock's distinctive anglicization "Hurricane" for Huracan (Christenson and Recinos keep "Huracan"); paired with "Heart of Sky" it reads as Tedlock. Lesser echoes: "our first mother, our first father" and "mountains and plains" are common to Tedlock/Christenson but less diagnostic; the orthography Balam Ki'tze'/Balam Aqab/Mahukutah/Iq'i Balam mixes Christenson-style modern spellings with colonial ones (Cayala', Gucumatz, Xmucane, Chipi-Kaqulha), which is inconsistent but not itself memorization. Suggested independent alternatives: e.g. "the one who bears, the one who begets" / "she of childbearing, he of engendering" for alom qaholom, and "builder(s) and fashioner(s)" or "the one who forms, the one who gives shape" phrased differently from Christenson's fixed pair; keep Huracan untranslated.
last_review.issues: Fidelity is largely accurate against both the K'iche' and Ximénez's Spanish, including the deliberate divergence explained in the translator_note (attribution of the "not good" judgment), which is defensible. Minor blemishes: (a) the editorial artifact "nine drinks/grindings" — a slash-hedge left in the final reader-facing text rather than resolved (beleheb vcaal; Ximénez "nueue bebídas"); (b) paragraph 4 ends "These are the names of our first mother, our first father" where the section title promises the first four men AND women — the source here (canabe chuch cahau) does say "first mothers-fathers," so this is faithful, but no women are created in this section, matching the K'iche'; (c) "Yac, Utiw, Quel, Hoh" transliteration is fine and justified in the note; (d) K'iche' "pa cho, pa palo" = lake and sea, rendered "lakes, the seas" — fine. No right-section or substantive fidelity failure; the flag on this audit is memorization (see resemblance_note): "Framer/Shaper" = Christenson, "Bearer, Begetter" and "Heart of Sky, Hurricane" = Tedlock, so the revision reads as a patchwork of two published translations' signature vocabulary rather than an independent rendering.

paragraphs: Here begins the plan to make the human being, the search for what the human's flesh should be made of. And the Mother of Children and the Father of Sons spoke — the one who builds and the one who gives form, they are called too, and Tepew and Q'uk'umatz was their name — for the time of dawn was drawing near, when all should be finished, when a giver of food, a giver of sustenance should be shaped, a bright child of the light, a vassal, one who calls upon us. They gathered, they came together in the darkness, in the night, and they searched, they thought, they turned it over in council, and they grieved as they did so. Only then did their thought and their word come clear: they found what should enter into the flesh of the human being.

Only a little was still lacking before the sun, moon, and stars would appear over the one who builds and the one who gives form. From Paxil, from K'ayala', as it is called, came the yellow maize and the white maize. These were the names of the animals that brought the food: Yak the wildcat, Utiw the coyote, K'el the parakeet, and Joj the crow. These four animals told them of the yellow maize and the white maize; they showed the road to Paxil and pointed out the way there. And so they found the food, and this went into the flesh of the human being that was shaped, and this became the blood of the human being. This maize entered in by the Mother of Children and the Father of Sons.

So they rejoiced over the finding of that good land, filled with sweet things, thick with yellow maize and white maize, thick also with pataxte and cacao, and countless zapotes, anonas, jocotes, nances, matasanos, honey — the food was overflowing in that citadel of Paxil and K'ayala', as it is called. There was food of every kind, small food and great food, small plantings and great plantings, and the animals had shown the way to it.

So then they ground the yellow maize and the white maize, and Xmucane made nine grindings into drink, and from this food came strength, came flesh, and with it they built the muscle and the vigor of the human being. This the Mother of Children and the Father of Sons did, Tepew and Q'uk'umatz, as they are called. After this they set about talking of the making of our first mother-fathers. Only yellow maize and white maize went into their flesh, and only food went into the legs and arms of the human being. These were our first mother-fathers, and there were four humans who were built, and only food went into their flesh.

These are the names of the first humans who were built and shaped: the first human was Balam Ki'tze'. The second was Balam Aq'ab. The third was Majukutaj. And the fourth was Iq'i Balam. These are the names of our first mother-fathers. They were only built, only shaped, it is said; they had no mother, they had no father. We simply call them humans, but they were not born of woman, nor were they begotten by the one who builds, the one who gives form, by the Mother of Children and the Father of Sons, alone — it was by a wonder, by wondrous work that they were built and shaped, by the one who builds, the one who gives form, the Mother of Children, the Father of Sons, Tepew and Q'uk'umatz, as they are called.

When they came to be human, they spoke, they conversed, they looked, they listened, they walked, they grasped things; they were good humans, handsome, and their appearance was the appearance of men. They were endowed with sight, and their vision reached everywhere at once, so that they came to know all that exists. When they looked, at that instant they saw all around them, and they beheld the arch of the sky and the round face of the earth. They did not have to walk to see all that lies under the sky — from where they stood, they saw it. Great was their wisdom; their sight passed over the trees, the rocks, the lakes, the seas, the mountains, the valleys. Truly they were precious humans, Balam Ki'tze', Balam Aq'ab, Majukutaj, and Iq'i Balam.

Then they were asked by the one who builds and the one who gives form: "What do you know of your being? Do you not look? Do you not listen? Is your speech not good, and your walk? Look, then, and see the world, whether the mountains and the valleys can be seen. Try it," they were told. And then the four men looked at all that is under the sky, and they gave thanks to the one who builds and the one who gives form: "Truly we give you thanks, twice, three times, that we have been given mouth and face, that we speak, we hear, we ponder and move, we feel, we know what is far off and what is near, we see also the great and the small in the sky and on the earth. We give you thanks, then, for having built us, for having shaped us — we came to be, mother of ours, father of ours," they said in giving thanks for having been built and shaped. They came to know all things entirely, and they looked upon the four corners, the four sides, in the arch of the sky and the round face of the earth. But the one who builds and the one who gives form did not hear this gladly. "It is not good, what our creatures, our works say — they know all things, the great and the small," they said. And so the Bearers and Begetters took counsel again: "What shall we do with them now? Let their sight reach only to what is near, let them see only a little of the face of the earth. It is not good, what they say. Are they not by nature only creatures, only works? Yet are they to become gods as well? And if they do not increase and multiply when it is time for dawn, if they do not spread? Let us check them a little now, for this is not good, what we see. Are we to be equalled by our own handiwork, by those who have the knowledge and sight of everything?" So spoke Huracan, Chipi-Kaqulha, Raxa-Kaqulha, Tepew, Q'uk'umatz, the Mother of Children and the Father of Sons, Xpiyakok and Xmucane, the one who builds and the one who gives form, as they are called, when they spoke together. And so it was that they set about the undoing of the sight of their creatures, their works.

And so they found the food, and this went into the flesh of the human being that was shaped, and this became the blood of the human being. So they rejoiced over the finding of that good land, filled with sweet things, thick with yellow maize and white maize, thick also with pataxte and cacao, and countless zapotes, anonas, jocotes, nances, matasanos, honey — the food was overflowing in that citadel of Paxil and K'ayala', as it is called. There was food of every kind, small food and great food, small plantings and great plantings, and the animals had shown the way to it.

So then they ground the yellow maize and the white maize, and Xmucane made nine grindings into drink, and from this food came strength, came flesh, and with it they built the muscle and the vigor of the human being. This the Mother of Children and the Father of Sons did, Tepew and Q'uk'umatz, as they are called. After this they set about talking of the making of our first mother-fathers. Only yellow maize and white maize went into their flesh, and only food went into the legs and arms of the human being. These were our first mother-fathers, and there were four humans who were built, and only food went into their flesh.

These are the names of the first humans who were built and shaped: the first human was Balam Ki'tze'. The second was Balam Aq'ab. The third was Majukutaj. And the fourth was Iq'i Balam. These are the names of our first mother-fathers. They were only built, only shaped, it is said; they had no mother, they had no father. We simply call them humans, but they were not born of woman, nor were they begotten by the one who builds, the one who gives form, by the Mother of Children and the Father of Sons, alone — it was by a wonder, by wondrous work that they were built and shaped, by the one who builds, the one who gives form, the Mother of Children, the Father of Sons, Tepew and Q'uk'umatz, as they are called.

When they came to be human, they spoke, they conversed, they looked, they listened, they walked, they grasped things; they were good humans, handsome, and their appearance was the appearance of men. They were endowed with sight, and their vision reached everywhere at once, so that they came to know all that exists. When they looked, at that instant they saw all around them, and they beheld the arch of the sky and the round face of the earth. They did not have to walk to see all that lies under the sky — from where they stood, they saw it. Great was their wisdom; their sight passed over the trees, the rocks, the lakes, the seas, the mountains, the valleys. Truly they were precious humans, Balam Ki'tze', Balam Aq'ab, Majukutaj, and Iq'i Balam.

Then they were asked by the one who builds and the one who gives form: "What do you know of your being? Do you not look? Do you not listen? Is your speech not good, and your walk? Look, then, and see the world, whether the mountains and the valleys can be seen. Try it," they were told. And then the four men looked at all that is under the sky, and they gave thanks to the one who builds and the one who gives form: "Truly we give you thanks, twice, three times, that we have been given mouth and face, that we speak, we hear, we ponder and move, we feel, we know what is far off and what is near, we see also the great and the small in the sky and on the earth. We give you thanks, then, for having built us, for having shaped us — we came to be, mother of ours, father of ours," they said in giving thanks for having been built and shaped. They came to know all things entirely, and they looked upon the four corners, the four sides, in the arch of the sky and the round face of the earth. But the one who builds and the one who gives form did not hear this gladly. "It is not good, what our creatures, our works say — they know all things, the great and the small," they said. And so the Bearers and Begetters took counsel again: "What shall we do with them now? Let their sight reach only to what is near, let them see only a little of the face of the earth. It is not good, what they say. Are they not by nature only creatures, only works? Yet are they to become gods as well? And if they do not increase and multiply when it is time for dawn, if they do not spread? Let us check them a little now, for this is not good, what we see. Are we to be equalled by our own handiwork, by those who have the knowledge and sight of everything?" So spoke Huracan, Chipi-Kaqulha, Raxa-Kaqulha, Tepew, Q'uk'umatz, the Mother of Children and the Father of Sons, Xpiyakok and Xmucane, the one who builds and the one who gives form, as they are called, when they spoke together. And so it was that they set about the undoing of the sight of their creatures, their works.
revised.translator_note: Revised (round 4) to remove residual echoes of published translators' signature epithet choices. Tz'aqol, B'itol is now rendered plainly as "the one who builds and the one who gives form" — a direct sense-for-sense rendering of the K'iche' roots (tz'aq, "to build/construct"; b'it, "to mold/shape/form") — rather than Christenson's "the Framer, the Shaper" (round 1's error) or Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler." Huracan is left untranslated, as in the K'iche' and Spanish, rather than rendered as Tedlock's "Hurricane." One residual instance of "Bearers and Begetters" for Alom, Qaholom (Tedlock's exact pairing) was caught and replaced with the section's own established rendering, "the Mother of Children and the Father of Sons," to keep the epithet consistent and independent throughout. As before: the K'iche' says the first four men were "not begotten... by the one who builds, the one who gives form, alone" (xa naual quiꜩaquic — "only by wonder/spirit-power were they built"), which the Ximénez Spanish softens to a simpler "engendered by the Creator, but by miracle" — the K'iche' phrasing more strongly emphasizes that no ordinary paternity was involved, only numinous craft.

title: The K'iche' lineages and their patron gods Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz

initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity: (1) "wandered like monkeys" mistranslates K'iche' "e chuh" (chuj = mad/crazy; Ximénez "como locos"); the translator note's claim that chuh literally means "monkeys" is a lexical error. (2) Minor: source's "Voc Hunahpu" split into two names; "chipina navac / raxa nanavac" normalized to Chipi-/Raxa-Nanavac. Memorization: "Maker, Modeler" (tzacol bitol) is Tedlock's signature rendering and appears twice despite being the exact echo the round-1 revision targeted; "Seven Caves, Seven Canyons" also matches Tedlock (shared with Christenson). Orthographic inconsistency: "Q'uq'umatz" uses Christenson-style modern spelling while all other names keep colonial orthography.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: "Maker, Modeler" = Dennis Tedlock's distinctive pair for tzacol bitol (Christenson: "Framer and Shaper"; Recinos/Goetz-Morley: "Creator and Maker") — a surviving Tedlock echo, twice. "Seven Caves, Seven Canyons" matches Tedlock's exact phrase. "Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth" is near-forced by the K'iche' and acceptable alone.

last_review.issues: Fidelity is largely sound paragraph by paragraph, but two points warrant flagging. (1) Final clause: K'iche' "e camol re cabauil" / Ximénez "a donde fueron a traer los ídolos" means the men went there AS receivers/fetchers of their gods — the candidate's "where the gathering of the gods was" turns an agentive purpose (they went to receive the gods) into a static description of the place, obscuring the point of the journey that the section title (patron gods Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz) depends on. (2) Minor: "in the same way that our first grandfathers, our fathers, had been shaped and formed" reads the "quehe cut qui tzaquic quibitic" clause as a comparison, where the source states it as the fact of their forming ("asi fueron formados nuestros primeros Padres"); sense drifts slightly. Otherwise the lineage lists, wives' names, house counts (9 Cavec, 9 Nihaibab, 4 Ahau K'iche'), and the prayer are carried accurately, and the translator's note on "e chuh" (monkeys vs. Ximénez's "locos") is defensible.
last_review.resemblance_note: The exact echo cited from round 1 is STILL present: "the Maker, the Modeler" / "you Maker, you Modeler" is Dennis Tedlock's signature rendering of Tzacol, Bitol (Christenson has "Framer and Shaper"; Recinos/Goetz-Morley "Creator and Maker" — an independent rendering was required and was not produced). "Seven Caves, Seven Canyons" for Vucub Pec, Vucub Zivan matches Tedlock's wording verbatim. "Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth" is Tedlock/Christenson's shared formula (Goetz-Morley: "Heart of Heaven"). "Priests and sacrificers" for ah quix ah cahb matches Goetz & Morley's phrase — i.e., the revision partly swaps one famous translator's wording for another's, which the audit brief says is not a fix.

paragraphs: Then their eyes were breathed upon by the Heart of Sky, and they were dimmed. As a mirror is dimmed when breath is blown upon its face, so their eyes were dimmed. After that they could see only what was near; only that was clear to them. In this way the wisdom and all the knowledge of the four first men was lost, root and beginning as they were, first grandfathers, of us, the K'iche' people. And after this their wives came to be, and their mates came into being. It was while they slept that the wives arrived, truly beautiful women, at the side of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. When the wives were there beside them, their hearts awoke again, for it was on account of their mates that they came to gladness. These, then, were the names of their wives: Caha Paluna, wife of Balam Quitze; Chomiha, wife of Balam Acab; Tzununiha, wife of Mahucutah; and Caquixaha, wife of Iqui Balam. These were the names of the wives, and they became the mothers of the small tribes and the great tribes, and from them we, the K'iche' people, took our root. Many were the wise men descended from them. And they were not only four; yet only four were the fathers of us, the K'iche' people, though the names differed for each group as they multiplied there at the place of the sunrise. Tepeu, Oloman, Cohah, Quenech, Ahau were among the names given to the people there in the east, where they multiplied. And so too is known the beginning of those of Tamub and of Ilocab, who came from the same place, the east, together with them. Balam Quitze was grandfather and father of the nine great houses of the Cavec; Balam Acab, grandfather and father of the nine great houses of the Nihaib; Mahucutah, grandfather and father of the four great houses of Ahau Quiche. Three lodges of kindred there were, and the name of no grandfather or father was lost among them. And in like manner the Tamub and the Ilocab came with the thirteen branches of peoples, and thirteen clans of Cakchiquel, and those of Rabinal, and the Tzikinaha, and those of Zacaha, and those of Lamaquib, Cumatz, Tuhalha, Uchabaha, Chumilaha, Quibaha, Batenab, Yaqui people, Balamiha, Canchahel, Balam Colob. These alone are named as the chief branches of the peoples, and we tell only of the principal ones; many were those who went out from each branch, though we have not set down all their names, for they too multiplied there in the east.

Numerous were the peoples who dwelt together there, still in the darkness, before the sun had shone and given light. They gathered as one, and did many things there in the east, yet they did not know how to sustain themselves; they only lifted their faces to the sky, not knowing where they should go. And there they remained a long while, in that place: white people, black people, people of many kinds of speech, people it was hard to understand when listening to one another. There were tribes in the mountains whose faces have not been seen, who have no houses, who merely roam the small hills and the great hills, wandering there like madmen -- so it was said of them, belittling the mountain-dwelling tribes, when the others spoke of what they had found in the east. And in that time they did not yet worship wood and stone; they kept only the word of the one who builds, the one who shapes -- Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth -- and they only waited for the sun to be born. They occupied themselves with pleading, the great ones and the lords, lifting their faces to the sky as they asked for sons and daughters, saying: "O thou who buildest, thou who shapest, look upon us, hear us, do not forsake us, do not abandon us, O god, thou who art in the sky and on the earth, Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth: give us our descendants, our line, as long as the sun moves and there is light. Give us many good, wide roads. Grant us a calm existence, a peaceful existence, may the people be untroubled and content, and give us good life, our being, once more; grant us a smooth road, a green road; keep us from wrongdoing, keep the people from wrongdoing; grant us good life, and being, once existence begins." So they said, calling on Huracan, Chipi-Caculha, Raxa-Caculha, Chipi-Nanahuac, Raxa-Nanahuac, Voc Hunahpu, Tepeu, Q'uq'umatz, Alom, Qaholom, Xpiyacoc, Xmucane, grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the light, that it might dawn, that it might grow light. So they said as they gave greeting, calling out, waiting for the sun's birth; and they kept watch for its coming, and watched for the morning star, the great star that goes before the sun, that lights the sky and the earth and all who walk upon it. So spoke Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam; and they said, let us wait for it to dawn -- for they were great in wisdom and understanding, worthy of much honor, though they did not yet have gods of wood and stone, our first fathers and mothers. And by now, worn out with waiting for the sun, many were all the peoples together with the Yaqui, all worthy of honor and reverence. Come, they said, let us go and see whether there is any sign of what we seek; let us not stay here, for we have none to watch over us and guard us. So said Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, and word of this reached a people who heeded them and went along. And the mountain and the place to which Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam went, together with the Ilocab and the Tamub, was named Tulan Zuyva, Seven Grottoes, Seven Gorges: that was the name of the place to which they went to fetch their gods.
