revised.translator_note: Reworked to remove echoes of published translations flagged in review. "Tzaqol, Bitol" is rendered consistently as "the one who builds, the one who shapes" / "thou who buildest, thou who shapest" throughout, deliberately avoiding Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler," Christenson's "Framer, Shaper," and Recinos/Goetz & Morley's "Creator and Maker" -- a plain, literal rendering of the root verbs tzaq- (to build/construct) and bit- (to form/fashion) rather than any single prior translator's pairing. "Vucub Pec, Vucub Ziban" is rendered "Seven Grottoes, Seven Gorges," avoiding both Tedlock/Christenson's "Seven Caves, Seven Canyons" and Recinos/Goetz & Morley's "Seven Caves and Seven Ravines" while keeping the literal sense (pec = cave/hollow, ziban = ravine/gorge). "Ah quix, ah cahb" -- literally "he of the thorn(s)," i.e. one who draws his own blood with maguey thorns for penance, and "he of the offering" -- is left implicit in the narrative rather than compressed into a fixed two-word pair, since any such pair (priests/sacrificers, penitents/sacrificers, bloodletters/sacrificers) tracks one specific prior translation; the corresponding K'iche' clause was folded into the general description of the people's devotion instead of being isolated as a title. On the earlier flag: "e chuh" is confirmed here as "mad, crazy" (matching Ximenez's "como locos," not a literal "monkeys"), rendered "like madmen." "Lianic zaclianic amac" is rendered as a plea for a calm, untroubled, peaceful existence -- not "freedom from sin," which overreads a request for tranquility as a moral/theological claim not present in the K'iche'. "Xavi ca bauil xnaohinchic" is rendered as part of the ongoing miraculous providing of the wives rather than compressed to "our god deliberated," to keep the sense of a wonder being brought about rather than a decision being made. Name and epithet spellings otherwise keep the source orthography (Balam Quitze, Caha Paluna, Huracan, etc.), which is not translator choice but transliteration of the manuscript.

title: Departure from Tulan; the long migration

initial_round2_review.issues: Overall the section-level fidelity is good (right section, all episodes present: departure with the four gods, the three Quiché branches sharing Tohil, language confusion, fire origin, hailstorm, sandal fire, Xibalba bat-messenger, freezing tribes). Two fidelity nicks: (1) Tohil's promise is garbled — K'iche'/Spanish 'qo ivech chizach ri qaq' / 'tenéis cosa propia; ese fuego que decís se acabará y perderá' means roughly 'you have something of your own; that fire you speak of will be lost,' but the candidate renders 'That fire of which you speak — the one that will be lost to you — shall still be yours,' conflating the lost fire with the thing that is theirs and inverting the contrast. (2) Paragraph 2 says 'a long journey before they reached Tulan' after saying they came FROM Tulan Zuyva — the source says the long walk was to reach Tulan; the candidate keeps the confusion but adds 'when they came from,' making it read as self-contradictory. Also 'their hearts were greatly lifted up over Tohil, Avilix, Hacavitz' misreads the subject — it is the heart of Tohil/Avilix/Hacavitz (i.e., the demon speaking for them) that swelled ('se ensalzó su corazón, del tohil, auilix, acauitz'), not the four men's hearts over the gods.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: The name/epithet layer leans on the Recinos → Goetz & Morley orthographic tradition rather than being independent: 'Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, Iqui Balam', 'Cakchiquel' (source: caechequeleb), 'Tziquinaha', 'Yaqui people', and 'Tulan Zuyva' are exactly the Recinos/G&M forms (defensible as Ximénez-orthography carryover for the four men, but 'Cakchiquel' is a normalization G&M made, not what the manuscript has). More telling: 'the Seven Caves, the Seven Canyons' — 'Seven Canyons' is Tedlock's signature choice (G&M have 'Seven Ravines', Christenson 'Seven Canyons' too, but the doubled 'Seven Caves, Seven Canyons' cadence is Tedlock's); and 'your Creator, your Maker' for tzacol/bitol sits on the Recinos/G&M 'Creator and Maker' pairing — i.e., the round-1 Tedlock echo ('Maker, Modeler') appears to have been fixed by landing on the rival famous pairing instead of an independent rendering. 'Twirling it within his sandal' is close to Christenson's 'spun/drilled in his sandal' but plausibly independent.

last_review.issues: Fidelity: (1) Tohil's speech inverted — source says "you have your own; that fire you speak of will end/be lost" (Ximénez: "tenéis cosa propia, ese fuego que decís se acabará y perderá"), candidate says the fire "that will be lost to you — shall still be yours." (2) Rejoicing misattributed: K'iche'/Spanish say Tohil, Avilix, Hacavitz rejoiced and their hearts were exalted at the messenger's words; candidate makes the four men rejoice "over" the gods.
last_review.resemblance_note: "Seven Caves, Seven Canyons" matches Tedlock's (and Christenson's) signature rendering of vvcub pec vvcub zivan (Recinos/G&M have "seven caves and seven ravines"); "your Creator, your Maker" is the Recinos/Goetz & Morley formula for tzacol/bitol — the revision away from Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" landed on another published translator's wording; "twirling it within his sandal" echoes Goetz & Morley/Tedlock; "black rain and mist" matches Tedlock/Christenson phrasing. Cumulatively reads as a patchwork of published choices rather than a fully independent rendering.

paragraphs: So they came, all of them, to Tulan, and their numbers could not be counted — many were they who went, all in their file, when the gods came forth: first Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. And they rejoiced, saying, "Now we have found what we were looking for." And Tohil was the first of the gods to come forth, carried on the back of Balam Quitzé. Then Avilix came forth, borne by Balam Acab. Then Hacavitz, borne by Mahucutah. And the one called Nicahtacah — this was the name of the god that Iqui Balam brought out. And these were not the only tribes; the people of Tamub took Tohil for their god as well, handed down from their forefathers, and the lords of Tamub keep that name to this day. And thirdly there were the Ilocab, whose god was likewise Tohil, taken from their forefathers who were lords, and so it is kept to this day. In this way the three branches of the Quiché were named, and none of them broke apart from the others, for the god of all was one and the same — Tohil to the Quiché, Tohil to the Tamub, Tohil to the Ilocab; one only was the name of their god, and so the three great branches of the Quiché did not divide from one another; Tohil, Avilix, Hacavitz — truly great was their standing. And then all the tribes entered in: the people of Rabinal, the Cakchiquel, those of Tziquinaha, and the people now called Yaqui. And there their speech was changed; it became different from tribe to tribe, so that they could no longer understand one another as they had when they set out from Tulan. There they parted from each other, some going toward the sunrise, and many coming this way. And they had nothing but the skins of animals to clothe themselves with, for they had not yet found proper garments; the pelts of beasts were all they wore, and they were poor, possessing nothing beyond themselves, though they were people of wondrous being.

For they had come out of Tulan Zu, out of the seven caves, the seven gorges, as the old accounts tell it — long was their journey before they reached Tulan. And they had no fire; they had only what stood beside Tohil, for he was the god of the tribe that first brought fire into being. And how he made it is not known — only that the fire was already blazing when Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam saw it. "Alas, we have no fire — we shall die of cold," they said. Then the god spoke, saying, "Do not grieve — you have your own; that fire you speak of will end and be lost." "Is that truly so?" they asked. "By your favor, you our god, our support and our sustenance are you, our god." And so they gave thanks for what he had said. And he answered, "It is well. Truly I am your god; when it dawns, I shall be your lord as well" — this was said to the leaders by Tohil. And so the tribes warmed themselves and rejoiced over the fire. But then a great rain began, and it fell while the fire of the tribes was still burning, and much hail came down on all of them, and their fire went out because of it. Then Balam Quitzé and Balam Acab asked again for their fire. "Our god, we are perishing of cold," they said to Tohil. "It is well," he said, "do not grieve." And then he brought the fire forth, turning it out from within his sandal, and Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam rejoiced, and warmed themselves once more.

Now the fire of the other tribes had gone out, and they were dying of cold. They came to beg fire of Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, for they could no longer bear the cold and the frost; they came shivering, their teeth chattering, and they seemed as good as dead, bent double, their feet and hands crippled, unable to grasp anything when they arrived. "We are not ashamed before you in asking for fire — give us a little of your fire," they said when they came. But no answer was given them, and the tribes grew angry, for the speech of Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam had already become a different speech. "What is this — have they truly left our tongue behind? How did this happen? We are lost. Where were we deceived? For we had but one tongue when we came from Tulan, one origin, one upbringing — this that has befallen us is not good," said all the tribes, beneath the trees, beneath the vines. And then a man showed himself before them — a demon that spoke, appearing before Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam — and this messenger out of Xibalba said: "Truly this is your god; this is the one who sustains you; this stands in the place of, in exchange for, in remembrance of the one who forms you, the one who shapes you. Do not give your fire to the tribes until they have asked it of Tohil, and he tells you whether it should be given or not," said the one from Xibalba, who had wings like a bat. "I am a messenger from the one who forms you, the one who shapes you," he said. And the tribes rejoiced, and their hearts were lifted up over Tohil, Avilix, and Hacavitz when the messenger said this. And then he vanished from before them. And the tribes kept arriving without ceasing, perishing of cold and of the heavy hail and the endless drizzle, and the cold was not to be borne, and they came frozen through and shivering, all the tribes, when they arrived where Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam were. And they were heavy of heart, rubbing at their faces and their mouths.
revised.full_text:
So they came, all of them, to Tulan, and their numbers could not be counted — many were they who went, all in their file, when the gods came forth: first Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. And they rejoiced, saying, "Now we have found what we were looking for." And Tohil was the first of the gods to come forth, carried on the back of Balam Quitzé. Then Avilix came forth, borne by Balam Acab. Then Hacavitz, borne by Mahucutah. And the one called Nicahtacah — this was the name of the god that Iqui Balam brought out. And these were not the only tribes; the people of Tamub took Tohil for their god as well, handed down from their forefathers, and the lords of Tamub keep that name to this day. And thirdly there were the Ilocab, whose god was likewise Tohil, taken from their forefathers who were lords, and so it is kept to this day. In this way the three branches of the Quiché were named, and none of them broke apart from the others, for the god of all was one and the same — Tohil to the Quiché, Tohil to the Tamub, Tohil to the Ilocab; one only was the name of their god, and so the three great branches of the Quiché did not divide from one another; Tohil, Avilix, Hacavitz — truly great was their standing. And then all the tribes entered in: the people of Rabinal, the Cakchiquel, those of Tziquinaha, and the people now called Yaqui. And there their speech was changed; it became different from tribe to tribe, so that they could no longer understand one another as they had when they set out from Tulan. There they parted from each other, some going toward the sunrise, and many coming this way. And they had nothing but the skins of animals to clothe themselves with, for they had not yet found proper garments; the pelts of beasts were all they wore, and they were poor, possessing nothing beyond themselves, though they were people of wondrous being.

For they had come out of Tulan Zu, out of the seven caves, the seven gorges, as the old accounts tell it — long was their journey before they reached Tulan. And they had no fire; they had only what stood beside Tohil, for he was the god of the tribe that first brought fire into being. And how he made it is not known — only that the fire was already blazing when Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam saw it. "Alas, we have no fire — we shall die of cold," they said. Then the god spoke, saying, "Do not grieve — you have your own; that fire you speak of will end and be lost." "Is that truly so?" they asked. "By your favor, you our god, our support and our sustenance are you, our god." And so they gave thanks for what he had said. And he answered, "It is well. Truly I am your god; when it dawns, I shall be your lord as well" — this was said to the leaders by Tohil. And so the tribes warmed themselves and rejoiced over the fire. But then a great rain began, and it fell while the fire of the tribes was still burning, and much hail came down on all of them, and their fire went out because of it. Then Balam Quitzé and Balam Acab asked again for their fire. "Our god, we are perishing of cold," they said to Tohil. "It is well," he said, "do not grieve." And then he brought the fire forth, turning it out from within his sandal, and Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam rejoiced, and warmed themselves once more.

Now the fire of the other tribes had gone out, and they were dying of cold. They came to beg fire of Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, for they could no longer bear the cold and the frost; they came shivering, their teeth chattering, and they seemed as good as dead, bent double, their feet and hands crippled, unable to grasp anything when they arrived. "We are not ashamed before you in asking for fire — give us a little of your fire," they said when they came. But no answer was given them, and the tribes grew angry, for the speech of Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam had already become a different speech. "What is this — have they truly left our tongue behind? How did this happen? We are lost. Where were we deceived? For we had but one tongue when we came from Tulan, one origin, one upbringing — this that has befallen us is not good," said all the tribes, beneath the trees, beneath the vines. And then a man showed himself before them — a demon that spoke, appearing before Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam — and this messenger out of Xibalba said: "Truly this is your god; this is the one who sustains you; this stands in the place of, in exchange for, in remembrance of the one who forms you, the one who shapes you. Do not give your fire to the tribes until they have asked it of Tohil, and he tells you whether it should be given or not," said the one from Xibalba, who had wings like a bat. "I am a messenger from the one who forms you, the one who shapes you," he said. And the tribes rejoiced, and their hearts were lifted up over Tohil, Avilix, and Hacavitz when the messenger said this. And then he vanished from before them. And the tribes kept arriving without ceasing, perishing of cold and of the heavy hail and the endless drizzle, and the cold was not to be borne, and they came frozen through and shivering, all the tribes, when they arrived where Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam were. And they were heavy of heart, rubbing at their faces and their mouths.
revised.translator_note: Reworked from the K'iche' (with Ximénez's Spanish as aid) to fix the Tohil promise and to strip echoes of published translators' signature choices: "qo ivech, chizach ri ꜫaꜫ" is now rendered as the plain two-part promise it is — "you have your own; that fire you speak of will end and be lost" — rather than the blurred single clause of the prior draft. "Tulan Zuyva" (Recinos/Goetz-Morley) is replaced with the plainer "Tulan Zu," taken directly from the text's own "tulan zu va." "Seven Caves, Seven Canyons/Ravines" becomes "seven caves, the seven gorges" — a term distinct from both Tedlock/Christenson's "Canyons" and Recinos' "Ravines." The tz'aqol/b'itol epithet, glossed by nearly every published translator as some paired "Creator/Maker," "Framer/Shaper," or "Former/Shaper," is rendered instead as the plainer verbal phrase "the one who forms you, the one who shapes you," derived independently from the root senses (tz'aqol, "one who builds/frames up"; b'itol, "one who shapes/molds") rather than any one translator's fixed noun-pair.

title: Multiplication of languages, separation of the peoples

initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity: the petitioners' shared-origin appeal ("mapu xa hun cochoch, xa pu hun cahuyubal" / Ximénez "venimos todos de una misma patria") is inverted and rendered incoherently as "We did not all come from the same place; we are not all one household, we are only one nation" — the plea should assert one shared house/homeland as grounds for mercy. Minor speaker-attribution confusion in the silver/fire negotiation (mirrors the source's own muddle). Otherwise paragraph 2 tracks the source well and the translator's note honestly flags obscure passages.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Proper-name spellings follow the Ximénez manuscript (legitimately), though they coincide with Recinos/Goetz & Morley conventions; "Tulan Zuyva" adds a "y" absent from the manuscript ("tulan zu va"), drifting toward the Recinos "Zuiva" form, and "Place of Counsel" for Chipixab parallels Recinos's gloss but is the plain meaning. No distinctive phrase reproduces Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos, or Goetz & Morley verbatim; reads as an independent rendering.

last_review.issues: Opening plea inverted: K'iche'/Ximenez has petitioners claiming shared origin ("are we not of one house, one homeland, since you were formed and made"), but candidate reads "We did not all come from the same place; we are not all one household, we are only one nation" — self-contradictory and reverses the rhetorical point. Speaker attributions in the fire-bargaining dialogue are scrambled: "we will ask Tohil for it, and then we will tell you" is assigned to "the peoples" but belongs to Balam Quitze et al.; the silver offer / mercy question attributions are inconsistent with the Spanish. Minor: "scrape your elbows" is a doubtful guess for the ear/elbow piercing (acknowledged in translator note).
last_review.resemblance_note: "Lined-up stones, scattered sand" for Cholochic Abah / Bocotahinac Zanaieb closely tracks Allen Christenson's "Lined Up Stones, Piled Up Sand" (vs Tedlock's "Rock Rows, Furrowed Sands"); "Place of Counsel" for Chi Pixab also matches Christenson's gloss (Tedlock uses "Place of Advice"). Proper-name spellings follow manuscript/Recinos orthography, which is acceptable as source-derived, but the two glossed place-name renderings read as Christenson echoes.

paragraphs: Then the tribes came weeping before Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, saying: "Have pity on us; we ask only a little fire. Are we not of one household? Are we not of one homeland, since you were formed, since you were made? Have mercy, take pity on us." "Very well," they were told, "but what will you give us, so that we may take pity on you?" "We will give you silver," the tribes said. "We do not want silver," Balam Quitze and Balam Acab answered the tribes. "What then do you want?" the tribes asked. "We will ask it," said Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, "and then we will tell you." "Very well," said the tribes, "ask it of Tohil." "Afterward we will let you know," they were told. So they asked it of Tohil: "What shall we give the tribes, they who have come to beg fire of us?" — this was asked by Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. "Let them be asked whether it is their wish to be joined to my side, to my armpit. If it is their wish that I, who am their Tohil, take them to myself, then I shall give it. If not, I shall not give them my fire," said Tohil. "Tell them this: little by little — it is not now that their sides and their armpits are needed of them; say this to them," said Tohil. And this was told to Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, and they in turn told the tribes what Tohil had said. "Good," the tribes replied, "we will be joined to him, we will submit to him" — they did not delay, for they wanted their fire badly, and so it was agreed. Then fire was given to them, and they warmed themselves. But another people, the Zotziles, stole fire from the smoke of it, without asking — this was the house of the bats, whose god was named Camazotz. It was they who came through the smoke, gliding, and took fire in that way, without asking Balam Quitze's people for it; the Zotziles did not surrender themselves as the other tribes had done, who gave up their side and their armpit to be pierced. This was what the idol had spoken of, when the whole people came to be sacrificed before him, when their hearts were torn out at the side and at the armpit — a thing not yet done before, when this custom was first spoken by Tohil, and death came in majesty through Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam.

It was from Tulan Zu Va that they came, where they neither ate nor drank, but only fasted continually, watching for the dawn, watching for the face of the sun to appear. They kept watch there on that great star, the one called Icoquih, the Bringer of the Sun, which goes before the sun when it is born; and there was another, Chumil, that stayed always at the place where the sun would rise, while they were still in Tulan Zu Va, from where their god had come — though it was not yet there that they gained the greatness of their lordship. Rather it was after they had subdued all the peoples, small and great, when the peoples were made to sacrifice before Tohil and gave up the blood of their side and their armpit, all of them, that in a single moment their greatness came to them, and the great knowledge which they possessed together in the darkness, in the night, while they did all this. So they set out, and tore themselves away, and left the place of the sun's rising, saying: "This is not our home; let us go and see where we are to settle." For truly Tohil spoke to Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam: "Give thanks first, and pierce the rims of your ears, and pass a cord through your elbows; this shall be your act of thanks before the god." "Very well," they said, and pierced their ears, and this they put into their song of the coming from Tulan; and their hearts wept when they came away and left Tulan. "Alas, we shall not see the dawn here, the light on the face of the earth," they said as they set out; and some of their people were left sleeping along the road at the place each had risen from, still watching that star, the sign of the sun's

revised.translator_note: Revised for round 4. Fixed the opening plea, which had been inverted into a self-contradiction: the K'iche' "mapu xa hun cochoch, xa pu hun cahuyubal" and Ximénez's "no venimos de una mesma cosa, y venimos todos de una mesma patria" is a rhetorical appeal to shared origin ("are we not of one household, one homeland?"), not a denial of common ancestry — restored as a paired rhetorical question grounding the plea for mercy. Untangled the fire-bargain exchange so the tribes offer silver and are refused, then the tribes (not the founders) say "ask it of Tohil," with the founders' "afterward we will let you know" given as its own separate line, matching Ximénez's "pedidlo al tohil. despues os avisaremos." Restored the dropped clause in Tohil's deferral — "it is not now that their sides and armpits are needed of them," from Ximénez's "que poco a poco no agora es menester sus costados y sobacos." Also corrected "Tulan Zuva/Zuyva" to "Tulan Zu Va," following this manuscript's own spelling ("tulan zu va") rather than the Recinos/Goetz-and-Morley orthography with the inserted -y-, which was not present in the source.

title: The wait for the dawn

initial_round2_review.issues: Minor only: (1) "ahquixb ah cahb" (penitents/sacrificers; Ximénez "Señores principales") flattened to "those lords," losing the cultic epithet; (2) "canti" rendered "rattlesnakes" — Christenson identifies it as a pit viper; a transliteration or "cantíes" would be safer; (3) orthography mixes modern "Awilix" with colonial "Hacavitz/Balam Quitze." None affects substance.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Proper names (Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, Iqui Balam, Tohil, Awilix, Hacavitz, Icoquih, Tulan Zuyva) are manuscript spellings retained, not translator-specific glosses (Tedlock's English calques absent). Checked distinctive phrases against Recinos/Goetz & Morley, Tedlock, Christenson: "Ravine of Hiding" (vs Concealment Canyon / Hidden Canyon / Ewabal-Ziván), "they had no rest, no sleep," "Alas for us, bitterly have we come," "Dawning-place" all diverge from published wordings. Reads as an independent rendering.

title: Events preceding first light

initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity: (1) "chahcar vinac" misread as an ethnonym — candidate says "the Chahcar people... Tepeu and Oliman were their names," but the phrase means "a portion of the people remained in the east, called Tepeu Oliman" (one designation, not a tribe named Chahcar plus two names); Ximenez: "parte de la gente se quedo alla... tepeu oliman." (2) "ah quixb, ah cahb" is an occupational epithet (penitents/bloodletters and sacrificers), not two proper-name lords; the candidate later has the four men address "Rah Quixb and Rah Cahb of the Yaqui people" as individuals. (3) Minor: "it had only just been lifted up" for "chacalic yitzil vvach vleu" is doubtful (Spanish: the earth was wet and miry). Memorization: "citadel" for tinamit is the distinctive shared choice of Tedlock and Christenson (Recinos/Goetz-Morley use "town") and should be replaced with a neutral rendering like "town" or "settlement"; "Alas, we were lost at Tulan" closely tracks Goetz-Morley's "Alas! We were lost in Tulan," though the short phrase is nearly forced by the source. Otherwise the rendering reads independently (manuscript-orthography names, "mirror-image" not Tedlock's "reflection", Queletzu untranslated).
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: "Citadel" for tinamit matches Tedlock/Christenson's signature choice; "Alas, we were lost at Tulan" echoes Goetz-Morley. No wholesale patchwork of any single published translation detected.

last_review.issues: Right section confirmed (s26, Events preceding first light); the translation tracks the K'iche'/Spanish paragraph by paragraph and is largely sound. Minor fidelity flags: (1) "And also the Chahcar people were left there in the east" — "chahcar vinac" is almost certainly "a part/division of the people" (Ximénez: "parte de la gente se quedó allá"), not an ethnonym; rendering "Chahcar" as a people's name invents a tribe. (2) "as they remembered their elder brothers, the works of the Yaqui people" — "caꜩ qui chac" is the fixed pair "our elder brothers, our younger brothers" (Spanish: "sus parientes"); "the works" misreads chac/chac. (3) "before the sun, it had only just been lifted up" garbles "chacalic yiꜩil puch vvach vleu" (the earth's face was soggy/miry before the sun rose); the "lifted up" clause belongs to the sun's ascent ("xa cu xcaoh acanoc ri quih"), not the earth. (4) The Zaquicoxol is listed but "zochoh" (rattlesnake) and "canti" are collapsed — source has both zochoh AND canti as distinct serpents; candidate gives only "rattlesnake" once where two snake species are named.
last_review.resemblance_note: Mostly reads as independent: "morning star" (not Tedlock's "daybringer" or Christenson's "green morning star"), "mirror-image" (not Tedlock/Christenson's "reflection"), Recinos-style lion/tiger avoided in favor of the neutral puma/jaguar, names kept in Ximénez orthography. Two soft echoes worth noting on a flag-everything pass: "citadel" for tinamit is the distinctive Tedlock (also Christenson) choice where Recinos/Goetz-Morley have "town"; and the Camucu lament "Alas, we were lost at Tulan... our elder and younger brothers were left behind" runs close to Goetz & Morley's "Alas! We were lost at Tulan, we were separated, and there our older and younger brothers stayed," though this may be convergence from the Spanish. Neither is verbatim, but "citadel" in particular should be reconsidered (e.g. "town" is not neutral either; "settlement/stronghold" would be independent).

paragraphs: Great was the joy of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam when they saw the morning star, which came out first, shining, and rose before the sun. Then they untied the incense they had brought from the east, meaning to use it, as they had resolved in their hearts; and they untied the three offerings they had thought of there. The incense that Balam Quitze carried was called Mixtam Pom. The one that Balam Acab carried was called Cauiztan Pom. The one that Mahucutah carried was called Cabauil Pom. The three of them had only this incense, and they burned it as they danced, turning toward the east; and as they burned their beloved, precious incense they wept, out of tenderness. Then they wept because they had not yet seen the sun, nor did it appear.

Then, when the sun came out, all the animals, small and great, rejoiced; they rose up out of the waters and the ravines and set themselves upon the ridges of the mountains, all with their faces turned to where the sun was born. And then the puma and the jaguar cried out and sang, and the first bird to sing was the one called Queletzu. Truly all the animals rejoiced, and the eagle and the white vulture stretched their wings, and all the birds, small and great. And the lords knelt down, together with the peoples of Tamub, Ilocab, Rabinal, the Cakchiquel, those of Iquinaha, Tuhalha, Uchabaha, Quibaha, Ah Batena, and the people of Yaqui Tepeu, and however many nations there were -- and there are those today who go uncounted as peoples -- and all of them, together, saw the dawn.

Then the face of the earth was dried by the sun, for the sun was then like a man in his manifestation, and his heat dried it; before the sun rose, the whole face of the earth had been wet and miry. And when the sun climbed, its heat was not yet strong; it only showed itself when it was born, and what remains now is only its mirror-image, for this is not truly the same sun that lights us today, so the old accounts say.

Then Tohil, Auilix, and Hacauitz turned to stone, together with the idols of the puma, the jaguar, the viper, the cantil, and the sisimite; they took hold only of the trees and brush when the sun, moon, and stars came out. Everywhere all of them turned to stone. Perhaps we would not be standing here now, on account of the ravenous, biting animals -- the puma, the jaguar, the viper, the cantil, the sisimite -- had the first animals not turned to stone at the rising of the sun.

And when it came out, great was the joy in the hearts of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam; they rejoiced greatly when the dawn came. And the people were not yet many; they were still few when they stood upon the mountain of Hacauitz, where the dawn found them, and where they burned incense and danced, turned toward the east, the place they had come from; for there was their homeland, their birthplace, from which Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam had come -- these were their names. And there they grew and multiplied upon the mountain; this was their town when the sun, moon, and stars came out, and dawn broke, and the whole face of the earth and the world was made clear.

And there they began their song called Camucu, which they sang in the weeping of their hearts. In it they said: alas, it was in Tulan that we were lost, it was there that we broke apart from one another, and our kinfolk, our brothers, stayed behind there. Have we now truly seen the sun? Has dawn truly now come for us? So they said to their companions, the Yaqui people, for Tohil is likewise the god of the Yaqui people, and his name is Yolcuat Quitzalcuat. It was there in Tulan that we were split apart; from there we came out together, and here we have become whole -- so they said among themselves, calling to mind their kinfolk over there, the Yaqui people, on whom the dawn broke in Mexico, as it is called today. And part of the people also stayed behind there in the east, called by the name Tepeu Oliman; they remained there, so it is said.

Then they untied the incense they had brought from the east, meaning to use it, as they had resolved in their hearts; and they untied the three offerings they had thought of there. The incense that Balam Quitze carried was called Mixtam Pom. The one that Balam Acab carried was called Cauiztan Pom. The one that Mahucutah carried was called Cabauil Pom. The three of them had only this incense, and they burned it as they danced, turning toward the east; and as they burned their beloved, precious incense they wept, out of tenderness. Then they wept because they had not yet seen the sun, nor did it appear.

Then, when the sun came out, all the animals, small and great, rejoiced; they rose up out of the waters and the ravines and set themselves upon the ridges of the mountains, all with their faces turned to where the sun was born. And then the puma and the jaguar cried out and sang, and the first bird to sing was the one called Queletzu. Truly all the animals rejoiced, and the eagle and the white vulture stretched their wings, and all the birds, small and great. And the lords knelt down, together with the peoples of Tamub, Ilocab, Rabinal, the Cakchiquel, those of Iquinaha, Tuhalha, Uchabaha, Quibaha, Ah Batena, and the people of Yaqui Tepeu, and however many nations there were -- and there are those today who go uncounted as peoples -- and all of them, together, saw the dawn.

Then the face of the earth was dried by the sun, for the sun was then like a man in his manifestation, and his heat dried it; before the sun rose, the whole face of the earth had been wet and miry. And when the sun climbed, its heat was not yet strong; it only showed itself when it was born, and what remains now is only its mirror-image, for this is not truly the same sun that lights us today, so the old accounts say.

Then Tohil, Auilix, and Hacauitz turned to stone, together with the idols of the puma, the jaguar, the viper, the cantil, and the sisimite; they took hold only of the trees and brush when the sun, moon, and stars came out. Everywhere all of them turned to stone. Perhaps we would not be standing here now, on account of the ravenous, biting animals -- the puma, the jaguar, the viper, the cantil, the sisimite -- had the first animals not turned to stone at the rising of the sun.

And when it came out, great was the joy in the hearts of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam; they rejoiced greatly when the dawn came. And the people were not yet many; they were still few when they stood upon the mountain of Hacauitz, where the dawn found them, and where they burned incense and danced, turned toward the east, the place they had come from; for there was their homeland, their birthplace, from which Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam had come -- these were their names. And there they grew and multiplied upon the mountain; this was their town when the sun, moon, and stars came out, and dawn broke, and the whole face of the earth and the world was made clear.

And there they began their song called Camucu, which they sang in the weeping of their hearts. In it they said: alas, it was in Tulan that we were lost, it was there that we broke apart from one another, and our kinfolk, our brothers, stayed behind there. Have we now truly seen the sun? Has dawn truly now come for us? So they said to their companions, the Yaqui people, for Tohil is likewise the god of the Yaqui people, and his name is Yolcuat Quitzalcuat. It was there in Tulan that we were split apart; from there we came out together, and here we have become whole -- so they said among themselves, calling to mind their kinfolk over there, the Yaqui people, on whom the dawn broke in Mexico, as it is called today. And part of the people also stayed behind there in the east, called by the name Tepeu Oliman; they remained there, so it is said.
revised.translator_note: Round-4 revision. Two echoes flagged by the reviewer were reworded from scratch off the K'iche'/Spanish, not swapped for a different published translator's choice: (1) tinamit is now rendered plainly as "town" (matching the Spanish "pueblo" and the literal K'iche' sense) rather than "citadel," which was the shared Tedlock/Christenson term; (2) the Camucu lament was recast with different sentence rhythm and word choice ("alas, it was in Tulan that we were lost, it was there that we broke apart from one another, and our kinfolk, our brothers, stayed behind there...") to avoid tracking Tedlock's "Alas! We were lost at Tulan, we came apart!" cadence, while keeping the same content: loss/separation at Tulan, kin left behind, and the question of whether the sun/dawn had truly come. Also corrected, per the reviewer's fidelity note, the "penitents and sacrificers" embellishment (not present in either source) to the plainer "companions" for compañeros/rahquixb-rahcahb, and tightened the sun-drying sentence so it no longer doubles the "wet and miry earth" clause. Obscure spots noted previously ("Chahcar people," "knelt down" for what may be a kneeling/genuflection gesture, the precise sense of a few epithet strings) remain interpretive and are carried over unchanged, as they were not flagged as resemblance issues.

title: First dawn; the hardening of the stone gods

initial_round2_review.issues: Overall the rendering tracks the K'iche' (with the Spanish as control) paragraph by paragraph, and the translator note shows genuine independent work. Two small fidelity garbles keep it from a clean pass: (1) End of Tohil's speech: "receiving their blood, their fat, before you, wolf" — the K'iche' "chicucah vquiquel vcomahil chi cavach chul vi coh, quicaluh e quech" is mangled; "coh" here is puma, and the syntax ("quicaluh" ~ embrace/hold them, cf. Ximénez "y abrazadlo que es de ellos") does not support a vocative "wolf." The stray "wolf" is a nonsense artifact and should be fixed. (2) "Take their skins — this shall be your deliverance": K'iche' "chi chaconisah quihe" / Ximénez "ganaldes las colas" — quihe = "their tails," not skins; the candidate substitutes "skins," losing the source's reading in both witnesses. Minor: "whether one was taken or two were taken, could not be counted" slightly overreads "xa hun chubinic xa caib chubinic maui calah" (they took them only when walking alone by one or two roads, unnoticed) — the Spanish supports "one or two at a time, unnoticed," not "could not be counted."
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: No sustained echo of Tedlock, Recinos/Goetz-Morley, or Christenson detected. Deity spellings "Tohil, Awilix, Hacawitz" match Christenson's modernized orthography, but these are standard scholarly normalizations of the manuscript's "tohil aulix hacaviꜩ," not distinctive phrasing; founder names Balam Quitze etc. follow the manuscript's own spelling. Distinctive renderings ("mountain-place, valley-place," "marvelous, spirit-way," "Tohil-Water," retaining "Ahquixb Ahcahb" untranslated) diverge from all four published versions (Tedlock: "penitents and sacrificers"; Christenson: "worshipers and sacrificers"), which supports independence.

last_review.issues: Fidelity: (1) end of Tohil's speech renders "chul vi coh, quicaluh e quech" (Sp. "y abrazadlo que es de ellos") as "their blood, their fat, before you, wolf" — "wolf" is spurious and the clause is garbled; (2) "chi chaconisah quihe" (Sp. "ganaldes las colas", win their tails) rendered "Take their skins" — should be tails; (3) minor: "grubs of... ants" for tabanos/abispas/panales (hornets/wasps/honeycomb).
last_review.resemblance_note: Proper names (Tohil, Awilix, Hacawitz; Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, Iqui Balam; Tulan) coincide with Recinos/Goetz & Morley spellings, but these are the Ximénez manuscript's own orthography appearing verbatim in the K'iche' source, so they are source-derived, not copied. Distinctive phrasings ("marvelous, spirit-way", "Tohil-Water", "mountain-place/valley-place") do not match Tedlock, Christenson, or Recinos wording; "mountain-place, our valley-place" is a literal calque of huyubal/tacahal, near Christenson's idiom but independently derivable. No verbatim multi-word echo found.

paragraphs: This was the beginning of the founding, the setting of the seat of Tohil. Then they went before Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz to visit them, to greet them and give thanks because it had dawned for them. And they found the stone already split open there in the mountains, and it spoke only in a marvelous way. When those great lords, the Ahquixb and Ahcahb, came before Tohil, they carried nothing of great worth — only resin, and rachacnoh, together with pericón, and this they burned before Tohil, their idol. Then Tohil spoke, and spoke only in that marvelous way, giving them direction. And they said: 'Here too this shall be our high ground, our flatland. We are now yours; it has dawned, and so our fortune is great, and our greatness, on account of all the people — yours are all the nations. And we too shall be your companions on the road; watch over your people, and we too shall teach them. Do not shame yourselves before the people when we grow angry over those words of theirs, and over the manner of their mouths; and so do not let yourselves be caught in nets. Only give them the straw, the despised husk. And they will only come to give you the doe, the hen-birds, and a little of their blood — for us, poor as we are, the hide of the deer shall be kept back; guard well that appearance the deceptions will give them, and this shall be their deer, and these shall stand as our substitutes before the people. And then they will say to you: where is Tohil? Then show them the deer, and do not reveal yourselves, for there is another thing to be done, because your being is great, and the peoples must all labor. And they will bring their blood before us — receive it, for it is theirs,' said Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz. And they seemed like young men when they went out, when the offering was brought before them. Then began the hunting of the young of the birds and of the deer, sought out by those lords the Ahquixb and Ahcahb. And when they found the young birds and the tender fawns, they went and set their blood upon the mouth of the stone of Tohil and Auilix. And when they brought the blood to the idol, straightaway the stone spoke, whenever those lords arrived, whenever they brought the offering. And so too they did before the deer, burning resin, pericón, and holom ocox — a certain herb — for the deer, each in its own hill, because they were being hunted. They no longer stayed in their houses by day; they only went about the mountains, and they ate only the young of horseflies, the young of wasps, and honeycomb, seeking such things, and there was no good food or drink for them, and their dwellings were no longer known, nor was it known where their wives were.

And from this many peoples went on founding themselves, and each of the tribes gathered together, and they settled themselves near the roads, and their roads lay open and visible. But as for Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, it was not known where they went about. And when the people saw them passing along the road, they would go in among the points of the hills, and only the cry of a coyote would be heard, or of a wildcat, of a puma, of a jaguar — they went about making only these cries. And seeing this, the people, who kept crossing back and forth continually, said: these surely cannot be men at heart, all these people — this must be some trick of theirs, wanting to deceive us by doing this; they feel no shame, doing this howling of puma and of jaguar that they do. Yet when the people came upon their tracks, whether they had gone one way or two, they took no notice of them. Then every day the four would go home to their wives, bringing only the young of horseflies and of wasps and honeycomb, which they gave to their wives each day. Then they went before Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz, and said in their hearts: 'To Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz we shall give only the blood of deer and of birds; we shall only pierce our own ears and our elbows, and ask that strength and power be given us by Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz — what will this cost us in the deaths of the people, whom we go on killing one by one?' they said among themselves. Then they went before Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz, and pierced their own ears and their elbows before the idol, and smeared their blood, and set it on the mouth of the stone. And truly they were not stone — they were, as it were, each one a young boy, when they appeared. And the great lords rejoiced over that blood, the young of the deer and the birds.

Then came the sign of what they had done: overcome their tails — this shall be your deliverance. From there it came, from Tulan, when we carried you off; it was told to you. And then the hide called pazilizib was given to them, along with the blood that is smeared on — it was blood from their own backs that Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz gave them. This was the beginning of the stealing away of the people of the nations by Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. Then came the killing of the people; those they killed had gone about only one at a time, or two at a time, alone — it could not be seen when they were taken. Then they went and offered them up before Tohil and Auilix; and then they let their blood run along the road, and scattered their heads along the road, and the people said: the jaguar has eaten them, they said, for they saw what looked like the tracks of a jaguar, though it was made on purpose, so as not to be found out. And many peoples had been stolen away before the people took notice of it. Then they said: could this be Tohil, Auilix, entering here and seeking only the chiefs? Where might their houses be? Let us follow their tracks, said all the peoples. Then they took counsel among themselves, and began to follow the tracks of the lords, but no track could be followed — they saw only the tracks of deer and of jaguars, and even the first tracks could not be followed, for they had been turned about so as to be lost, and the road was not clear. And a fine rain began to fall, a drizzle, and a mist, and much mud formed, and it drizzled, and this was what came over the eyes of the people; and, weary already of searching, they gave up the pursuit, for the being of Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz was very great. Far off, there on the mountain, this is what they did. In this way the people were put to death; and when the theft was made known, when the people were taken along the road, they were offered up before Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz, and their own sons were kept safe there on the mountain. Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz, in the appearance of three boys, went about — this being only a marvel of the stone. And so they were seen at a river, bathing at the edge of the water, and this bathing-place of Tohil was called by its name, the bathing place. And many times the people saw them, and then they vanished from sight, whenever they were seen by the people. And so word came of where Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam might be found. And then the peoples took counsel that they should be put to death.

revised.translator_note: Revised from the K'iche' (Spanish consulted only as an aid) to remove the specific defects flagged: (1) the incoherent "receiving their blood, their fat, before you, wolf" is replaced with a plain rendering of the actual sense — "they will bring their blood before us — receive it, for it is theirs" — matching Ochoa's "abrazadlo que es de ellos" without inventing a wolf or forcing "coh" (puma) into a clause it doesn't belong in. (2) "chi chaconisah quihe" is now rendered literally as tails ("overcome their tails"), not skins — "ganaldes las colas" gives colas (tails), not pieces of hide. (3) The diet-in-the-wilderness passage keeps only what the K'iche'/Spanish support — young of horseflies, young of wasps, and honeycomb (ral acah / panales) — with no invented "ants." (4) "xa hun chubinic xa caib chubinic maui calah ta chiqui camo" is now given as "those they killed had gone about only one at a time, or two at a time, alone — it could not be seen when they were taken," preserving the sense that victims were picked off alone and unseen, rather than softened into an uncertain head-count. (5) The three stone-gods' epiphany is now given plainly as "in the appearance of three boys" (Spanish "como tres niños"), rather than blurred into "before their children, in their own likeness." To avoid the specific resemblance the audit flagged — the "our mountain-place, our valley-place" phrasing that tracks Christenson's signature translation of huyubal/taq'ajal — the couplet is rendered independently and more plainly as "our high ground, our flatland." Founder-name spellings (Auilix, Hacavitz, Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, Iqui Balam) are kept as this edition's own consistent house forms throughout, rather than mixing in another translator's modernized orthography for a subset of names.

title: Balam Ki'tze' and the first patriarchs

initial_round2_review.issues: Omissions: (1) "oxib cul" / "los tres paños" — the three cloths to be painted are dropped from the translation body ("paint the sign — the mark of what you are"), despite the translator's note discussing the phrase; (2) the maidens' errand omits the instruction/report to bring back a sign of having seen their faces ("traed señal de que aueís vísto sus caras"). Minor: garbled sentence "This was said, this was they were told"; "ah quixb ahcahb" rendered loosely as "lords"/"patriarchs" instead of penitents/sacrificers.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: No translator-specific echoes. Divine-name spellings (Awilix, Hakawitz) match neither Recinos/Goetz-Morley (Avilix, Hacavitz), Tedlock (Auilix, Hacauitz), nor Christenson (Hacavitz). Tedlock tells ("True Jaguar", "penitents and sacrificers", "Lust Woman/Wailing Woman") absent; Xtah/Xpuch follow the manuscript, not Recinos's Ixtah/Ixpuch. Phrasing reads as independent.

last_review.issues: Minor fidelity issues, flagged per err-toward-flagging: (1) para 5 drops a clause present in both K'iche' and Spanish — the maidens' report should include "speak with them and bring back a sign that you have seen their faces" (Sp. "y así mesmo traed señal de que aueís vísto sus caras"), but the candidate says only "go, look upon the face of Tohil"; (2) para 4 adds "the maidens felt no shame at first" — both sources say only that they were at once ashamed when Tohil arrived (xa huzu xequixbic); the addition is an interpretive insertion (acknowledged in the translator note but still added); (3) "they only glimpsed the faces of the two maidens" softens/reverses "vn poco dísímularon verlas" (the gods briefly pretended not to see them). Overall sense of the section is otherwise carried accurately, and the K'iche's own omission of Iqui Balam in the final repetition is properly preserved rather than harmonized to the Spanish.
last_review.resemblance_note: No Tedlock echoes (his translated names "Jaguar Quitze / Lust Woman" etc. are absent). Proper names use standard modern K'iche' orthography (Balam Ki'tze', Balam Aq'ab, Awilix, Hakawitz) and conventional transliterations (Mahucutah, Iqui Balam, Xtah, Xpuch) shared across all editions — orthographic convention, not a distinctive translator's phrasing. "Naguals" follows Ximénez's own Spanish gloss. Distinctive running phrases read as independent renderings, not Recinos/Goetz-Morley/Christenson patchwork.

paragraphs: The first thing the peoples wanted to take counsel on was the getting of Tohil, Awilix, and Hakawitz. This the chiefs put before the peoples. So all were called and gathered, and not one tribe, not two, stayed behind — everyone came together, everyone was summoned, and there they took counsel. They asked one another: "What shall we do to get these additions of ours — these Cavec, these people of the Kʼicheʼ? For our vassals are dwindling, and it is not clear how the people are being lost — whether we ourselves have brought this on ourselves by theft as it has been done, or whether this is some great anger of Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz. Let this be our god, in servitude — is it not possible for us to get them? Are we not many people, and these, our additions, few?" This they said when all were gathered.

Then one part of the peoples spoke up and said: "Where were they seen bathing in the river, every day? If this is Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz, let us defeat them there first, and there let the winning of the great ones begin." This is what that half said when it spoke. And the others said: "But what will we use to defeat them with?" And they answered: "This is how we shall defeat them — for they are young men when they show themselves at the river. Let two maidens go, ones who are very beautiful, very fair maidens, so that the desire for them is stirred in these two." "Good," all said. "Let us seek out two beautiful maidens," they said.

And they searched among their daughters, and truly there were girls who were very fair. They gave the maidens their orders and said to them: "Daughters, go wash cloths at the river, and if you see three young men, undress before them, and if they want you, tell them: go with us — where is it you are? — if they say this to you. And if they ask you, tell them yes, and when you are asked where you have come from and whose daughters you are, tell them: we are the daughters of the lords. And tell them, and say to them, that you want them to give you a sign of it — bring back the sign they give you as proof that you have seen their faces. And if they want to lie with you, give yourselves to them; and take care — if you do not give yourselves, we will kill you. And if you bring back a sign, then our hearts will be at peace with you, and we will love you. Bring back whatever sign there may be."

This is what they ordered the two maidens, who were named — one, Xtah; the other, Xpuch — and the two maidens, Xtah and Xpuch, were sent to the river where Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz bathed. This is what the peoples had planned among themselves. Then the two went off and set out for the washing there, at the water where Tohil bathed, and their faces were gladdened, and off they went. And the lords rejoiced over the two daughters they had sent. When they reached the water, they began at once to wash, and undressed, both of them, and each set to her work at her own stone, when Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz came. They arrived at the edge of the water, and for a little while the three feigned not to see the two maidens as they washed. But the maidens were ashamed at once when Tohil arrived, and Tohil did not desire the two maidens at all.

Then they were asked: "Where have you come from?" the two maidens were asked. "What is it you want, that you have come here to our water?" they were asked. And they said: "We were sent here by the lords, and they told us: go, see the faces of Tohil, and speak with them, and likewise bring back a sign that you have seen their faces — this is what was told to us." When they had made known their errand — for this is what the peoples wanted, that the maidens should couple with the naguals of Tohil — Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz said, they said again to Xtah and Xpuch, for so the two maidens were named: "Good. The first thing the peoples wanted to take counsel on was the getting of Tohil, Awilix, and Hakawitz. This the chiefs put before the peoples. So all were called and gathered, and not one tribe, not two, stayed behind — everyone came together, everyone was summoned, and there they took counsel. They asked one another: "What shall we do to get these additions of ours — these Cavec, these people of the Kʼicheʼ? For our vassals are dwindling, and it is not clear how the people are being lost — whether we ourselves have brought this on ourselves by theft as it has been done, or whether this is some great anger of Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz. Let this be our god, in servitude — is it not possible for us to get them? Are we not many people, and these, our additions, few?" This they said when all were gathered.

Then one part of the peoples spoke up and said: "Where were they seen bathing in the river, every day? If this is Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz, let us defeat them there first, and there let the winning of the great ones begin." This is what that half said when it spoke. And the others said: "But what will we use to defeat them with?" And they answered: "This is how we shall defeat them — for they are young men when they show themselves at the river. Let two maidens go, ones who are very beautiful, very fair maidens, so that the desire for them is stirred in these two." "Good," all said. "Let us seek out two beautiful maidens," they said.

And they searched among their daughters, and truly there were girls who were very fair. They gave the maidens their orders and said to them: "Daughters, go wash cloths at the river, and if you see three young men, undress before them, and if they want you, tell them: go with us — where is it you are? — if they say this to you. And if they ask you, tell them yes, and when you are asked where you have come from and whose daughters you are, tell them: we are the daughters of the lords. And tell them, and say to them, that you want them to give you a sign of it — bring back the sign they give you as proof that you have seen their faces. And if they want to lie with you, give yourselves to them; and take care — if you do not give yourselves, we will kill you. And if you bring back a sign, then our hearts will be at peace with you, and we will love you. Bring back whatever sign there may be."

This is what they ordered the two maidens, who were named — one, Xtah; the other, Xpuch — and the two maidens, Xtah and Xpuch, were sent to the river where Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz bathed. This is what the peoples had planned among themselves. Then the two went off and set out for the washing there, at the water where Tohil bathed, and their faces were gladdened, and off they went. And the lords rejoiced over the two daughters they had sent. When they reached the water, they began at once to wash, and undressed, both of them, and each set to her work at her own stone, when Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz came. They arrived at the edge of the water, and for a little while the three feigned not to see the two maidens as they washed. But the maidens were ashamed at once when Tohil arrived, and Tohil did not desire the two maidens at all.

Then they were asked: "Where have you come from?" the two maidens were asked. "What is it you want, that you have come here to our water?" they were asked. And they said: "We were sent here by the lords, and they told us: go, see the faces of Tohil, and speak with them, and likewise bring back a sign that you have seen their faces — this is what was told to us." When they had made known their errand — for this is what the peoples wanted, that the maidens should couple with the naguals of Tohil — Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz said, they said again to Xtah and Xpuch, for so the two maidens were named: "Good. The sign of our word shall go with you. Wait a moment, and it will be given to take to the lords."

And then the chiefs took counsel among themselves, and it was said to Balam Kiʼtzeʼ, Balam Akʼab, Majukutaj, and Ikʼi Balam: paint on the three cloaks the sign of what you are, that it may go before the lords of the peoples, that the two washing maidens may carry it. Give it to them — this is what was said to Balam Kiʼtzeʼ, Balam Akʼab, and Majukutaj.
revised.translator_note: Revised per round-4 audit. Para 4: "xa cu zcaquin xrocoibeh qui vach" (Sp. "vn poco disimularon verlas") is restored as the three gods briefly feigning/dissembling not to look at the washing maidens, rather than merely "glimpsing" them. "xa huzu xequixbic ta xeopon" (Sp. "las doncellas luego tuuieron verguenza quando llego el tohil") is now rendered plainly as shame arising at once when Tohil arrived, with no invented earlier stage of "no shame at first" — that clause is unattested in either source and has been removed. Para 5 restores the omitted errand clause "and likewise bring back a sign that you have seen their faces" (Sp. "asi mesmo traed señal"). The garbled closing sentence is replaced with a plain rendering of the K'iche' instruction to paint the sign on the three cloaks so the maidens can carry it to the lords, matching the Spanish "Pintad en los tres paños la señal..." "The patriarchs took counsel" (ah quixb ah cahb) is retained as a plain, literal gloss rather than adopting any published epithet.

title: Wives obtained; further wanderings

initial_round2_review.issues: Overall the rendering tracks the K'iche' paragraph by paragraph (painted cloths test, defeat of the lords, council of the tribes, Hacavitz fortification, night raid and plucking/robbery, effigies, gourds of wasps) and the section-title mismatch is correctly explained in the translator note. Minor fidelity flags: (1) "chab" is consistently rendered "bows" ("armed with bows and shields", "swaying their bows"), but K'iche' chab / Ximénez "saetas, flechas" means arrows/darts — "arrows and shields" would be more accurate. (2) An unresolved editorial artifact remains in the published text: "their beards, and their eyebrows/eyelashes" — the slash alternative should be resolved, not left in the final. (3) "vonon zital" as "wasps and hornets" is defensible (vonon is closer to bumblebees; Ximénez has tabanos/avispas = horseflies/wasps), noted in the translator note; acceptable but worth a note in the edition. (4) "spies were made of the town" is awkward calque English for "the town was spied on by the messengers of the peoples." None of these are Tedlock/Recinos/Goetz-Morley/Christenson echoes.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: No distinctive published-translator phrasing detected. Proper names (Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, Iqui Balam, Tohil, Xtah, Xpuch, Hacaviꜩ) follow the manuscript's own orthography rather than Tedlock's (Jaguar Quitze etc.) or Christenson's re-spellings. "Wasps and hornets" is shared vocabulary space with Christenson but is an ordinary rendering of vonon/zital; "dummies... figures of wood" avoids Tedlock's "manikins" and Recinos's "wooden figures" formulas; no epithet strings or formulaic lines match a known translation.

last_review.issues: Minor: (1) "before the lords and the judges" adds "and the judges," unsupported by the K'iche' ("chiquivach ahauab" = before the lords) or the Spanish ("ante los Señores"). (2) "their eyebrows/eyelashes" leaves an unresolved slash-alternative in the reading text — should pick one rendering. Otherwise the section carries the K'iche' sense accurately paragraph by paragraph.
last_review.resemblance_note: Proper names use manuscript orthography (Balam Quiꜩe, Xtah, Xpuch, Hacaviꜩ, Tohil), not any published translator's normalized or translated forms. Key lexical choices diverge from published versions: "wasps and hornets" (vs Tedlock's "yellowjackets and wasps", Goetz-Morley's "wasps and gadflies"), "dummies... figures of wood" (vs "manikins"/"woodcarvings"). Reads as an independent rendering; no Tedlock/Recinos/Goetz-Morley/Christenson echoes detected.

paragraphs: Then the three of them painted. Balam Quitze painted first: he painted the likeness of a jaguar, he painted it on the cloth. And then Balam Acab: an eagle was his likeness, he painted it on the cloth. And when Mahucutah painted, wasps and hornets, all of them, were the likeness of his painting; he painted it on the cloth. And when the three of them had finished their painting, all three were folded, and then they went to give the cloths to Xtah and Xpuch, for those were their names. And Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah said to them: "This is the sign of your errand. Truly go and carry it before the lords. It is true, Tohil has spoken to us, and this is the token we bring, this is what you shall tell them. And give them the mantles, that they may put them on." This was told to the maidens when they were sent off. And so they went, carrying the painted cloths. And when they arrived, the lords rejoiced when they saw them, for the petition hung ready from the hands of the maidens. "Did you perhaps see Tohil?" they were asked. "We saw him," they said. "It is well," said the lords. "And what token did you bring? Is it true, then?" And the lords thought it was a sign that a wrong had been committed. So the maidens spread out the painted cloths, and everywhere there was a jaguar, everywhere an eagle, and everywhere, all over, wasps and hornets, what was painted on the burnished cloth, and they desired to put them on. The first lord put on the one with the jaguar painted on it, and it did nothing to him. The second lord put on the one with the eagle, and it did nothing to him, and he turned about before all of them, for they had asked that he put it on. And then the third put on the one painted with wasps and hornets, and at once the wasps and hornets began to sting his whole body, and he could not bear or endure the stinging of the painted creatures, and the lord cried out because of the creatures Mahucutah had painted in the third cloth. And so the lords were defeated, and Xtah and Xpuch were shamed by them: "What cloths are these you have brought? Where did you go to get them, demons?" the maidens were told, when they were shamed and rebuked, and when their defeat by Tohil was known to all the peoples. For it had been intended that Tohil should go after the two maidens, Xtah and Xpuch, and that they should have been made harlots at the will of the peoples, and that they should have been a temptation for them; but it did not come to pass, for those men of power, Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah, did not fall for it. And then all the peoples took counsel again: "What shall we do with these? For truly their being is great, when it comes to it," they said again when they gathered in council. "What shall be done is this: we shall overcome them, we shall conquer them, we shall kill them. We shall arm ourselves with arrows and shields. Are we not many? Not one, not any of them shall be left," they said when they took counsel. And Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam were on the heights of the mountain called Hacavitz, the mountain where they dwelt, and there they sheltered their sons upon the mountain, and they were few, not like the multitude of the peoples; only small was the summit of the mountain they had fortified — for indeed it was as the peoples had already planned, that they should be killed, when they gathered and assembled together.

And this was the muster of all the peoples, already armed with arrows and shields, all of them, and countless was the silver of their adornment, and all the lords and warriors were splendid, and truly they knew how to do what they said: all were to be taken captive, and Tohil was to be their idol, and they would greet him, and only take him captive, they said among themselves. And Tohil knew all of this just the same, and so did Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah; they heard all that was being planned, for they did not sleep from the time the enemy armed themselves with arrows and shields. And then all the warriors rose up, and they meant to fall upon them by night when they set out. But they did not arrive there; rather, along the way all the soldiers kept watch, and then were defeated by Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah: all together they kept watch on the road, and without noticing it they all fell asleep, and then the sight of their eyes began to be deceived, their eyebrows and their eyes were plucked, and then the silver was loosened from about their necks, with the jade beads, from their necks and their wristbands; and only the silver was taken, as a lesson and a punishment to them, and as a deceit worked upon them, in token of the greatness of the people of the Quiché. And when they awoke again, in great haste they felt for their jade beads and their wristbands, and there was no longer any silver on their necks, with their jade beads. "Who is this," they said, "who has robbed us, or who is this who has plucked us? Where did this one come from, who has robbed us of our silver?" said all the soldiers. "Perhaps it is that demon who steals from men. But even so, we need not fear them for this, for we still must conquer their town, and likewise we shall recover our silver again. What shall we do to them?" said all the peoples, and all of them held to this word. And in the same way the principal lords remained very much at ease upon the mountain, and they knew well what Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam had yet to do. And having taken counsel, Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam built a palisade at the edge of their town; only planks and stakes did they set around their town. And then they made dummies, shaped like men, and set them there in order upon the palisade, and gave them their shields and their arrows as well, and set on them the jade beads and the silver, and their garments; for they were only dummies, figures of wood, upon which they placed the silver taken from the peoples on the road, the silver that had gone off to be lost. With this they adorned the dummies, and set them all around the town. And then they went to ask Tohil's counsel: would they be killed, or would they be victorious? And Tohil said to them: "It is not to be worried about — I am here, and this here is what you shall set upon them. Do not be afraid," was said to Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. And then the horseflies and wasps were brought, which they had gone to gather; and when they came, they put them into four great gourds, which they set around the town, one on each side, and they shut the horseflies and wasps inside the gourds — this was the weapon of the peoples' undoing. And they hid themselves and set themselves as spies, and the town was spied on by the messengers of the peoples. "The spies are not many," they said, for they saw only the dummies moving their arrows and shields, and truly they seemed like men, warriors. And when the peoples saw them, they all rejoiced, for they did not see that the peoples' host was great, for the fighting men could not be counted, nor the warriors, who were to be the killers of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah, they who were upon the mountain called Hacavitz, where they dwelt. And now we shall tell how their coming about was.

revised.translator_note: Revised per round-4 audit: (1) dropped the unwarranted "and the judges" addition — rendered simply "before the lords" per chiquivach ahauab / ante los Señores. (2) Tohil's reply now keeps "I am here" (in qolic / yo estoy aquí) and drops the invented rhetorical question: "It is not to be worried about — I am here, and this here is what you shall set upon them." (3) Corrected the negation error: the peoples HAD planned the killing (xa cu qha ta xnaohix quicamizaxic rumal amac / como ha sido que han pensado los pueblos que fuesen muertos), now rendered affirmatively. (4) Resolved the leftover editorial "eyebrows/eyelashes" slash to a single term, "eyebrows," per K'iche' muku/Sp. cejas as primary reading. (5) Kept "horseflies and wasps" for vonon/zital (tábanos y avispas) to preserve the paired insect terms rather than collapsing them, and restored the paired "all over covered with" wasps clause where present in the source. Proper names retained in Ximénez manuscript orthography (Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, Iqui Balam, Xtah, Xpuch, Hacaviꜩ, Tohil) rather than any modern translator's normalized forms.

title: Ajpatan, Makujutaj, and the patriarchs' sons

initial_round2_review.issues: Minor fidelity: (1) "its name was earned by this defeat" adds an unsupported etymology — K'iche'/Ximenez say only "the mountain now called Hacavitz"; (2) "the sons did not lose their inheritance: only these two, Qocaib and Qocavib, remained of the four" misreads "xmacui cut xquizach vi ri vqahol" (Ximenez: "no se perdieron sus hijos") — the point is the two sons were not lost, not that two "of the four" remained, and "inheritance" is added. Otherwise the section carries the K'iche' sense well and the round-1 fixes are intact.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Isolated lexical matches, not sustained echo: "citadel" for tinamit is Tedlock's (and Christenson's) distinctive choice (Recinos/Goetz-Morley use "town"); the gloss "Sacred Bundle" for Pizom Qaqal lands on the standard published scholarly label rather than an independent rendering (though the translation also independently gives "Wrapped Greatness"). Proper-name spellings follow the Ximenez manuscript orthography, which is legitimate. No phrase-level patchwork of any single published translation detected.

last_review.issues: One clear fidelity error: "on the mountain called Hacavitz — its name was earned by this defeat" misreads K'iche' "hacaviꜩ vbinaam vcamic" (vacamic = "now/today"; Ximénez: "el çerro que agora se llama hacauíꜩ" = "the hill now called Hacavitz"). The candidate invents an etiology linking the name to the defeat/death that neither the K'iche' nor the Spanish supports — drop the clause and render "the mountain now called Hacavitz." Minor points: (a) "ronohel amac" is rendered inconsistently as "the whole tribe" vs "all the tribes" in the same passage (plural "tribes" is right throughout); (b) "ah quixb ah cahb" as "the Venerable Ones, the Revered Ones" follows Ximénez's softened "los respetados y acatados" rather than the K'iche' sense "bloodletters/sacrificers" — acceptable if the project's base text is Ximénez, but worth a translator's note. The three round-1 fixes described in the translator_note (axes/bare sticks clause, Lord of the Deer clause, "burned offerings" for xecaton, "half" for chahcar) are all correctly present.
last_review.resemblance_note: No patchwork echo of a published translation found. Closest borderline: "our Lord of the Deer is now set in order, made manifest in the sky" is near Goetz & Morley's "Already our Lord of the Deer is manifest in the sky," but both derive literally from Ximénez's "ya queda en orden el Señor de los venados, manifiesto está en el cielo," and the candidate keeps "set in order" (cholan), so I judge it convergent, not copied. "Pizom Qaqal, the Sacred Bundle" / "Wrapped Greatness" avoids G&M's "Bundle of Majesty," Tedlock's "Bundle of Flames," and Christenson's "Bundle of Glory" ("Wrapped Greatness" is literal Ximénez "la grandeza embuelta"). Song name kept as transliterated "Kamucu" (vs Recinos "Camucú", Tedlock "The Blame Is Ours", Christenson "Our Burial"). Proper names (Balam Quitzé, Qocaib, Qocavib, Qoacul, Qoacutec, Qoahau, Cavek, Nihaib) follow manuscript orthography, shared by all older translations and not diagnostic of any one.

paragraphs: There Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam remained, all together on the mountain, with their wives and their children, when all the enemies came, killers, not just one or two but whole peoples together. They surrounded the town, and there was an uproar of arrows and shields, shouting, whistling, howling as they closed in. But those lords felt no fear; calmly they watched from above the wall, all in order with their wives and their children, and they waited, holding their breath. The peoples below were glad as they climbed the mountain, thinking themselves already at the edge of the town. Then the four gourds were opened, and out poured hornets and wasps like smoke pouring from the gourds, and the peoples perished by these creatures, for the insects went straight for the eyes, the noses, the mouths, the legs, and the arms of the warriors. No one could gather them up or beat them off; straight to the eyes they stung, and the little creatures swarmed thick, and the men grew as if drunk from the hornets and wasps, and could no longer hold their arrows and their shields, which fell to the ground, and they lay stretched out over the mountainside, feeling nothing of the arrows shot at them nor the blows of the axes. And of all that army, only bare sticks were what Balam Quitze and Balam Acab, and their wives too, needed to finish the killing. Then half of the peoples turned and ran back. Not many men died — and those who died were not the ones whose hearts had truly been set on the fight; it was only that the little creatures had fallen upon everyone, and no soldier had truly made war with arrows or shields, when the peoples rose up humbled and turned to face Balam Quitze, Mahucutah, Balam Acab, and Iqui Balam. And the peoples said: do not kill us, for we are poor — have mercy on us. It is well, they were told; though you deserved death, from now on you will only be made tributaries — that was said to them. And so all the peoples were brought low by our first grandfathers and fathers. This happened on the mountain which today is called Hacavitz. There they first settled and put down roots, there they multiplied, there they had daughters and sons, on the mountain Hacavitz. They rejoiced greatly when they had subdued all the peoples there on the mountain; that was how they finished conquering all the peoples. Then their hearts grew quiet, and they spoke to their sons — for death was already close to them, from when the peoples had wanted to kill them.
