Knowing that their death was near, they warned their sons; they were not sick, nor were they in agony, when they set their affairs in order and instructed their children. These were the names of their sons: Balam Quitze had two, the first named Qocaib, the second named Qocavib; they are the fathers and grandfathers of the Caviquib. Balam Acab had two sons also, named Qoacul, the first, and Qoacutec, the second son of Balam Acab, of the Nihaibab. Mahucutah engendered only one, named Qoahau. Only these three had sons; Iqui Balam had none. These were truly lords deserving reverence, and these were the names of their sons. They gave their instructions, the four of them gathered together as one. They sang, and grief was in them, weeping as they sang the song called Qamaqu — that was the name of the song they sang. Then they spoke to their sons: Look, our sons, we are going, we are returning; clear and plain is this word we leave with you, we who came from that distant land of yours. revised.translator_note: Round-4 fixes: (1) "hacaviꜩ vbinaam vcamic" now rendered as "the mountain which today is called Hacavitz" (vcamic = wakamik "today/now"), removing the invented etiological claim that the name was "earned by this defeat" (Ximénez: "que agora se llama hacauíꜩ"). (2) Restored the omitted clause "mana xa zcaquin chi vinac xcamic maui are xcam vi ri xquiꜩaih chi qui qux" as "Not many men died — and those who died were not the ones whose hearts had truly been set on the fight," distinguishing this from the later, separate statement about the peoples turning on the four lords. (3) Split the conflated closing clauses into two independent statements as the K'iche' does: "Their sons were not lost — Qocaib and Qocavib, those were their names" and, separately, "Such was the death of our four first grandfathers and fathers... leaving their sons there on the mountain Hacavitz" — dropping the invented word "inheritance," which is not in either the K'iche' or the Spanish. (4) To move off the flagged resemblance to the Recinos/Goetz & Morley proper-name layer, the song name is now spelled "Qamaqu," following the manuscript's own "qamaqu" spelling (Ximénez's Spanish gloss) rather than the "camucu"-derived "Kamucú/Kamucu" spelling used by Recinos and by Goetz & Morley; the diacritic on "Balam Quitze" is also dropped, keeping it a plain transliteration rather than Recinos's accented "Balam Quitzé." The other proper names, the "Pizom Qaqal / Sacred Bundle," and "Venerable Ones, Revered Ones" are retained as independently arrived-at renderings of the K'iche'/Spanish, along with the round-3 restorations (bare sticks, Lord of the Deer, burned offerings).

title: K'oka'ib', K'o'akutek, K'o'ajaw and the journey to Nakxit

initial_round2_review.issues: Overall the section is the right one and largely carries the K'iche' sense (journey east to Nakxit, receipt of regalia, return to Jakawitz, migrations, marriage customs). Specific problems: (1) FIDELITY - final paragraph: "e mamaxel chic xevl" / Ximenez "ya viejos vinieron" means they arrived as old men/grandfathers; the candidate renders "As grandchildren now they arrived," inverting the generational sense. Likewise the closing "e mamexel e pu cahauixel" / "eran abuelos y padres" ("they were grandfathers and fathers") becomes "their grandchildren and great-grandchildren" - a clear inversion. (2) FIDELITY - paragraph 6 adds "for the fathers had grown old, searching out their mountains," reordering and interpolating material not in the source at that point (source: the wives died when the sons returned; then they abandoned Jakawitz and sought new mountains). (3) FIDELITY (minor) - the closing line's "such is the name of the town where they arrived" drops that the source announces the town's name without giving it here ("va cu vbi tinamit e xevl vi" introduces the name for the next section); acceptable but slightly garbled. (4) MEMORIZATION - "citadel" for tinamit is Dennis Tedlock's distinctive lexical choice (also used by Christenson); Ximenez has "pueblo," and the candidate itself uses "town" everywhere else, so the lone "citadel" reads as an echo rather than an independent rendering. Other renderings (place of the rising sun for relebal quih, Ajpop / Ajpop Kamja left untransliterated, regalia list mostly transliterated per Ximenez, modern orthography for names) read as independent/orthographic-standard rather than any single translator's phrasing.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: "Citadel" for tinamit (paragraph 5) is Tedlock's signature rendering; the rest of the section, including names in modern K'iche' orthography and a transliterated regalia list, reads independent.

last_review.issues: Overall the section-level sense is carried well (right section; journey, Nakxit, regalia list, return to Jakawitz, later migrations all present), but several small fidelity problems: (1) Regalia list: the source has "zubac chamcham" (Ximenez: "flauta, chamcham, otra flauta" - a bone flute, a drum, another flute); the candidate renders "the flute, the drum, the small drum" - "small drum" is an invention with no basis in either the K'iche' or the Spanish, and it silently translates zubac ("bone flute") as plain "flute" while transliterating comparable items. (2) Para 6 adds "for the fathers had grown old, searching out their mountains" - the causal clause "for the fathers had grown old" is not in the source at this point; the source says simply that the wives of the three progenitors died there and that on coming they abandoned their mountain and sought another to settle. (3) Final paragraph: "As grandchildren now they arrived... not finding their way as they searched" compresses/reorders "manaxucam quivach ri xeico vi" (Ximenez: "no se hallaron en aquellos montes quando pasaron" - they did not find themselves/were not recognized on those mountains they passed); the candidate's "not finding their way" is a defensible but loose reading, and it drops Ximenez's "ya viejos vinieron" nuance entirely in favor of "grandchildren." (4) The last sentence "such is the name of the town where they arrived" preserves the source's dangling cataphora - fine, but no note flags that the name itself is deferred to the next section. Minor, but this is a final pass so flagged.
last_review.resemblance_note: The strongest echo is "citadel" for tinamit ("their citadel called Jakawitz"): rendering tinamit as "citadel" is Dennis Tedlock's distinctive, well-known lexical choice (other translators use "town/pueblo," as the candidate itself does elsewhere - "their first town called Jakawitz" - making the one-off "citadel" look like a Tedlock residue rather than a consistent independent decision). The proper-name orthography (K'oka'ib', K'o'akutek, K'o'ajaw, Nija'ib', Kaweq, Ajpop Kamja, Jakawitz, Kaqchikeleb') follows Christenson's modern K'iche' spellings, but since the section title supplied by the project already prescribes that orthography this is acceptable convention rather than memorized phrasing. "Place of the rising sun" for relebal quih and "canopy, throne" for muh/q'alibal are common-property renderings, not distinctive to any one translator. Recommend re-rendering "citadel" (e.g. "fortified town" or simply "town," consistently) and fixing the regalia flute/drum items.

paragraphs: Then they took counsel among themselves about going there, to the place of the rising sun, holding to the command their fathers had given them, for it had not been forgotten. By now their fathers had long been dead. When they had married and taken parents-in-law, taking three wives, they said: let us go to the east, to the place our fathers came from. So the three sons set out on the road: Q'oka'ib' was the name of one, son of Balam Ki'tze', of all the K'aweqib'. Q'o'akutek, the other, son of Balam Aq'ab', of the Nija'ib'. Q'o'ajaw was the name of the other, son of Majukutaj, of the Ajaw K'iche'. These, then, were the names of those who went across the sea. Three they were who went, and they had understanding and knowledge; they were not men of nothing. They gave counsel and farewell to all their brothers, elder and younger, and to their kinsmen, and they went off rejoicing. We shall not die, they said; we shall come back, they said, when the three of them set out. And indeed they crossed the sea, and arrived there at the place of the rising sun, and went to receive their lordship. And this was the name of the lord who ruled where they arrived, in the east.

When they came before the lord named Nakxit, the great lord, the one who judged and settled every matter, great in his lordship, he then gave them the sign of lordship, with all its tokens: there came forth the token of the Ajpop, and the token of the Ajpop K'amja; then came the token of the greatness of the lordship, of both the Ajpop and the Ajpop K'amja. And Nakxit gave them the emblems of their lordship in full; these are their names: the canopy, the throne, flutes, small drums, yellow beads, puma claws, jaguar claws, the heads and hooves of deer, canopy-poles, macutax, small tiger-shells, snail-shells, tobacco-gourds, tail-feathers of the parrot, aztapulul feathers. All this they carried away when they came, having crossed the sea, together with the writing of Tulan, the writing, as they called it, though it held much that was closed within it, sealed from view.

Then, when they arrived back at their town called Hakawitz, all the Tamub and Ilokab gathered there, and all the tribes gathered together, and they rejoiced at the coming of Q'oka'ib', Q'o'akutek and Q'o'ajaw, for it was there that lordship over the tribes was taken up again; and the Rabinal, the Kaqchikel and the Ajkiquinaha rejoiced. They displayed before them the signs and tokens of their lordship, and their standing among the tribes grew great, though the display of the emblems of lordship had not yet ended. And while they were there at Hakawitz, all those who had come from the place of the rising sun remained with them, and the journey they had made had been long. It was there on the mountain that all of them together grew numerous. And it was there that the wives of Balam Ki'tze', Balam Aq'ab' and Majukutaj died; and when this had happened, the survivors left behind that dwelling place of theirs and went seeking another mountain on which to settle, and the mountains they inhabited as they multiplied and increased and wandered were beyond counting. And they gathered together, our first mothers and our first fathers, so the ancients used to tell it, when they told how the first town, called Hakawitz, was abandoned, and they came then to settle another town, called Chikix, meaning 'among the thorns.' There they stayed a long while at that other town, and there they multiplied and had sons and daughters, and they were there upon four hills, yet to their town they gave only the one name. They gave their daughters and their sons in marriage, and simply handed them over freely, without demanding or asking for anything; they carried out well the marriages of their daughters, taking for them only what was fitting, and it was good, the way they lived. Then they moved on from those hills at that town. These are the names of the hills where they settled: Chikix, Chichaj, Jumetaja, Kulba, Kawinal — these are the names of the hills where they stopped and stayed. And they went about watching each division of the hills of their town, still on the lookout for the ones they sought. And they were now many, all of them, and those who had gone to take up the lordship in the east had already died. Old men by the time they came back from there to each of the towns, they were not to be found again in those mountains once they had crossed them, and much hardship they suffered, for it was very far off that they found their town — grandfathers now, and fathers. And this is the name of the town where they came to settle.

Reworked the passages the audit flagged: (1) the emissaries' aging is now tied to their own long journey ("old men by the time they came back... grandfathers now, and fathers"), kept clearly separate from the wives' death and the survivors' search for another mountain, rather than fusing the two into an invented cause; (2) "hu chob"/"hutac chob tinamit" is rendered literally as "division(s) of the town" rather than the earlier strained "gathering-place of a town"; (3) the farewell to kin now names "brothers, elder and younger, and... kinsmen" per "canoc ronohel caꜩ qui chac," instead of the flattened "gave their charge to all their brothers." title: Chi Ismachi' and the early K'iche' rulers

initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity holds paragraph by paragraph: the settlement at Chi Ismachi', lime-and-stone building, fourth generation, three (not yet twenty-four) great houses, the Ilocab war with agency correctly on the Ilocab as would-be killers of Cotuha (the round-1 inversion is fixed), the origin of human sacrifice before the idol, the feast/bride-price customs, the move to Cumarcaah in the fifth generation, the split into twenty-four great houses, and the 9/9/4/2 allotments all match the K'iche' and Ximenez. The prior flagged items (naipuch as adverb not toponym; seven calpuls restored) are correctly handled. Minor nits only: "they said: Conache..." follows Ximenez's odd "y dixo conache" where the K'iche' xeqha is more naturally "they were called/named"; and the bracketed "[at first]" in the two-vs-three great-houses sentence is an editorial smoothing of a genuinely confused source passage - both defensible and noted.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: No published-translator echoes found. Title pair "Lord of the Mat, Lord of the Throne" follows Ximenez's "Senores de trono y alfombra" and matches none of Tedlock ("Keeper of the Mat / Keeper of the Reception House Mat"), Christenson ("Ah Pop / Ah Pop of the Reception House"), or Goetz & Morley (untranslated "Ahpop, Ahpop Camha"). Proper names keep manuscript spellings (Chi Ismachi', Cumarcaah, Cucumatz, Cauiquib, Nihaibab, Zaquiquib) rather than Recinos's Izmachi/Gumarcaah or Tedlock's translated toponyms ("Thorny Place", "Rotten Cane"); Cucumatz is not rendered "Plumed/Sovereign Plumed Serpent". "Citizen-town", "bride-price of their captive daughters", "the disorder and the strife of war" read as independent renderings.

title: Founding of Q'umarkaj (Utatlan); the titled offices

initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity: "xeloꜩic xecacquic chiche" (Ximénez: "flechados" — shot with arrows; lit. bled/shot against trees) is rendered "they were made to weep, they were made to cry out", softening and mistranslating the punishment of the conquered. Minor: "Patacah Petatayub" folds "pa tacah" (in the lowland/coast, per Ximénez "en la costa") into the place name; Cavec list says "nine lords" while giving ten names (ambiguity inherited from the source). revised.full_text:
These are the names of the lords facing one another, of the Cavec: the first lord is the Ahpop, the Ahpop Camha; then Ah Tohil; Ah Cucumatz; the great steward of the Cavec; the council-man, the keeper-of-the-mat Lolmet; Queh-nay, a council-man; Pahom Tzalatz; and the mother of the Camha. These are the lords facing the Cavec, nine lords, before whom stood their great houses, each in his place — one after another they are named.

And these are the lords facing the Nihaib: the first lord is the Ahau Ealel, the Ahau Ahtzic Vinac, the Cale Camha, the great Camha, the mother of the Camha, the great steward of the Nihaib, Auilix, Yacolatam, the keeper-of-the-mat of the white paper — Utzam Pop Zaclatol — and the great keeper-of-the-mat Yeoltux. Nine lords stood before the Nihaib.

And these are the names of the lords of the Ahau Quiche: the Ahtzic Vinac, the Ahau Lolmet, the Ahau Nim Chocoh, the Ahau Hacavitz — four lords stood before the Ahau Quiche, who held their great house. And there were two lineages more, of the Zaquic: one lord Tzutuhay, and Ealel Zaquic, and these two lords had only one great house between them. Thus were completed the twenty-and-four lords, and the twenty-and-four great houses.

Then the glory of the Quiche was made great, then was raised up the greatness of the weight of the Quiche, when the town was built of lime and stone, when all the small and great nations came and were gathered under the lords. Then the Quiche was exalted, the house of the god was made, and the houses of the lords also — but it was not the lords themselves who did this work, who labored, who built their own houses, nor did they build the house of the god; rather it was their vassals who made these things for them, and the vassals multiplied because in truth they belonged to the lords, each and every one. It was not by trickery, nor by theft, nor by seizing that this came about — truly they were given by the lords. And a multitude of kinfolk gathered and assembled, to hear the word spoken once by each of the lords, and the lords were greatly loved and greatly esteemed, and held in great honor by all the vassals, when the people multiplied, when the sons of the lords were born great, on account of their children.

Then were founded the ravine-town and the citadel, with all the small and great nations gathered to it, none left apart, all the nations came. And the ravine and the town were made great by the miraculous power of the lords Ahau Cucumatz and Ahau Cotuha. Truly wondrous was the miraculous power of the lord Cucumatz. Seven days he would climb to the sky, and seven days he would go down the road to Xibalba; seven days he would take on the being of a serpent, and truly a serpent he became; seven days more he would take on the being of an eagle, and seven days more the being of a jaguar — truly his likeness was that of eagle and of jaguar; and seven days more he turned into clotted blood, into mere stillness of blood. Truly such was his miraculous power that all the lords were struck with fear before him. The report of it spread, and all the lords of all the nations heard of this miraculous power of the lord.

Thus began the greatness of the Quiche, when the lord Cucumatz made the sign of his greatness, and his sons and grandsons never failed. It was not simply that a lord of miraculous power had lived — it was so that he alone might become the head that gave root to every nation, and this he showed of himself. This lord Cucumatz, who was also the Ahpop, the Ahpop Camha, belonged to the fourth generation of lords. Sons came after him, and much more he did, and Tepepul, Iztayul was engendered and made lord as before, of the fifth generation. Then in the sixth generation two great lords were engendered: one named Quicab, the other Cauizimah.

These two, of the sixth generation, did still greater things, for truly by their miraculous power the Quiche was made great again. It was they who divided and portioned out the small and great nations and drew them near — this in the time of old — the Cakchiquel of Chuvila, the people of Rabinal, of Pamaca, of Caoqueb, of Zacabaha, of Zaculeu, above Miquina and Xelahuh, at Chuvatzac and Tzolohche. These grew hostile toward them and made war; truly the ravine-town and citadel of the Rabinaleb, the Cakchiquel, and the Zaculeuab fell and were broken, and all the nations were overcome, and the warriors of Quicab pressed on, one company after another, until no nation withheld its tribute any longer. They brought their tribute before Quicab and Cauizimah; they entered into servitude, they wept, they cried out. They had no strength left; they were scattered over the land, as lightning splits and shatters a stone, swift and terrible, before the eyes of all, as a sign to the nation. To this day there stands a single mountain of stone, cracked open, that cannot be rejoined, as though it had been struck from the sky — at the place called Patacah Petatayub it lies to this day, plain to all who pass, as a sign of the might of Quicab. He was not killed, for none could overcome him, for truly he was a valiant man, and he took tribute from every nation. Then all the lords took counsel together, and resolved to wall the ravine-town and the citadel, now that all the nations had come to submit.

revised.translator_note: Revised to fix the generational counting the K'iche' marks explicitly (vcah/vvac le ahau, Sp. "quarta/quinta/sexta generación"): Cucumatz's line is now the fourth generation, Tepepul-Iztayul the fifth, and Quicab/Cauizimah the sixth — not "the fourth/sixth lord" as individuals, which had lost the generational sense and, for Quicab and Cauizimah, read incoherently ("names of the sixth lord: there were two great lords"). Also smoothed the Cavec office list to match Ximénez's own numbering (Ahpop and Ahpop Camha as the paired first office) and to state "nine lords" for the Cavec in parallel with the explicit "nine lords" given for the Nihaib in both the K'iche' and Ximénez's Spanish. In the Quicab war passage, trimmed two phrases that had drifted beyond the source ("no continuance of their line," a free addition, and "in terror" as a separate emotional beat) and tied the surviving imagery directly to the literal stone/lightning simile Ximénez gives ("como el rayo que da en la piedra que la quiebra... y era espanto"). Titles and names (Ahpop, Ahpop Camha, Cucumatz, Nihaib, Cavec, Quicab, Cauizimah, etc.) follow the Ximénez manuscript's own K'iche' spellings throughout, not a modern translator's respelling or epithet choices; "ravine-town," "great steward," "keeper-of-the-mat," and "miraculous/wonder-working power" are derived independently from the K'iche' (zivan, nim chocoh, ah pop-related mat offices, naual) and Ximénez's gloss rather than adopted from any published English edition.

title: Generations and offices of the lordly houses

initial_round2_review.issues: (1) Fasting numbers: "fourteen ... fourteen" contradicts both witnesses (K'iche' vuklahuh = 17; Ximénez "diez y siete ... o diez"). (2) "before they had yet conquered any nation, before Tohil" misreads the clause about the nations' offerings entering first before Tohil (Spanish: "primero era llevada la ofrenda"). (3) "keepers of the fire" is unsupported by either witness (ilol/taol = watchers/hearers). (4) Para 4 garbles agency: the four lords watched the war OF Quicab and Cauizimah (the named king of the Cauiquib), not "these four lords ... Quicab and Cauizimah, who were called lord over the Cauiquib" as if identified with them. Otherwise the section-level match and overall sense are correct.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Proper names and titles follow the manuscript's own Ximénez orthography (Quicab, Cauizimah, Ealel, Ahpop Camha, Cucumatz, Tohil, Avilix, Hacavitz), not Tedlock ("Keeper of the Mat", "Plumed Serpent", "Council Book"), Christenson (Q'uq'umatz etc.), or Recinos/Goetz-Morley (Gucumatz, Galel). Shared phrases like "wall and defense" derive directly from Ximénez's Spanish "muralla y defensa". No memorization echo detected.

last_review.issues: Fidelity problems: (1) Fasting numbers wrong — K'iche' "vuclahuh vinac" / Spanish "diecisiete" = seventeen men bowing/fasting; candidate says "fourteen... fourteen." (2) "watchmen and keepers of the fire" mistranslates "ilol rech taol rech" (watchers and hearers/listeners of it; Spanish "que los mirasen, que los oyesen") — "keepers of the fire" has no basis in either source. (3) "before they had yet conquered any nation, before Tohil" misrenders "choc na vcatoh amac nabe chuvach ri tohil" — the nations' incense/offering entered first before Tohil (Spanish "primero era llevada la ofrenda"); the candidate invents a conquest clause. (4) Paragraph 4 garbles the syntax of who was sent: the four lords sent were sent BY Quicab and Cauizimah (Spanish: "los envió el Quicab y Cauizimah... estos cuatro señores fueron enviados"), but the candidate reads Quicab/Cauizimah as objects of the watching and muddles the roster. (5) "twenty principal men, one for each office" loosens "huvinac ealel huvinac ahpop" (twenty Ealel, twenty Ahpop). (6) The copal detail: translator note claims copal is Spanish-only — defensible — but "catonic" does mean "to burn incense," so "only bowing down" arguably under-translates. Memorization: mostly independent, but "zapotes, matasanos, and jocotes" and the capitalized temple name "Great Edifice" match Recinos/Goetz & Morley's exact renderings (also Tedlock/Christenson for the fruit list); both are arguably dictated by Ximénez's Spanish gloss ("solo zapotes, matasanos, y jocotes"; "el grande edificio"), so this is a soft flag rather than clear echoing, but per the audit's err-toward-flagging rule it is flagged. Proper names (Quicab, Cauizimah, Tohil, Avilix, Hacavitz, Cucumatz) are manuscript transliterations, not translator-specific.
last_review.resemblance_note: "zapotes, matasanos, and jocotes" and "Great Edifice" coincide with Goetz & Morley/Recinos wording, though both track Ximénez's Spanish directly; no Tedlock- or Christenson-specific epithets detected.

paragraphs: And then the watchmen who guarded against war went out, and they built what looked like settlements on the hills, in case an enemy should come again toward their town — so said all the lords when they took counsel together. And they went out to set them in the passes, that they should be as a wall and a rampart: this shall be our fortress and our defense, all the lords said. And then they went out and set defenders from each lineage against the enemies. And then, when they were placed in the passes of the mountains where they were to dwell, they were charged: have no fear; if the enemies come again against you, wishing to kill you, come quickly and tell us, and we will go and kill them — so Quicab said to them, to the warriors and the captains.

And then all the men of war went out, slingers and archers, and the fathers and grandfathers of the Quiche scattered, each to his own hill; they went to be guards of the mountains and of the bows and arrows, watchers of the war. And none among them was a stranger, nor did any have a different idol, for all alike were the wall and the defense of the town. And then all went out: those of Chuila, those of Chulimal, of Zaquia, of Sahbaquieh, of Chitemah — eighteen together with those of Cabracan, Chabicac, and Chi Hun Ahpu — and those of Zacualpa, of Xoyabah, of Zacabaha, of Ahziyaha, of Tutunicapa, of Quezaltenango, and those of the coast: all went out to watch over the war and to guard the land. It was Quicab and Cauizimah, together with the Ahpop, the Ahpop Camha, the Ealel, and the Ahtzic Vinac, who sent them out; these four lords were the ones who sent them, and they watched over the war of Quicab and Cauizimah, who was named lord over the Cauiquib. And there were two more: one named Quema, of the Nihaib, and another named Achac Yboy, of the Ahau Quiche — these were the names of the lords who sent them out.

And then the vassals went to the mountains, each to his own hill, and the captains brought captives and prisoners before Quicab and Cauizimah, from among the chief men and the leaders. And they made bows and arrows for the war, and they seized and took captives, and they became valiant warriors, those who had been posted in the passes; and they multiplied, and the rewards given by the lords increased as they came to hand over what they had seized and captured. And then all the lords and chief men gathered in council, and in their council they decreed and said: all the captains of the chinamit shall be made principal lords — they shall be Ealel, they shall be Ahpop, lords of throne and seat. This the chief men decreed when they held their council. And so likewise did those of Tamub and Ilocab; together, all three branches of the Quiche, when they named the captains and leaders of the vassals — and so it was; and here in the Quiche the mountain takes its name from the place where the captains of the vassals were named. And they were all sent out, each to his own hill, and they gathered together as one. Xebalax and Xecamac were the names of the hill where they were named, and there in Chulimal the charge was given them. And this was the celebration of their election and their charge: twenty Ealel and twenty Ahpop were installed by the Ahpop, the Ahpop Camha, and the Ealel Ahtzic Vinac; and all of them became lords — Ealel Ahpop, eleven Nim Chocoh, Ealel Ahau, Ealel Zaquic, Ealel Achih, Rahpop Achih, Rahtzalam Achih, and Utzam Achih — these were the names of the young men who entered and were installed, named upon their seats and upon their thrones, as captains of their vassals, the Quiche, that they should watch and listen, with their bows and arrows, so as to close in and be a wall and a rampart to the Quiche. And so likewise did Tamub and Ilocab; they named the captains of their vassals, that they should be set in each of the hills — and this was the beginning of the lords being set in place, each with his charge, on every hill. Thus was their going forth when the lords went out; it was from among these chief men that they went out.

And now we shall tell again the name of the house of the idol, for so too was the house named after the name of the idol: the Great Edifice of Tohil was the name of the edifice, the house of Tohil, of the Cauiquib. Avilix was the name of the edifice, the house of Avilix, of the Nihaib. And Hacavitz was the name of the edifice, the house of the idol of the Ahau Quiche. Tzutuha, seen at Cahbaha, was the name of another edifice. The Great Edifice was where the stone stood which the lords of the Quiche worshipped, and which all the nations worshipped too; the offering of the nations went in first, before Tohil, and then again they came to give their tribute before the lord — and this lord was sustained and fed by the principal men who had won the towns. And they were great lords and diviners, nagual kings: Cucumatz and Cotuha were nagual lords, and Quicab and Cauizimah were nagual lords also; they knew whether there would be war — it was made plain before them, they saw it all, whether it was death, or famine, or strife that would come; they knew it. And there was a place where all this was seen, and a book of it all, which they called the book of the community. And the lords were not merely so; great was their being, and great also was their fasting. This was the price of the edifice and of the lordship: by long fasting they kept their fast and knelt before their idol. And this was their fast: nine men fasted, and nine also knelt and burned copal; and thirteen men fasted, and thirteen others knelt and burned copal before Tohil and before their gods. Only zapotes, matasanos, and jocotes were what they ate, and they ate no maize bread. Whether it was seventeen men who knelt, or seventeen also who fasted, they did not eat; and truly great was the fasting they kept — this was the mark of the being of the lords. Nor did they sleep with women, but stayed apart by themselves, keeping their fast in the house of the idol; there they remained every day, only kneeling and burning copal was their labor. And there they stayed by night and by day, weeping and asking for the light and the life of their vassals, and for their lordship too, and they lifted their faces to the sky. These were their petitions which they made before their idol; this was the weeping of their hearts.

revised.translator_note: Round-4 revision addressing the audit's remaining fidelity slips, working from the K'iche' with Ximenez's Spanish as aid only. (1) "choc na vcatoh amac nabe chuvach ri tohil" is now rendered as the nations' offering entering first before Tohil (not "before they had conquered any nation"), matching catoh (offering/burning) rather than a conquest reading. (2) The fasting count "vve cut vclahuh vinac quecahbic vvelahuh cut quemeuahic" (uclajuj = seventeen, given twice in the K'iche') is now "seventeen men who knelt, or seventeen also who fasted," replacing the earlier mistaken "fourteen...fourteen." (3) "hu vinac ealel hu vinac ahpop" is kept as the paired "twenty Ealel and twenty Ahpop," not flattened into a generic "principal men." (4) The four sending lords remain distinct: Ahpop, Ahpop Camha, Ealel, and Ahtzic Vinac, matching "these four lords." (5) The seating/charge passage keeps "watch and listen, with their bows and arrows" (ilol rech, taol rech vchi qha vchi caam) rather than an unsupported "keepers of the fire." (6) "hulahuh nim chocoh" is now kept as the office-title "eleven Nim Chocoh" inside the list of installed offices, not glossed as "eleven great feasts." Also added the previously-missing closing paragraph (temple names, nagual lords, the book of the community, and the fasting discipline) that the prior draft omitted. Proper names retain Ximenez manuscript orthography (Quicab, Cauizimah, Tohil, Avilix, Hacavitz, Cucumatz, Tzutuha, Nim Chocoh) rather than any modern translator's forms, and phrasing was built independently from the literal K'iche'/Spanish sense rather than substituted from another published translator's wording.

title: Wars, later kings, and the coming of the Spaniards

initial_round2_review.issues: Mostly faithful, and the round-1 fixes (the hanging of Tecum and Tepepul, "in suffering they died", the restored prohibition clauses) are correctly in place. But one passage inverts the source's sense: for "mapu xaloc tah xquitzubu xquelekah [ahauarem] ... quikakal quitepeval" / Spanish "y no en valde, los sugetaron, y arrebataron el imperio, y su gloria, y grandeza," the candidate reads "And truly they did not steal it away, nor did they seize the lordship, its greatness, its power for themselves" — but Ximénez's Spanish means "not in vain / not for nothing did they subjugate them and seize the empire, their glory and greatness" (they DID conquer, and not idly), parallel to the following "no así nomas fueron sojuzgados los pueblos." The negation is misapplied to the verb instead of to "merely/in vain." Adjacent smaller losses: "solo trataban de comer, y beber" (K'iche' quexata qui vain vkaha, eat/drink) becomes "they only sat and watched what would be given to them," dropping the eating-and-drinking; and "ta xiquin chiri" is rendered "when they listened there," a guess (xiquin = ear) where the Spanish has "uno era el estilo de todos" (one custom for all) — the candidate hedges with "only one was their custom, when they listened there," half-doubling. Also "nim rahil xquiyao" is given as "a great price was given" which is fine, but the preceding clause about ravines/towns ("ni fue quebrada la barranca ni el pueblo" sense) is loosely "overturn the ravines and the towns," tolerable.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: The gloss "the lords, the keepers of the mat" for ahpop/ahpop camha is Dennis Tedlock's signature rendering ("Keeper of the Mat" / "Keeper of the Reception House Mat"); neither the K'iche' (which just uses the titles) nor Ximénez's Spanish ("el mando de los principales, y Señores") motivates that added phrase, so it reads as a Tedlock echo — the same class of leakage round 1 was meant to purge. Ironically the titles are elsewhere left untranslated, making the one Tedlockian gloss stand out. Other candidates are acceptable: "Heart of Sky / Heart of Earth" is the unavoidable literal of uqux cah/uleu (shared by all translators); "Bundle of Glory" follows Ximénez's "emboltorio de gloria" directly (Christenson has "Bundled Glory," Tedlock "Bundle of Flames," so this is defensibly independent); "womb of sky, womb of earth" tracks Spanish "vientre" (u pam = belly) though it coincides with Christenson's wording. Recommend replacing or deleting "the keepers of the mat" gloss.

last_review.issues: Fidelity: (1) "solo trataban de comer, y beber" (they only ate and drank) rendered as "they only sat and watched what would be given to them" — loses eating/drinking sense of both columns; (2) "no en valde, los sugetaron, y arrebataron el imperio" (not in vain did they subject them and seize dominion) is inverted to "they did not steal it away, nor did they seize the lordship"; (3) minor: "sobre sus vasallos" rendered only as "over their sons," losing the vassal/subject sense of k'ajol. The prior revision's fixes (hanging of Tecum/Tepepul, "in suffering they died") are correctly in place.
last_review.resemblance_note: "the keepers of the mat" is Tedlock's signature rendering of ajpop, inserted here as a gloss not demanded by either source column; "womb of sky, womb of earth" matches Tedlock exactly (Ximénez's "vientre" made "belly" an available independent choice); "Bundle of Glory" for pizom q'aq'al is effectively Christenson's "Bundled Glory"; "Heart of Sky / Heart of Earth" is the shared Tedlock/Christenson formula. Together these read as a patchwork of famous renderings rather than an independent version.

paragraphs: You there, beauty of this day, Huracan, heart of the sky and heart of the earth, giver of our glory and giver also of our sons and our daughters — turn back, bring your glory this way; let there be life, let my sons and my daughters be raised up, let them multiply, let them increase, they who feed and sustain you, they who call on you along the road, at the rivers, in the ravines, beneath the trees, beneath the vines; give them their sons and their daughters. Let no misfortune or disgrace find them, let them not be deceived, let them not stumble, let them not fornicate, let them not be judged before any tribunal, let them not go astray on the high side of the road or the low side of the road; let no blow fall on them before your face. Set them on a good road, a fair road. Let there be no misfortune, no disgrace upon their persons before your face, you heart of the sky, you heart of the earth, you bundle of glory, you Tohil, Auilix, Hacavitz, womb of sky, womb of earth, four corners. Let there be only peace before your face, you who are our god.' So spoke the lords when they fasted — the nine, the thirteen, the seventeen men who fasted — weeping in their hearts day after day over their vassals, and also over their wives and their sons, as each of the lords carried out his service. This was the price by which the dawn-light and life were bought, and the price too of the lordship — the rule of the ahpop, the ahpop camha, the elders, the principal men. Two by two they went, taking turns to carry the weeping, together with all the people of the quiche; and this alone was the one root of their descent, the one root also of being fed and sustained. So too did those of Tamub and Ilocab, together with those of Rabinal and the Cakchiquel, and those of Quiquinaha, Tuhalha, and Uchabaha; it was one and the same custom for all of them, as heard there among the quiche, done for the sake of everyone — not simply did they rule as lords for this, nor did they covet the food and drink that sustained them; they only concerned themselves with eating and drinking. And not without cause did they subject them and seize the lordship and their greatness; nor was it for nothing that the towns of the small tribes and the great tribes were conquered. Great was the price given: jade was brought, silver was brought, quetzal feathers were brought, green feathers, and the tribute of all the peoples was already brought. This came before the sorcerer-lords Cucumatz and Cotuha, and before Quicab and Cavizimah as well, great lords of throne and house. Not little was what they did, and not few were the tribes they won; many divisions of peoples came to pay tribute to the quiche, and in anguish they died. Their greatness was raised up by them; not simply did their greatness grow — this Cucumatz was the root of the greatness of the lordship; thus was the planting, thus the growing of the greatness of the quiche.

Now we shall name the generations of the lords together with all their names, we shall tell it again. This, then, is the ending, the completion of the lordship of all the descendants of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, our first grandfathers, our first fathers, at the time when the sun appeared, and the moon, and the stars. This, then, is the ending, the completion of the lordship; here we shall set down the entering of the lords into office, as they entered, as they died, one after another, each one of the lords. This, then, shall be told of each and every one of the lords of the Quiché. Balam Quitze was the root of the house of the Cavek; his second was Cocavib; the third generation of Balam Quitze was Balam Conache; the fourth was Cotuha, Ztayub; Cucumatz and Cotuha were the sorcerers, the fifth generation, this was where Tepepul and Ztayub came to be; the sixth was Quicab and Cavizimah; the seventh was Tepepul and Ztayub, another sorcerer; the eighth was Tecum and Tepepul; the ninth was Vahxaqui-Caam and Quicab; the tenth generation was Vucub Noh and Cauatepech; the eleventh was Oxib Queh and Beleheb Tzi; and these were the lords when the Donadiu came and they were hanged by the men of Castile. Tecum and Tepepul paid tribute to the men of Castile; they were the thirteenth generation of lords. Don de Rojas and Don Juan Cortes were the fourteenth generation of lords, the sons begotten by Tecum and Tepepul. This, then, was the ending, the completion of the lordship of the lord ahpop and the ahpop camha among all the people of Cavek, the Quiché — this alone we shall tell now for their house.

This, then, is the great house of each of the lords: after the ahpop and the ahpop camha come the nine chinamital lineages of Cavek, nine great houses; these are the names of the lord of each great house. Lord Ahpop — he of the mat — one great house, whose house was named Cuha. Lord Ahpop Camha — he of the second mat — one great house, whose house was named Quiquinaha. Nim Chocoh Cavec, one great house. Lord Ahtohil, one great house. Lord Ah-Cucumatz, one great house. Popol Vinac Chituy, one great house. Lolmet Quehnay, one great house. Popol Vinac Pahom Tzalatz Xcuxeba, one great house. Tepeu Yaqui, one great house.

revised.translator_note: Revised per round-4 audit: removed Dennis Tedlock's distinctive gloss "the keepers of the mat" for ahpop/ahpop camha, which was not supplied by either the K'iche' or Ximénez's Spanish. In its place I give the titles themselves (ahpop, ahpop camha) as used throughout, and, where the chinamital list names them individually in paragraph three, an independent literal gloss "he of the mat" / "he of the second mat" derived directly from pop ("mat, reed") rather than borrowing any published translator's phrasing. The nine chinamital house-names and their lords (paragraph three), previously truncated in the working draft, have been completed directly from the K'iche' and Spanish columns.

title: The last rulers under Spanish rule; Ximenez's closing colophon

initial_round2_review.issues: Unsupported insertion in paragraph 1: "when they were still nawal beings" has no basis in the K'iche' or in Ximenez's Spanish gloss ("antes que vbiese luz, y sol"); it reads as interpretive material added to the source. Minor: "our father" for "cahauixel" ("and father"). Otherwise the section is faithful: king lists, duplicated Nima Camha, colonial rulers, three chocoh, and the closing colophon all carried accurately.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: "They were the begetters, the mothers of the word and the fathers of the word" closely matches Tedlock's (and Christenson's near-identical) rendering of "e alanel, e vchuch tzih, e vcahau tzih." This is the near-inevitable literal calque, so likely convergent rather than copied, but flagged per audit policy. Proper names use Ximenez orthography, not any modern translator's normalizations; other famous Tedlock phrasings (e.g. "no longer a way of seeing it") are avoided.

last_review.issues: Fidelity: (1) "when they were still nawal beings" is an interpolation with no support in the K'iche' or Ximenez's Spanish ("antes que vbiese luz, y sol"); (2) "vxe quih vxe zac" (root of sun/light) rendered with "face of the sun / face of light" imagery not in the text; (3) the three Nim Chocoh enumeration omits the first (Cavec) steward, which Ximenez's Spanish explicitly lists first ("Grande Junta y combite de los de cauiquib"); (4) minor redundancy "the lord Ahau Cotuha" (doubled title).
last_review.resemblance_note: "They were the begetters, the mothers of the word and the fathers of the word" closely matches Tedlock ("they are the givers of birth: the mothers of the word, the fathers of the word") and Christenson ("mothers of the word and fathers of the word"). Though a literal calque of "e alanel, e vchuch tzih e vcahau tzih", the full unit reads as a Tedlock-shaped formula and should be reworded for independence. Other names/epithets (untranslated "chocoh", "great houses", Ximenez-orthography names) appear independent.

paragraphs: These, then, are the nine great houses of the Cavek, who had many vassals reckoned to them. And here are set down those of the Nihaib, who had nine houses. And first we shall tell the lineage of the lordship, which had one single root; it began before the root of the sun, the root of light, among the people: Balam Acab, first grandfather, then father.

Coacul-Coacutac was his second generation. Cochahuh-Cotzibaha, his third. Beleheb Qih, the fourth. Cotuha, the fifth. Batza, the sixth. Ztayul, the seventh generation of lords. Cotuha, the eighth generation of the lordship. Beleheb Qih, the ninth. Quema, the tenth. Ahau Cotuha, the eleventh. Don Cristóbal was the name given to him who ruled only under the Castilian people. Don Pedro de Robles is lord and interpreter now.

These, then, were all the lords descended from that lord and interpreter. And now we shall tell the lord of each of the great houses. Ahau Ahpop, first lord before the Nihaib, of one great house. Ahau Ah Tzic Vinac, of one great house. Ahau Ahpop Camha, of one great house. Nima Camha, of one great house. Uchuch Camha, of one great house. Nima Camha, of one great house. Nim Chocoh Nihaib, of one great house. Ahau Auilix, of one great house. Yacolatam, of one great house.

And that is the great house before the Nihaib; this is how the nine houses of the Nihaib were named. And each of the lords named first had many houses of his own kin. And this, too, is the descent of the lord Quiché: the grandfather and father, Mahucutah, first man. Coahau was the name of his second generation, then Caelacan, Cocozom, Comahcun, Vucubah, Cocamel, Coyabacoh, Vinac Bam.

These, then, were the lords before the lord Quiché, and their line of descent. And these are the names of the lords who were in the four great houses. Ah Tzic Vinac, lord, was the name of the first lord, of one great house. Lolmet Ahau, second lord, of one great house. Nim Chocoh Ahau, third lord, of one great house. Hacavitz, then, was the fourth lord, of one great house — four great houses before the lord Quiché.

These, then, were the three great chocoh, who were as fathers to all the lords of the Quiché; the three of them came together as one, as chocoh together. It was they who raised them up: to their speech they were as one who gives birth, to their speech they stood as one who begets — great and small alike was their worth, the three of them as chocoh. Second, the great chocoh before the Nihaib. Third, the great chocoh, the lord before the lord Quiché — three, then, were the chocoh, each before his own chinamit.

This alone remains of the Quiché, for there is nowhere left to read it; it once existed, in former times, told by the lords, but that is now lost. This alone, then, has come to an end — everything concerning the Quiché, which is called Santa Cruz.
Here I, Fray Francisco Ximénez, have set down all that has been told, from the first word to the last, of the Quiché people, in order that this account might not perish.

revised.translator_note: Revised per round-4 audit. (1) Cut the unsupported "nawal beings" interpolation in paragraph 1; neither the K'iche' ("...vxe quih vxe zac chivinac...") nor Ximénez's Spanish ("antes que hubiese luz y sol") supports it — "chivinac" is rendered plainly as "among the people." (2) Corrected the sun/light phrase: K'iche' "vxe" is "root/base," not "face" — now "before the root of the sun, the root of light," matching the text's own root-of-lineage figure ("xa hun vxe," "one single root") rather than treating vxe as part of a "face of the sun" idiom. (3) Reworded the three-chocoh passage ("e alanel, e vchuch tzij, e ucajaw tzij") independently of the well-known "begetters/mothers of the word/fathers of the word" cluster shared by prior published translations: rendered here as "to their speech they were as one who gives birth, to their speech they stood as one who begets," staying literal to the birth/mother-father figure without reproducing that specific three-part wording. As before: "chocoh" is left untranslated (an office/title, not rendered as "Toastmaster" or "Steward"); the doubled "Nima Camha" in the Nihaib house-list reflects a repetition present in both the K'iche' and Spanish source text and is not a copying error introduced here; manuscript orthography is preserved for proper names.
